Then we introduce the $\mathcal { M } _ { d _ { 1 } , d _ { 3 } }$ –valued process (recall (4.1)): 

$$
U _ {t} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \delta_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \left(f (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) - \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (f)\right).\tag{4.2}
$$

In a similar way, for $g$ and h like in (2.1), we set 

$$
U _ {t} ^ {\prime n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \left(g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) - \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h)\right).\tag{4.3}
$$

Our aim in this section is then to prove the following two CLT’s: 

Proposition 4.1 Under (SH), if f is at most of polynomial growth, the sequence of processes $U ^ { n }$ in $( 4 . 2 )$ is C-tight. If further f is even, then it converges stably in law to the process U defined componentwise $b y$ 

$$
U _ {t} ^ {j k} = \sum_ {j ^ {\prime} = 1} ^ {d _ {1}} \sum_ {k ^ {\prime} = 1} ^ {d _ {3}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \delta_ {u} ^ {\prime j k, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}} d W _ {u} ^ {\prime j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}},\tag{4.4}
$$

where 

$$
\sum_ {l = 1} ^ {d _ {1}} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {d _ {3}} \delta_ {u} ^ {\prime j k, l m} \delta_ {u} ^ {\prime j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}, l m} = \sum_ {l, l ^ {\prime} = 1} ^ {d _ {2}} \Big (\rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (f ^ {l k} f ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) - \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (f ^ {l k}) \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (f ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) \Big) \delta_ {u} ^ {j l} \delta_ {u} ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}},\tag{4.5}
$$

and $W ^ { \prime }$ is a d d –dimensional Wiener process defined on an extension of $( \varOmega , \mathcal F , ( \mathcal F _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 } , \mathsf P )$ and which is independent of the σ–field ${ \mathcal F } .$ 

Proposition 4.2 Under (SH) and if g and h are continuous with at most polynomial growth, the sequence of processes $U ^ { \prime n }$ is C-tight. If further g and h are even, then it converges stably in law to the process $U ( g , h )$ described in (2.13). 

Before proceeding to the proofs, let us mention the following estimates, which are obvious under (SH): 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\| \beta_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq C _ {q}.\tag{4.6}
$$

Next, saying that $f$ is of at most polynomial growth means that for some constants $C > 0$ and $p$ (we can always choose $p \geq 2 )$ , 

$$
x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \quad \Rightarrow \quad | f (x) | \leq C (1 + \| x \| ^ {p}).\tag{4.7}
$$

Observe also that Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 imply respectively 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \delta_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} f (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \xrightarrow {\mathsf {P}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \delta_ {u} \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (f) d u,\tag{4.8}
$$

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \xrightarrow {\mathsf {P}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (g) \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (h) d u.\tag{4.9}
$$

Proof of Proposition 4.1. We have $\begin{array} { r c l } { U _ { t } ^ { n } } & { = } & { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } } \end{array}$ , where $\zeta _ { i } ^ { n } =$ $\delta _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } \big ( f ( \beta _ { i } ^ { n } ) - \rho _ { i - 1 } ^ { n } ( f ) \big ) / \sqrt { n }$ . Recalling (4.6) and (4.7), we trivially have 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = 0, \qquad \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {4} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \leq \frac {C}{n ^ {2}},\tag{4.10}
$$

$$
\mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j k} \zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = \frac {1}{n} \Delta_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {j k, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}},
$$

where $\varDelta _ { u } ^ { j k , j ^ { \prime } k ^ { \prime } }$ is the right side of (4.5). Moreover since σ is c`adl`ag we deduce from (4.7) that $s \mapsto \rho _ { \sigma _ { s } } ( f )$ also is c`adl`ag. Thus by the Riemann integrability we get 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j k} \zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \to \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varDelta_ {u} ^ {j k, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}} d u.\tag{4.11}
$$

Then (4.10) and (4.11) are enough to imply the tightness of the sequence $( U ^ { n } )$ 

Now, assume further that $f$ is even. Since the variables $\varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } W$ and $- \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } W$ have the same law, conditionally on $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ , we get 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j k} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W ^ {l} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {d _ {2}} \delta_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {j m} \mathbf {E} (\varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W ^ {l} f (\sqrt {n} \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W) ^ {m k} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = 0.\tag{4.12}
$$

Next, let N be any bounded martingale on $( \varOmega , \mathcal F , ( \mathcal F _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 } , \mathsf P )$ , which is orthogonal to W. For $j$ and k fixed, we consider the martingale $M _ { t } = \mathbf { E } ( g ( \beta _ { i } ^ { n } ) ^ { j k } | \mathcal { F } _ { t } )$ ， for $\textstyle t \geq { \frac { i - 1 } { n } }$ . Since W is an $( \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) .$ –Brownian motion, and since $\beta _ { i } ^ { n }$ is a function of $\sigma _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ and of $\varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } W$ , we see that $( M _ { t } ) _ { t \geq ( i - 1 ) / n }$ is also, conditionally on $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ,$ , a martingale w.r.t. the filtration which is generated by the process $\dot { W _ { t } } - \dot { W } _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } }$ . By the martingale representation theorem the process M is thus of the form $M _ { t } = M _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } + \textstyle \int _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } ^ { t } \eta _ { s } d W _ { s }$ for an appropriate predictable process η. It follows that M is orthogonal to the process $\begin{array} { r } { N _ { t } ^ { \prime } = N _ { t } - N _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } \ ( \mathrm { f o r } \ t \geq \frac { i - 1 } { n } ) } \end{array}$ or in other words the product $M N ^ { \prime }$ is an $\left( \boldsymbol { \mathcal { F } } _ { t } \right) _ { t \geq \frac { i - 1 } { n } }$ –martingale. Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathbf {E} (\varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} N g (\sqrt {n} \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W) ^ {j k} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = \mathbf {E} (\varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} N ^ {\prime} M _ {i / n} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \\ = \mathbf {E} (\varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} N ^ {\prime} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} M | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = 0, \end{array}
$$

and thus 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} N | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) = 0.\tag{4.13}
$$

If we put together (4.10), (4.11), (4.12) and (4.13), we deduce the result from Theorem IX.7.28 of [9]. □ 

Proof of Proposition 4.2. A simple computation shows that $\begin{array} { r l } { U _ { t } ^ { \prime n } } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 2 } ^ { [ n t ] + 1 } \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } + \gamma _ { 1 } ^ { n } - \gamma _ { [ n t ] + 1 } ^ { n } } \end{array}$ , where 

$$
\zeta_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \left(g (\beta_ {i - 1} ^ {n}) (h (\beta_ {i - 1} ^ {\prime n}) - \rho_ {i - 2} ^ {n} (h)) + (g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) - \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g)) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h)\right),
$$

$$
\gamma_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \left(g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) - \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g)\right) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h).
$$

We trivially have (4.10), while (4.12) and (4.13) (for any bounded martingale N orthogonal to W) are proved exactly as in the previous proposition. We will write $\begin{array} { r } { \rho _ { i - 2 , i - 1 } ^ { n } ( g , h ) = \int g ( \sigma _ { \frac { i - 1 } { \infty } } x ) h ( \sigma _ { \frac { i - 2 } { \infty } } x ) \rho ( d x ) } \end{array}$ , where $\rho$ is the $\mathcal { N } ( 0 , I _ { d ^ { \prime } } )$ 7 law. An easy computation shows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j k} \zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \\ = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {l, l ^ {\prime} = 1} ^ {d _ {2}} \Big [ g (\beta_ {i - 1} ^ {n}) ^ {j l} g (\beta_ {i - 1} ^ {n}) ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}} \left(\rho_ {i - 2} ^ {n} (h ^ {l k} h ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) - \rho_ {i - 2} ^ {n} (h ^ {l k}) \rho_ {i - 2} ^ {n} (h ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}})\right) \\ \quad + g (\beta_ {i - 1} ^ {n}) ^ {j l} \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) \left(\rho_ {i - 2, i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}}, h ^ {l k}) - \rho_ {i - 2} ^ {n} (h ^ {l k}) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}})\right) \\ \quad + g (\beta_ {i - 1} ^ {n}) ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}} \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h ^ {l k}) \left(\rho_ {i - 2, i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j l}, h ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) - \rho_ {i - 2} ^ {n} (h ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j l})\right) \\ \quad + \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h ^ {l ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}}) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h ^ {l k}) \left(\rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j l} g ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}}) - \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j l}) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g ^ {j ^ {\prime} l ^ {\prime}})\right) \Big ]. \end{array}
$$

and thus by (4.8) and since the components of g and h satisfy (4.7) and are continuous and σ is c`adl`ag (hence in particular $\rho _ { i - 2 , i - 1 } ^ { n } ( g , h ) - \rho _ { i - 2 } ^ { n } ( g h )$ goes to 0, uniformly in $i \le [ n t ] + 1 )$ , we get with the notation (2.14): 

$$
\sum_ {i = 2} ^ {[ n t ] + 1} \mathbf {E} (\zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j k} \zeta_ {i} ^ {n, j ^ {\prime} k ^ {\prime}} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \to \int_ {0} ^ {t} A (\sigma_ {u}, g, h) ^ {j k, k ^ {\prime} j ^ {\prime}} d u.
$$

Then exactly as in the previous proof we deduce that the processes $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \zeta _ { i } ^ { n }$ are C–tight, and that they converge stably in law to the process $U ( g , h )$ of (2.13) when further $g$ and h are even. 

On the other hand $\gamma _ { i } ^ { n }$ is the transpose of the jump at time $i / n$ of the process $U ^ { n }$ of (4.2) when $\delta _ { u } = \rho _ { \sigma _ { u } } ( h ^ { * } )$ and $f = g ^ { * }$ , so Proposition 4.1 yields $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { i \leq [ n t ] } \| \gamma _ { i } ^ { n } \| \stackrel { \textsf { P } } { \longrightarrow } 0$ for any t: hence the results. □ 

## 5 A second simplified problem

So far $Y$ has played no role, but it will come in this section. Recalling (4.1), we set 

$$
\xi_ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n}, \qquad \xi_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}.\tag{5.1}
$$

Observe that 

$$
\xi_ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} a _ {u} d u + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} (\sigma_ {u -} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d W _ {u}\right),
$$

and a similar equality for $\xi _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ , with the integrals between $i / n$ and $( i + 1 ) / n$ Then under (SH) we have for any $q \in [ 2 , \infty )$ , by Burkholder Inequality: 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\| \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \xi_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \xi_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq C _ {q}.\tag{5.2}
$$

We can now consider the processes $U ^ { n } ( g , h )$ of (2.15): in view of (5.2), the conditional expectations in (2.15) are finite as soon as g and h have polynomial growth. 

Theorem 5.6. Under (SH) and $i f g$ and h are continuous with at most polynomial growth, the sequence of processes $U ^ { n } ( g , h )$ of (2.15) is C–tight. If further g and h are even, it converges stably in law to the processes $U ( g , h )$ of (2.13). 

We first prove three lemmas. The first one is very simple: 

Lemma 5.1. Let $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \right)$ be an array of random variables satisfying for all t: 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \stackrel {{\mathsf {P}}} {{\longrightarrow}} 0.\tag{5.3}
$$

If further each $\zeta _ { i } ^ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i + 1 ) / n }$ –measurable, the array $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } - \mathbf { E } ( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) \right)$ is AN. 

Proof. Of course the result is well known when $\zeta _ { i } ^ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { i / n }$ –measurable. Otherwise, we set $\eta _ { i } ^ { n } = \mathbf { E } ( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { i / n } )$ . This new array satisfies also (5.3) and now $\eta _ { i } ^ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { i / n }$ –measurable: so the array $\left( \eta _ { i } ^ { n } - \mathbf { E } ( \eta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) \right)$ is AN. 

Next, (5.3) and Lenglart’s inequality (see e.g. I-3.30 in [9]) yield $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \mathbf { E } ( \Vert \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \Vert ^ { 2 } \ | \ \mathcal { F } _ { i / n } ) \ \xrightarrow { \textsf { P } } 0 _ { ! } } \end{array}$ , so the afore mentioned well known result also yields that the array $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } - \eta _ { i } ^ { n } \right)$ is AN, and the result follows. □ 

Lemma 5.2. Under (SH) we have for all $t > 0 .$ 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} \left(\| \xi_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {2} + \| \beta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {2}\right)\rightarrow 0.\tag{5.4}
$$

Proof. First, the boundedness of a yields 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\| \xi_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {2}) \leq C \left(\frac {1}{n} + n \mathbf {E} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \| \sigma_ {u -} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| ^ {2} d u\right)\right).
$$

We also trivially have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} (\| \beta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {2}) \leq C \mathbf {E} (\| \sigma_ {\frac {i}{n}} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| ^ {2}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq C n \mathbf {E} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\| \sigma_ {u -} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| ^ {2} + \| \sigma_ {u -} - \sigma_ {\frac {i}{n}} \| ^ {2}\right) d u\right). \end{array}
$$

Hence the left side of (5.4) is smaller than 

$$
C \left(\frac {t}{n} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathbf {E} \left(\| \sigma_ {u -} - \sigma_ {[ n u ] / n} \| ^ {2} + \| \sigma_ {u -} - \sigma_ {([ n u ] + 1) / n} \| ^ {2}\right) d u\right).
$$

Since $\sigma$ is c`adl`ag, the expectation above goes to 0 for all u except the fixed times of discontinuity of the process $\sigma ,$ that is for almost all $u ,$ and it stays bounded by a constant because of (SH): hence the result by Lebesgue’s theorem. □ 

For further reference, the third lemma is stated in a more general setting: 

● $f$ and k are functions on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ satisfying (4.7); 

$\gamma _ { i } ^ { n } , \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n } , \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n }$ are $\mathbb { R } ^ { d _ { - } }$ –valued variables, 

(5.5) 

$Z _ { i } ^ { n } = 1 + \| \gamma _ { i } ^ { n } \| + \| \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n } \| + \| \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } \|$ satisfies $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { E } \big ( ( Z _ { i } ^ { n } ) ^ { p } \big ) \leq C _ { p } . } \end{array}$ 

Lemma 5.3. Under (5.5) and if further k is continuous and 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| ^ {2}) \to 0,\tag{5.6}
$$

then we have for all $t > 0 .$ 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} \Big (f (\gamma_ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {2} (k (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) - k (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n})) ^ {2} \Big) \to 0.\tag{5.7}
$$

Proof. Set $\theta _ { i } ^ { n } = ( f ( \gamma _ { i } ^ { n } ) ( k ( \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n } ) - k ( \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } ) ) ) ^ { 2 }$ and $m _ { A } ( \varepsilon ) = \operatorname* { s u p } ( | k ( x ) - k ( y ) | ~ ;$ $\| x - y \| \leq \varepsilon .$ , x A). For all $\varepsilon \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ and $A > 1$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \theta_ {i} ^ {n} \leq C \left(A ^ {2 p} m _ {A} (\varepsilon) ^ {2} + A ^ {4 p} 1 _ {\{\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| > \varepsilon \}} \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + (Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {4 p} (1 _ {\{\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {n} \| > A \}} + 1 _ {\{\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| > A \}} + 1 _ {\{\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| > A \}}) \Big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq C \left(A ^ {2 p} m _ {A} (\varepsilon) ^ {2} + \frac {A ^ {4 p} \| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| ^ {2}}{\varepsilon^ {2}} + \frac {(Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {4 p + 1}}{A}\right). \end{array}
$$

Then in view of (5.5) we get 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\theta_ {i} ^ {n}) \leq C \left(A ^ {2 p} m _ {A} (\varepsilon) ^ {2} + \frac {1}{A} + \frac {A ^ {4 p}}{n \varepsilon^ {2}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| ^ {2})\right).
$$

This holds for all $\varepsilon \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ and $A > 1$ . Since $m _ { A } ( \varepsilon ) \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } \varepsilon \to 0$ , for every A, (5.7) readily follows from (5.6). □ 

Proof of Theorem 5.6. In view of Proposition 4.2, it is clearly enough to prove that $U ^ { n } ( g , h ) - U ^ { \prime n } \xrightarrow { \mathrm { ~ P ~ } } 0$ . Set 

$$
\zeta_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \Big (g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) h (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \Big)\tag{5.8}
$$

and observe that $\begin{array} { r } { U ^ { n } ( g , h ) _ { t } - U _ { t } ^ { \prime n } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } - \mathbf { E } ( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) \right) } \end{array}$ and that $\zeta _ { i } ^ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i + 1 ) / n }$ -measurable. Then by Lemma 5.1 it sufices to prove that 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {2}) \to 0.\tag{5.9}
$$

For proving (5.9) it is clearly enough to consider the case where both $g$ and h are 1–dimensional. Recalling $\sqrt { n } ~ \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } Y = \beta _ { i } ^ { n } + \xi _ { i } ^ { n }$ , we then have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| \zeta_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq \frac {C}{n} \Big (h (\sqrt {n}   \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) ^ {2}   (g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n} + \xi_ {i} ^ {n}) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n})) ^ {2} \\ \qquad + g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {2}   (h (\beta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} + \xi_ {i + 1} ^ {n}) - h (\beta_ {i + 1} ^ {n})) ^ {2} + g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {2} (h (\beta_ {i + 1} ^ {n}) - h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n})) ^ {2} \Big). \end{array}
$$

Then (5.9) immediately follows from (4.6) and (5.2) and from Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3. □ 

## 6 The proof of Theorem 2.1

As stated in Section 2, we can and will assume (SH). We use the notation $\zeta _ { i } ^ { n }$ of (5.8), and set 

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {n} = \mathbf {E} \Big (g (\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) h (\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big), \quad \eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h)
$$

and $\begin{array} { r c l } { V _ { t } ^ { n } } & { = } & { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \eta _ { i } ^ { n } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r l r } { V _ { t } ^ { \prime n } } & { { } = } & { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } } \end{array}$ . Theorem 5.6 implies that ${ \frac { 1 } { n } } \big ( X ^ { n } ( g , h ) - V ^ { n } \big ) \ { \xrightarrow { \textsf { P } } } \ 0 ,$ , and Riemann integrability yields ${ \begin{array} { l } { { \frac { 1 } { n } } } \end{array} } V ^ { \prime n } \to X ( g , h )$ pointwise in $\omega$ and locally uniformly in time. So we need to prove that $\Sigma ^ { \left( { \large 1 } , { \large 1 } \right. \left( V ^ { n } - V ^ { \prime n } \right) } \ { \large \stackrel { \textsf { P } } { \longrightarrow } } \ 0$ . Since $\eta _ { i } ^ { n } - \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } = \sqrt { n } \ \mathbf { E } ( \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } )$ , it clearly suffices to prove that 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta_ {i} ^ {n} \|) \to 0.\tag{6.1}
$$

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the left side of (6.1) is smaller than $\begin{array} { r } { \left( t \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \mathbf { E } ( \| \zeta _ { i } ^ { n } \| ^ { 2 } ) \right) ^ { 1 / 2 } } \end{array}$ and thus (6.1) follows from (5.9). □ 

## 7 Technical preliminaries for Theorem 2.3

As said before, for proving Theorem 2.3 we can and will assume (SH), and also (SH’) when at least one of the components of $g$ or h satisfies (K’) instead of (K). In fact, this theorem is deduced from Theorem 5.6, provided we can show that $\sqrt { n } \left( X ^ { n } ( g , h ) _ { t } - U ^ { n } ( g , h ) _ { t } \right)$ goes to 0 in probability, locally uniformly in t. This amounts to proving that the array 

$$
\zeta_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \mathbf {E} \Big (g (\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) h (\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big) - \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (g) \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (h) d u
$$

is AN. Obviously, we can work componentwise, and so we will assume w.l.o.g. that both $g$ and h are 1–dimensional (they still are functions on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , though). We have $\zeta _ { i } ^ { n } = \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } + \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n }$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \zeta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \left(\mathbf {E} \Big (g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) h (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}\right) \\ - \mathbf {E} \Big (g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \mathbf {E} \Big (h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big) \Big), \end{array}\tag{7.1}
$$

$$
\zeta_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} = \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (g) \rho_ {\sigma_ {u}} (h) - \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (g) \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h)\right) d u.\tag{7.2}
$$

So we are left to prove that both arrays $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { { \prime } n } \right)$ and $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } \right)$ are AN. For the second one this is relatively simple, but for the first one it is quite complicated, and we need to split the diference in (7.1) into a large number of terms, which are treated in diferent ways: this section is devoted to estimates for these various terms. 

## 7.1 Some notation

First, we fix a sequence of numbers $\varepsilon _ { n } \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ (which will be chosen later in such a way that $\varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 } n \geq 1 )$ , and we set $E _ { n } = \{ x \in E : \psi ( x ) > \varepsilon _ { n } \}$ . Then, recalling the product–matrix notation, under (SH1) we can introduce a (long) series of $\mathbb { R } ^ { d _ { - } }$ –valued random variables: 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} (a _ {u} - a _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d u + \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} a _ {s} ^ {\prime} d s \right.\\\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} (\sigma_ {s -} ^ {\prime} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime}) d W _ {s} + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} (v _ {s -} - v _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d V _ {s}\left. \right) d W _ {u}\\\zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} a _ {s} ^ {\prime} d s + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\sigma_ {s -} ^ {\prime} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime}\right) d W _ {s} \right.\\\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \left. + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} (v _ {s -} - v _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d V _ {s}\right) \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} W,\\\zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \left(\frac {1}{n}   a _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} + \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} (W _ {u} - W _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d W _ {u} \right.\\\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \left. + v _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} (V _ {u -} - V _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d W _ {u}\right),\\\zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n}   \left(\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W + v _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} V\right) \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} W,\\\zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} w (s -, x) (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x)\right) d W _ {u},\end{array}
$$

$$
\zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} w (s -, x) (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x)\right) \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} W,
$$

$$
\zeta (4) _ {i} ^ {n} = - \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n}} \left(w (s -, x) - w \Big (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x \Big)\right) \nu (d s, d x)\right) d W _ {u},
$$

$$
\zeta (4) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = - \sqrt {n} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \int_ {E _ {n}} \left(w (s -, x) - w \left(\frac {i - 1}{n}, x\right)\right) \nu (d s, d x)\right) \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} W,
$$

$$
\zeta (5) _ {i} ^ {n} = - \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n}} w \Big (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x \Big) \nu (d s, d x)\right) d W _ {u},
$$

$$
\zeta (5) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = - \sqrt {n} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \int_ {E _ {n}} w \Big (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x \Big) \nu (d s, d x)\right) \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} W,
$$

$$
\zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n}} \left(w (s -, x) - w \left(\frac {i - 1}{n}, x\right)\right) \mu (d s, d x)\right) d W _ {u},
$$

$$
\zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \int_ {E _ {n}} \left(w (s -, x) - w \Big (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x \Big)\right) \mu (d s, d x)\right) \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} W,
$$

$$
\zeta (7) _ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n}} w \Big (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x \Big) \mu (d s, d x)\right) d W _ {u},

$$

We also set 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l l} \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} = \zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {n} + \zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {n} + \zeta (4) _ {i} ^ {n} + \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n}, & \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} = \zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {n} + \zeta (5) _ {i} ^ {n} + \zeta (7) _ {i} ^ {n} \\ \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} = \zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + \zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + \zeta (4) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {\prime n}, \\ \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} = \zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + \zeta (5) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + \zeta (7) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \\ \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \widehat {\xi} _ {i + 1} ^ {n} + \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}, & \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \widetilde {\xi} _ {i + 1} ^ {n} + \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}. \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.3}
$$

In view of (5.1), a tedious but simple computation shows that 

$$
\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n} = \xi_ {i} ^ {n} = \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} + \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n}, \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \xi_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n}.\tag{7.4}

Next, we put $\begin{array} { r } { \varphi ( \varepsilon ) = \int _ { \{ \| \psi ( x ) \| \leq \varepsilon \} } \psi ( x ) ^ { 2 } F ( d x ) } \end{array}$ , so that 

$$
\left.\begin{array}{l l}\varepsilon \downarrow 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \varphi (\varepsilon) \rightarrow 0\\\theta \in [ 0, 2 ] \quad \Rightarrow \quad \int_ {\{\psi (x) > \varepsilon \}} \psi (x) ^ {\theta} F (d x) \leq \frac {C}{\varepsilon^ {2 - \theta}},\\\theta \geq 2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \int_ {\{\psi (x) \leq \varepsilon \}} \psi (x) ^ {\theta} F (d x) \leq \varphi (\varepsilon) \varepsilon^ {\theta - 2}.\end{array}\right\}\tag{7.5}
$$

Finally, set 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q} = \frac {1}{n ^ {q / 2}}\\\quad + \mathbf {E} \left(\left(n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\| a _ {u} - a _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| ^ {2} + \| \sigma_ {u -} ^ {\prime} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime} \| ^ {2} + \| v _ {u -} - v _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| ^ {2} \right. \right. \right.\\\quad \left. + \int_ {E _ {n}} \left\| w (u -, x) - w \left(\frac {i - 1}{n}, x\right)\right\| ^ {2} F (d x)\right) d u\left. \right) ^ {q / 2}\left. \right),\end{array}\tag{7.6}
$$

## 7.2 Estimates for $\zeta ( k ) _ { j } ^ { n }$ and $\zeta ( k ) _ { j } ^ { \prime n }$

Here we estimate moments of the variables $\zeta ( k ) _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\zeta ( k ) _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ . A repeated use of the H¨older and Burkholder inequalities gives us for $q \geq 2$ , and under (SH1): 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq C _ {q}   \alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q} / n ^ {q / 2}, \\ \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq C _ {q} / n ^ {q / 2}. \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.7}
$$

Lemma 7.4. Under (SH1), and for any even integer $q \geq 2$ , we have 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq C _ {q} \varphi (\varepsilon_ {n}) \frac {\varepsilon_ {n} ^ {q - 2}}{n}.\tag{7.8}
$$

Proof. $\mathrm { A p p l y }$ the H¨older and Burkholder inequalities repeatedly to get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) \leq C _ {q} \mathbf {E} \left(\left(n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left\| \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} w (s, x) (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x) \right\| ^ {2} d u\right) ^ {q / 2}\right) \\ \leq C _ {q} n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \mathbf {E} \left(\left\| \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} w (s, x) (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x) \right\| ^ {q} d u\right) \\ \leq C _ {q} n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \mathbf {E} \left(\left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} \| w (s, x) \| ^ {2} \mu (d s, d x)\right) ^ {q / 2}\right) d u \\ \leq C _ {q} \mathbf {E} \left(\left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} \psi (x) ^ {2} \mu (d s, d x)\right) ^ {q / 2}\right): \\ = \mathbf {E} ((Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {n}) ^ {q / 2}), \end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { Z _ { t } ^ { n } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \int _ { E _ { \ast } ^ { c } } \psi ( x ) ^ { 2 } \mu ( d s , d x ) } \end{array}$ is an increasing pure jump L´evy process, whose Laplace transform is 

$$
\lambda \mapsto \mathbf {E} (e ^ {- \lambda (Z _ {s + t} ^ {n} - Z _ {s} ^ {n})}) = \exp t \int_ {E _ {n} ^ {c}} \left(e ^ {- \lambda \psi (x) ^ {2}} - 1\right) F (d x).
$$

We compute the $q / 2$ –moment of $Z _ { s + t } ^ { n } - Z _ { s } ^ { n }$ by diferentiating $q / 2$ times the Laplace transform at 0: this is the sum, over all choices $u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { k }$ of positive integers with $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } u _ { i } = q / 2$ , of suitable constants times the product for all $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ of the terms $\begin{array} { r } { t \int _ { E _ { n } ^ { c } } \psi ( x ) ^ { 2 u _ { i } } F ( d x ) } \end{array}$ ; moreover this term is smaller than $t \varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 u _ { i } - 2 } \varphi ( \varepsilon _ { n } )$ . Since further $\varepsilon _ { n } \leq 1$ and $\varphi ( 1 ) < \infty ,$ , we deduce that 

$$
\mathbf {E} ((Z _ {s + t} ^ {n} - Z _ {s} ^ {n}) ^ {q / 2}) \leq C _ {q} \varphi (\varepsilon_ {n}) \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {q / 2} t ^ {k} \varepsilon_ {n} ^ {q - 2 k} \leq C _ {q} \varphi (\varepsilon_ {n}) (t \varepsilon_ {n} ^ {q - 2} + t ^ {q / 2}).
$$

We deduce (7.8) for $\zeta ( 3 ) _ { i } ^ { n }$ (recall $n \varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 } \geq 1 )$ ), and the same holds for $\zeta ( 3 ) _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ . Lemma 7.5. Under (SH1), for any $q > 2$ we have 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (4) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (4) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (5) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q}) + \mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (5) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq \frac {C _ {q}}{\varepsilon_ {n} ^ {q} n ^ {q}}.\tag{7.9}
$$

Proof. Applying the H¨older and Burkholder inequalities and $\| w ( s , x ) \| ~ \leq$ $\psi ( x )$ yields for $j = 4 , 5 \colon$ 

$$
\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (j) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q} + \| \zeta (j) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \leq C _ {q} \mathbf {E} \left(\left(n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E _ {n}} \psi (x) \nu (d s, d x)\right) ^ {2} d u\right) ^ {q / 2}\right) \\ \leq C _ {q} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d s \int_ {E _ {n}} \psi (x) F (d x)\right) ^ {q} \leq \frac {C _ {q}}{n ^ {q}} \left(\int_ {E _ {n}} \psi (x) F (d x)\right) ^ {q}. \end{array}\tag{7.10}
$$

The result readily follows from (7.5). 

For $\zeta ( j ) _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\zeta ( j ) _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ with $j = 6 , 7$ the analogous estimates are not quite enough for our purposes, and we need a bit more. Below, we consider a pair $( r , B )$ , where $r \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ and B is a closed subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , with Lebesgue measure 0, and such that (2.11) holds when $r < 1$ and that $r = 1$ if $B = \varnothing$ . Let also 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l l l} r = 1 & \Rightarrow & \widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n} = 1 \\ r <   1 & \Rightarrow & \widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n} = 1 + \frac {1}{d (\gamma_ {i} ^ {n} , B)}, \text {with either} \gamma_ {i} ^ {n} = \beta_ {i} ^ {n} \text {or} \gamma_ {i} ^ {n} = \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.11}
$$

Lemma 7.6. Under $( S H \bot )$ and the previous assumptions, and iffurther $( S H ^ { \prime } )$ holds whenever $r \ < \ 1$ , for any $q \in ( 1 , 2 )$ and $l \in [ 0 , 1 )$ we can find u $> 1$ (depending on q and l) such that 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} \left(\| \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}\right) + \mathbf {E} \left(\| \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}\right) \leq \frac {C _ {l , q} (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n , 2}) ^ {1 / u}}{n ^ {q / 2}}, \\ \mathbf {E} \left(\| \zeta (7) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}\right) + \mathbf {E} \left(\| \zeta (7) _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {q} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}\right) \leq \frac {C _ {l , q}}{n ^ {q / 2}}. \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.12}
$$

Proof. We set $\begin{array} { r } { M _ { i } ^ { n } \ = \ \operatorname* { s u p } _ { s \in \left[ ( i - 1 ) / n , i / n \right] } \| W _ { s } \ - \ W _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } \| } \end{array}$ and $w _ { n } ( s , x ) \ =$ $\begin{array} { r } { w ( s - , x ) - w ( \frac { i - 1 } { n } , x ) } \end{array}$ for $\textstyle { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } < s \leq { \frac { i } { n } }$ , and 

$$
Z _ {t} ^ {n} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {E _ {n}} \psi (x) \mu (d s, d x), \quad Z _ {t} ^ {\prime n} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| \mu (d s, d x).
$$

Observe that $Z ^ { n }$ and $Z ^ { \prime n }$ are nondecreasing, piecewise constant, and $Z _ { t } ^ { \prime n } \mathrm { ~ - ~ }$ $Z _ { s } ^ { \prime n } \leq 2 ( Z _ { t } ^ { n } - Z _ { s } ^ { n } )$ whenever $s < t$ . Then 

$$
\| \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n} \| \leq C \sqrt {n} M _ {i} ^ {n} (Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {\prime n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime n}).
$$

Set $\begin{array} { r } { u ^ { \prime } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( 1 + \frac { 1 } { l } \bigwedge \frac { 1 } { q - 1 } \right) } \end{array}$ , which satisfies $u ^ { \prime } > 1$ because $l < 1$ and $q \in ( 1 , 2 )$ With $\delta _ { i } ^ { n } = ( \sqrt { n } M _ { i } ^ { n } ) ^ { u ^ { \prime } q } ( \widehat { \gamma } _ { i } ^ { n } ) ^ { u ^ { \prime } l }$ we then have (since $u ^ { \prime } > 1$ and $u ^ { \prime } q - u ^ { \prime } + 1 > 0 )$ 

$$
\| \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l} \leq C _ {q} \left(\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {n}) ^ {u ^ {\prime} q - u ^ {\prime} + 1}\right) ^ {\frac {1}{u ^ {\prime}}} (Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {\prime n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime n}) ^ {\frac {u ^ {\prime} - 1}{u ^ {\prime}}},
$$

and H¨older’s inequality yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} \left(\| \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {q} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}\right) \\ \qquad \leq C _ {q} \left(\mathbf {E} \left(\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {n}) ^ {u ^ {\prime} q - u ^ {\prime} + 1}\right)\right) ^ {\frac {1}{u ^ {\prime}}} \left(\mathbf {E} (Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {\prime n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime n})\right) ^ {\frac {u ^ {\prime} - 1}{u ^ {\prime}}}. \end{array}\tag{7.13}
$$

Now, if we combine (2.11) and (3.6), we see that when $r \textless 1$ (so (SH’) holds) the variable $d ( \gamma _ { i } ^ { n } , B )$ has a conditional law knowing $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ which has a density which is bounded uniformly in $n , i$ and $\omega ,$ so $\mathbf { E } \big ( \big ( \widehat { \gamma } _ { i } ^ { n } \big ) ^ { \dot { s } } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } \big )$ is bounded by a constant $C _ { s }$ for all $s \in [ 0 , 1 )$ , whether $r = 1$ or $r < 1 . { \mathrm { A l s o } } ,$ $\mathbf { E } \bigl ( \bigl ( \sqrt { n } \ M _ { i } ^ { n } \bigr ) ^ { p } \ \bigr | \ \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } \bigr ) \ \leq \ C _ { q }$ for all $p > 0$ . Then by H¨older’s inequality we get E $\left( \delta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { \left( i - 1 \right) / n } \right) \leq C _ { q , l }$ . Since further the variable $Z _ { i / n } ^ { n } - Z _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ^ { n }$ is independent of $\delta _ { i } ^ { n }$ , conditionally on $\mathcal F _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } }$ , we deduce 

$$
\mathbf {E} \left(\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {n}) ^ {u ^ {\prime} q - u ^ {\prime} + 1}\right) \leq C _ {q, l} \mathbf {E} ((Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {n}) ^ {u ^ {\prime} q - u ^ {\prime} + 1}).\tag{7.14}
$$

Next, we estimate the moments of $Z ^ { n }$ and $Z ^ { \prime n }$ . Observe that $Z ^ { \prime n } = A ^ { \prime n } +$ $N ^ { \prime n }$ , where 

$$
A _ {t} ^ {\prime n} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| \nu (d s, d x), N ^ {\prime n} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x).
$$

On the one hand, since $F ( E _ { n } ) \leq C / \varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 }$ by (7.5) and $n \varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 } \geq 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (A _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {\prime n} - A _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime n}) ^ {2} \leq \frac {1}{n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d s \left(\int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| F (d x)\right) ^ {2} \\ \leq \frac {1}{n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d s F (E _ {n}) \int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| ^ {2} F (d x) \\ \leq \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d s \int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| ^ {2} F (d x). \end{array}
$$

On the other hand $N ^ { \prime n }$ is a square–integrable martingale, and thus 

$$
\mathbf {E} \left((N _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {\prime n} - N _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime n}) ^ {2}\right) \leq \mathbf {E} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d s \int_ {E _ {n}} \| w _ {n} (s, x) \| ^ {2} F (d x)\right),
$$

and thus 

$$
\mathbf {E} \left((Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {\prime n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime n}) ^ {2}\right) \leq \frac {C \alpha_ {i} ^ {n , 2}}{n}.\tag{7.15}
$$

If we replace $\| w _ { n } ( s , x ) \|$ by ψ(x), we obtain in a similar fashion 

$$
\mathbf {E} \left((Z _ {\frac {i}{n}} ^ {n} - Z _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {n}) ^ {2}\right) \leq \frac {C}{n}.\tag{7.16}
$$

Then if we combine (7.13), (7.14), (7.15) and (7.16), and since $u ^ { \prime } q - u ^ { \prime } + 1 \leq 2 .$ we obtain the result for $\zeta ( 6 ) _ { i } ^ { n }$ , with $\begin{array} { r } { u = \frac { 2 u ^ { \prime } } { u ^ { \prime } - 1 } > 1 } \end{array}$ , and the proof for $\zeta ( 6 ) _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ is similar. Finally if we replace $w _ { n }$ by w (then $\alpha _ { i } ^ { n , 2 }$ is replaced by a constant), we get the result for $\zeta ( 7 ) _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\zeta ( 7 ) _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ □ 

## 7.3 Estimates for the variables of (7.3)

Here we derive estimates on the variables defined in (7.3). Below, the pair $( B , r )$ and the variable $\widehat { \gamma } _ { i } ^ { n }$ are like in Lemma 7.6. We also consider positive random variables $Z _ { i } ^ { n }$ which satisfy 

$$

$$

Observe that $\xi _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\xi _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ do not depend on the sequence $\varepsilon _ { n } ,$ , but $\widehat { \xi } _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\widehat { \xi _ { i } ^ { \prime n } }$ do. Remember also the variables $\alpha _ { i } ^ { n , q }$ defined ibn (7.6). 

Lemma 7.7. Assume (SH1) and (SH’) and (7.11) and (7.17). Let $p \geq 2$ and $l \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . Then if $\theta \in ( 1 , 2 )$ we have 

$$
\mathbf {E} \Big ((Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {p} \| \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {\theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l} \Big) + \mathbf {E} \Big ((Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {p} \| \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| ^ {\theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l} \Big) \leq \frac {C _ {p , \theta , l}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}},\tag{7.18}
$$

Moreover one can find a sequence $\varepsilon _ { n } > 0$ with $n \varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 } \geq 1$ and a sequence $z _ { n } > 0$ with $z _ { n }  0$ , both sequences depending on l only, and also two numbers $q , q ^ { \prime } \geq$ 1 depending on l only, such that 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{r l} & {\mathbf {E} ((Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {p} \| \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} \| (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}) \leq \frac {C _ {p , l}}{\sqrt {n}} \Big (z _ {n} + (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q}) ^ {1 / q} + (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, 2}) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} \Big),} \\ & {\mathbf {E} ((Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {p} \| \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l})) \leq \frac {C _ {p , l}}{\sqrt {n}} \Big (z _ {n} + (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q}) ^ {1 / q} + (\alpha_ {i + 1} ^ {n, q}) ^ {1 / q}} \\ & {\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, 2}) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} + (\alpha_ {i + 1} ^ {n, 2}) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} \Big).} \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.19}
$$

Proof. We prove (7.18) and (7.19) for $\xi _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\widehat { \xi } _ { i } ^ { n }$ only, the proofs for $\xi _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ and $\widehat { \xi _ { i } ^ { \prime n } }$ being similar. We have seen in the proof of Lemma 7.6 that, by (7.11), 

$$
s \in [ 0, 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathbf {E} ((\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {s}) \leq C _ {s}.\tag{7.20}
$$

Although $\xi _ { i } ^ { n }$ does not depend on the sequence $\varepsilon _ { n } .$ , we need to introduce a suitable sequence $\varepsilon _ { n }$ to prove (7.18): so we prove (7.18) and (7.19) simultaneously, with some fixed $\theta \in [ 1 , 2 )$ for the first result, and with $\theta = 1$ for the second one. If $\begin{array} { r } { t = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( 1 + \frac { 1 } { l } \wedge \frac { 2 } { \theta } \right) } \end{array}$ , by (7.17) and H´older’s inequality we get 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {E} ((Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {p} \| \xi_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {\theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}) \leq C _ {p, \theta , l} \left(\mathbf {E} (\| \xi_ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t \theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l})\right) ^ {1 / t}, \\ \mathbf {E} ((Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {p} \| \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} \| (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {l}) \leq C _ {p, l} \left(\mathbf {E} (\| \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l})\right) ^ {1 / t}. \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.21}
$$

Next, let s be the biggest number in $( 1 , 1 / t l )$ such that its conjugate exponent $s ^ { \prime }$ is of the form $s ^ { \prime } ~ = ~ 2 m / t \theta$ for some m $\in \mathcal { N }$ with $m \ \geq \ 2 .$ and put $\textit { q } = \textit { s } ^ { \prime } t \theta$ . Note that $s ^ { \prime }$ and q depend on θ and l only. The set $\{ y > 0 : y ^ { q } \varphi ( y / { \sqrt { n } } ) \leq 1 \}$ is an open or semi–open interval whose left end point is $0 ,$ and whose right end point is denoted by $a _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ , and since $\varphi ( y ) \to 0$ as $y  0$ it is clear that $a _ { n } ^ { \prime } \to \infty$ . At this point, we set $a _ { n } = 1 \bigvee ( a _ { n } ^ { \prime } - 1 / n ) \colon$ then $a _ { n } \to \infty$ , and for all n big enough $a _ { n } < a _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ and thus $a _ { n } ^ { q } \varphi ( a _ { n } / { \sqrt { n } } ) \leq 1$ Then we choose the sequence $\varepsilon _ { n }$ as $\varepsilon _ { n } = a _ { n } / { \sqrt { n } }$ , thus $n \varepsilon _ { n } ^ { 2 } \geq 1$ . Observe that both sequences $\varepsilon _ { n }$ and $a _ { n }$ only depend on θ and l. 

Now we apply (7.8) and (7.9) with $q$ and $\varepsilon _ { n }$ as above, plus (7.20) and H¨older’s inequality, to get 

$$
\left(\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (3) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t \theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l}) ^ {1 / t} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l} \varphi (\varepsilon_ {n}) ^ {1 / s ^ {\prime} t} a _ {n} ^ {\theta - 2 / s ^ {\prime} t}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l}}{n ^ {\theta / 2} a _ {n} ^ {2 / s ^ {\prime} t}} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}},\right)\tag{7.22}
$$

In a similar way, (7.20) and (7.7) and H´older’s inequality give (with the same q as above): 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} \big (\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (1) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t \theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l}) ^ {1 / t} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l} (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n , q}) ^ {\theta / q}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}}, \\ \big (\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (2) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t \theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l}) ^ {1 / t} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}}. \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.23}
$$

Finally applying (7.12) and $t \theta < 2$ yields 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} \big (\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (6) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t \theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l}) ^ {1 / t} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l} (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n , 2}) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}}, \\ \big (\mathbf {E} (\| \zeta (7) _ {i} ^ {n} \| ^ {t \theta} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {t l}) ^ {1 / t} \leq \frac {C _ {\theta , l}}{n ^ {\theta / 2}} \end{array} \right\}\tag{7.24}
$$

for some $q ^ { \prime } > 1$ depending on tθ and $t l .$ , hence on θ and l only. 

Then if we put together (7.21), (7.22), (7.23) and (7.24), and in view of (7.3) and (7.4), we readily get (7.18), and also (7.19) with $z _ { n } = a _ { n } ^ { - 2 / s ^ { \prime } t } + a _ { n } ^ { - 1 }$ (note that for (7.19) we take θ = 1). □ 

## 7.4 Final estimates

The previous subsection gave us estimates on the variables of (7.3), which in view of (7.4) are the building blocks for obtaining the diference occuring in (7.1). Now we procees to give estimates for this diference itself. We start with a lemma about the variables of (7.6). 

Lemma 7.8. Under (SH1) we have for all $q \geq 2$ and $q ^ { \prime } \geq 1$ and $t > 0 .$ 

$$
\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q} \leq C _ {q}, \quad \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q}) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} \rightarrow 0.\tag{7.25}
$$

Proof. We can of course forget about the term $1 / n ^ { q / 2 }$ in (7.6), whereas the first part of (7.25) is obvious. For the second part we set 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\gamma_ {n} (u) = \| a _ {u} - a _ {[ n u ] / n} \| ^ {2} + \| \sigma_ {u -} ^ {\prime} - \sigma_ {[ n u ] / n} ^ {\prime} \| ^ {2} + \| v _ {u -} - v _ {[ n u ] / n} \| ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad + \int_ {E} \left\| w (u -, x) - w \Big (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x \Big) \right\| ^ {2} F (d x).} \end{array}
$$

Then the H¨older inequality yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} (\alpha_ {i} ^ {n, q}) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} \leq \frac {[ n t ]}{n} \left(\frac {1}{[ n t ]} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} \left(\left(n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \gamma_ {n} (u) d u\right) ^ {q / 2}\right)\right) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} \\ \leq \frac {[ n t ]}{n} \left(\frac {1}{[ n t ]} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} \left(n \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \gamma_ {n} (u) ^ {q / 2} d u\right)\right) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}} \\ \leq t ^ {\frac {q ^ {\prime} - 1}{q ^ {\prime}}} \left(\mathbf {E} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {t} \gamma_ {n} (u) ^ {q / 2} d u\right)\right) ^ {1 / q ^ {\prime}}. \end{array}
$$

Since $\gamma _ { n }$ is uniformly bounded and converges pointwise to 0, we get the result. 

Let us now introduce a list of growth or smoothness assumptions on a real–valued function $f$ on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , with complement (4.7). Below, $C \ > \ 0$ and $p \geq 2$ are suitable constants, and the pair $( B , r )$ is given, with the properties stated before (7.11). We list some conditions, for which we assume that $f$ is diferentiable on the complement $B ^ { c }$ . Below, each $\varPsi _ { A , \varepsilon }$ is an increasing continuous function on $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ with $\varPsi _ { A , \varepsilon } ( 0 ) = 0$ 

$$
x \in B ^ {c} \quad \Rightarrow \quad | \nabla f (x) | \leq C (1 + \| x \| ^ {p}) \left(1 + \frac {1}{d (x , B) ^ {1 - r}}\right),\tag{7.26}
$$

$$
x, y \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \Rightarrow | f (x + y) - f (x) | \leq C (1 + \| x \| ^ {p} + \| y \| ^ {p}) \| y \| ^ {r},\tag{7.27}
$$

$$
\| x \| \leq A, \| y \| \leq \varepsilon^ {\prime} <   \varepsilon <   d (x, B) \Rightarrow \| \nabla f (x + y) - \nabla f (x) \| \leq \Psi_ {A, \varepsilon} (\varepsilon^ {\prime})\tag{7.28}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 <   \| y \| \leq \frac {d (x , B)}{2} \\ \implies \| \nabla f (x + y) - \nabla f (x) \| \leq C (1 + \| x \| ^ {p} + \| y \| ^ {p}) \frac {\| y \|}{d (x , B) ^ {2 - r}}. \end{array}\tag{7.29}
$$

The connections with our assumptions (K) and (K’) are as follows (with B and r identical in (K’) and above, or $B = \varnothing$ and $r = 1$ in the case of (K)): 

$$
(\mathrm{K}), \text {   or   } (\mathrm{K} ^ {\prime}) \text {   with   } r = 1 \Rightarrow (4. 7), (7. 2 6), (7. 2 7) \text {   and   } (7. 2 8),\tag{7.30}
$$

$$
\left(\mathrm{K} ^ {\prime}\right) \text {   with   } r <   1 \Rightarrow (4. 7), (7. 2 6), (7. 2 7) \text {   and   } (7. 2 9)\tag{7.31}
$$

Next, we consider the setting of (5.5), with k is diferentiable on $B ^ { c }$ . We let $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n }$ be either $\beta _ { i } ^ { n }$ or $\beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ , and we introduce the following subsets of Ω: 

$$
A _ {i} ^ {n} = \{\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| > d (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}, B) / 2 \},\tag{7.32}
$$

(observe that $A _ { i } ^ { n } = \emptyset$ when $B = \varnothing )$ . Let also $\overline { { \gamma } } _ { i } ^ { n }$ be an auxiliary variable which for each ω is on the segment joining $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ and $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n }$ , and let $\widehat { \gamma } _ { i } ^ { n }$ be 1 when $r = 1$ and $1 + 1 / d ( \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } , B )$ when $r < 1$ . Then we set 

$$
\varPhi_ {i} ^ {n} = f (\gamma_ {i} ^ {n}) \Big ((k (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) - k (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n})) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}} - \nabla k (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}) (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}}
$$

$$
\left. + \left(\nabla k \left(\bar {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}\right) - \nabla k \left(\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}\right)\right) \left(\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}\right) 1 _ {\left(A _ {i} ^ {n}\right) ^ {c}}\right),\tag{7.33}
$$

$$
\widehat {\varPhi} _ {i} ^ {n} = f (\gamma_ {i} ^ {n}) \nabla k (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}) (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n})\tag{7.34}
$$

(by the fact that B has Lebesgue measure 0, we see that k is a.s. diferentiable at the point $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n }$ , which is either $\beta _ { i } ^ { n }$ or $\beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ , so (7.33) and (7.34) make sense). 

## Lemma 7.9. Assume the following:

(i) (SH1) and (5.5) and k satisfies (7.26) and (7.27); 

(ii) $\boldsymbol { f r } = 1$ then k satisfies (7.28); 

(iii) $i f B \ne \emptyset$ then (SH’) holds; 

(iv) $i f r < 1$ then k satisfies (7.29). 

(a) $I f \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } = \beta _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n } - \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } = \xi _ { i } ^ { n }$ , or $i f \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime } { } ^ { n } = \beta _ { i } ^ { \prime } { } ^ { n }$ and $\gamma _ { i } ^ { { \prime } n } - \gamma _ { i } ^ { { \prime } { \prime } n } = \xi _ { i } ^ { { \prime } n }$ , we have for all $t > 0$ 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (| \varPhi_ {i} ^ {n} |) \to 0.\tag{7.35}
$$

(b) $I f \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime { n } } = \beta _ { i } ^ { n }$ and $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n } - \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } = \widehat { \xi } _ { i } ^ { n } , ~ o r ~ i f \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } = \beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ and $\gamma _ { i } ^ { { \prime } n } - \gamma _ { i } ^ { { \prime } { \prime } n } = \widehat { \xi _ { i } ^ { \prime n } }$ , we have for all $t > 0$ 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (| \widehat {\varPhi} _ {i} ^ {n} |) \to 0.\tag{7.36}
$$

Proof. 1) We first prove (7.35) when $r = 1$ . We choose $\varepsilon _ { n } = 1$ for all n and putting together all estimates in (7.7), (7.8), (7.9) and (7.12) (with $l = 0$ , so this estimate holds for $q = 2$ as well) to get 

$$
q \geq 2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathbf {E} (\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| ^ {q}) \leq \frac {C _ {q}}{n}.\tag{7.37}
$$

Then (4.7) and (7.26) and $A _ { i } ^ { n } \subset \{ d ( \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } , B ) < \varepsilon \} \cup \{ \| \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime n } - \gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } \| \geq \varepsilon / 2 \}$ yield for all $A > 0 , \varepsilon > 2 \varepsilon ^ { \prime } > 0 \colon$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \varPhi_ {i} ^ {n} | + | \widehat {\varPhi} _ {i} ^ {n} | \leq C (Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {2 p} \bigg (\varPsi_ {A, \varepsilon^ {\prime}} (\varepsilon) + \frac {\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \|}{A} \\ \qquad \qquad + \| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| \left(\frac {1}{\varepsilon} + \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {\prime}}\right) + 1 _ {\{d (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}, B) \leq \varepsilon \}} \bigg) \| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \|. \end{array}\tag{7.38}
$$

If $B = \varnothing$ the indicator function above vanishes. Otherwise, the variable $\gamma _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n }$ has a conditional law knowing $\mathscr { F } _ { \underline { { i - 1 } } }$ which has a density (on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ that is smaller than some (non–random) Lebesgue integrable function $\varphi \ ( \mathrm { s e e \ ( 3 . 6 ) } )$ ), so it also has an unconditional density smaller than $\varphi .$ Therefore 

$$
\mathsf {P} (d (\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n}, B) \leq \varepsilon) \leq \alpha_ {\varepsilon} := \int_ {\{x: d (x, B) \leq \varepsilon \}} \varphi (x) d x,
$$

and lim $\iota _ { \varepsilon \to 0 } \alpha _ { \varepsilon } = 0$ . Then (5.5), (7.37), (7.38) and the multivariate H¨older inequality yield 

$$
\mathbf {E} (| \varPhi_ {i} ^ {n} |) + \mathbf {E} (| \widehat {\varPhi} _ {i} ^ {n} |) \leq \frac {C}{\sqrt {n}} \left(\varPsi_ {A, \varepsilon} (\varepsilon^ {\prime}) + \frac {1}{A} + \frac {1}{n ^ {1 / 4}} \left(\frac {1}{\varepsilon} + \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {\prime}}\right) + \alpha_ {\varepsilon} ^ {1 / 4}\right).
$$

Hence (7.35) readily follows: choose A big, then $\varepsilon$ small, then $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$ small. 

2) Now we suppose that $r < 1$ , hence $B \neq \varnothing$ . We have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \Phi_ {i} ^ {n} \right| \leq \left(Z _ {i} ^ {n}\right) ^ {2 p} \left(\left\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \right\| ^ {r} 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}} + \left\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \right\| 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {\left\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \right\|}{d \left(\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} , B\right) ^ {1 - r}} 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}} + \frac {\left\| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \right\| ^ {2}}{d \left(\gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} , B\right) ^ {2 - r}} 1 _ {(A _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {c}}\right) \\ \leq C (Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {2 p} \| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| ^ {1 + r / 2} (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {1 - r / 2}, \end{array} \tag {7.3}\tag{7.39}
$$

where the first inequality follows from (7.26), (7.27) and (7.29) for $k ,$ while the second one is obtained by using the definition of the set $A _ { i } ^ { n }$ . Hence Lemmas 7.7 and 7.8 readily give (7.35). 

3) Finally, in all cases we have 

$$
| \widehat {\varPhi} _ {i} ^ {n} | \leq C (Z _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {2 p} \| \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime n} - \gamma_ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n} \| (\widehat {\gamma} _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {1 - r}.\tag{7.40}
$$

Therefore (7.36) follows from Lemmas 7.7 (see (7.19)) and 7.8 again. 

## 8 The proof of Theorem 2.3

1) As said at the beginning of the previous Section, we can assume that g and h are 1–dimensional, and that (SH1), and also (SH’) when either g or $h$ satisfies (K’) instead of (K), and we need to prove that the arrays defined in (7.1) and (7.1) are AN. 

2) Let us prove first that $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } \right)$ is AN. If f is continuously diferentiable, and f and $\nabla f$ have polynomial growth, we readily deduce from Lebesgue’s theorem that $\Sigma \mapsto \rho _ { \Sigma } ( f ) = \mathbf { E } ( f ( \Sigma U ) )$ ) (where U is an $\mathcal { N } ( 0 , I _ { d } )$ –random vector) is bounded, continuously diferentiable and with bounded derivatives over the set $\mathcal { M } ^ { \prime }$ defined in connection with formula (3.6). Hence if both $g$ and h satisfy (K) we have (recall the notation (3.6), and set $\varphi ( \Sigma ) = \rho _ { \Sigma } ( g ) \rho _ { \Sigma } ( h ) )$ : 

$$
\Sigma , \Sigma^ {\prime} \in \mathcal {M} ^ {\prime} \Rightarrow \left\{ \begin{array}{l} | \varphi (\Sigma) | + \| \nabla \varphi (\Sigma) \| \leq C \\ | \varphi (\Sigma) - \varphi (\Sigma^ {\prime}) | \leq C \| \Sigma - \Sigma^ {\prime} \| \\ | \varphi (\Sigma) - \varphi (\Sigma^ {\prime}) - \nabla \varphi (\Sigma^ {\prime}) (\Sigma - \Sigma^ {\prime}) \| \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \Psi (\| \Sigma - \Sigma^ {\prime} \|) \| \Sigma - \Sigma^ {\prime} \| \end{array} \right.\tag{8.1}
$$

for some constant $C$ (depending on $A _ { 0 }$ in $\left( 3 . 6 \right) )$ and some increasing function Ψ on $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ , continuous and null at 0 (here, ϕ is $\mathcal { M } _ { d , d } \mathrm { - v a l u e d }$ , and $\nabla \varphi ( \Sigma ^ { \prime } ) ( \Sigma -$ $\Sigma ^ { \prime } )$ is R–valued). 

If g or h (or both) satisfy (K’) only we also have (SH’), and since 

$$
\rho_ {\Sigma} (f) = \int \frac {1}{(2 \pi) ^ {d / 2} \mathrm{det} (\Sigma \Sigma^ {\star}) ^ {1 / 2}} f (x) \exp \left(- \frac {1}{2} x ^ {\star} (\Sigma \Sigma^ {\star}) ^ {- 1} x\right) d x
$$

we see that as soon as $f$ has polynomial growth the function $\Sigma \mapsto \rho _ { \Sigma } ( f )$ is $C ^ { \infty }$ with bounded derivatives of all orders on the set $\mathcal { M } ^ { \prime }$ . Hence we also have (8.1), which thus holds in all cases. 

Since we can write (7.2) as $\begin{array} { r } { \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime { n } } = \sqrt { { n } } \int _ { ( i - 1 ) / { n } } ^ { i / { n } } ( \varphi ( \sigma _ { u } ) - \varphi ( \sigma _ { ( i - 1 ) / { n } } ) d u _ { \mathrm { { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { ~  ~ } } } } } \end{array}$ , we have $\zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } = \eta _ { i } ^ { n } + \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ where 

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \nabla \varphi (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\sigma_ {u} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}\right) d u,
$$

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i -}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \Big (\varphi (\sigma_ {u}) - \varphi (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) - \nabla \varphi (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) (\sigma_ {u} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \Big) d u.
$$

and we need to prove that the two arrays $( \eta _ { i } ^ { n } )$ and $( \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } )$ are $\mathrm { A N } .$ 

We decompose further $\eta _ { i } ^ { n }$ as $\eta _ { i } ^ { n } = \mu _ { i } ^ { n } + \mu _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ , where 

$$
\mu_ {i} ^ {n} = \sqrt {n} \nabla \varphi (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d u \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} a _ {s} ^ {\prime} d s,
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \sqrt {n} \nabla \varphi (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \left(\int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \sigma_ {s -} d W _ {s} + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} v _ {s -} d V _ {s} \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {u} \int_ {E} w (s -, x) (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x) \Bigg) d u. \end{array}
$$

On the one hand, we have $| \mu _ { i } ^ { n } | \le C / n ^ { 3 / 2 }$ by (8.1) and the boundedness of $a ^ { \prime } .$ so the array $( \mu _ { i } ^ { n } )$ is AN. On the other hand, we also get by (SH1) and (8.1) and Cauchy–Schwarz applied twice: 

$$
\mathbf {E} \Big (\mu_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big) = 0, \qquad \mathbf {E} \Big ((\mu_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big) \leq \frac {C}{n ^ {3}}.
$$

Then the array $( \mu _ { i } ^ { \prime n } )$ is AN, as well as the array $( \eta _ { i } ^ { n } )$ 

Finally, using (8.1) once more, we see that for all $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {| \eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} | \leq \sqrt {n} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \Psi (\| \sigma_ {u} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \|) \| \sigma_ {u} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| d u} \\ & {\quad \leq \sqrt {n} \Psi (\varepsilon) \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \| \sigma_ {u} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| d u + \frac {C \sqrt {n}}{\varepsilon} \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} \| \sigma_ {u} - \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \| ^ {2} d u.} \end{array}
$$

Since $\mathbf { E } ( \| \sigma _ { u } - \sigma _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } \| ^ { 2 } ) \leq C / n$ when $u \in ( ( i - 1 ) / n , i / n ]$ , we deduce that 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {[ n t ]} \mathbf {E} (| \eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} |) \leq C t \left(\varPsi (\varepsilon) + \frac {1}{\varepsilon \sqrt {n}}\right).
$$

From this we deduce the AN property of the array $( \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } )$ because $\varepsilon > 0$ is arbitrarily small and lim $_ { \xi \longrightarrow 0 } \varPsi ( \varepsilon ) = 0$ . Hence, finally, the array $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime n } \right)$ is AN. 

3) Now we start proving that the array $\left( \zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } \right)$ also is AN. Since $\varphi ( \sigma _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) =$ $\dot { \bf E } ( g ( \beta _ { i } ^ { n } ) h ( \beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } ) \mid \bar { \mathcal { F } } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } )$ , we have $\zeta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } = \mathbf { E } \big ( \delta _ { i } ^ { n } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } \big )$ , where 

$$
\delta_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \left(g (\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) h (\sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n})\right).
$$

Let us set 

$$
\begin{array}{c} A _ {i} ^ {n} = \{\| \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n} \| > d (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}, B) / 2 \}, \\ A _ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \{\| \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} \| > d (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}, B ^ {\prime}) / 2 \}, \end{array}
$$

where B (resp. $B ^ { \prime } )$ is either empty or is the set associated with $g \ ( { \mathrm { r e s p . ~ } } h )$ according to whether that function satisfies (K) or (K’). We can express the diference $g ( \sqrt { n } ~ \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } Y ) - g ( \beta _ { i } ^ { n } )$ using a Taylor expansion if we are on the set $( A _ { i } ^ { n } ) ^ { c }$ , and we can thus write 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \\ & \quad = (g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n})) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}} - \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n}) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}} \\ & \qquad + (\nabla g (\overline {{\gamma}} _ {i} ^ {n}) - \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n})) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n}) 1 _ {(A _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {c}} \\ & \qquad + \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n}), \end{array}\tag{8.2}
$$

where $\overline { { \gamma } } _ { i } ^ { n }$ is some (random) vector lying on the segment between ${ \sqrt { n } } \ \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } Y$ and $\beta _ { i } ^ { n } \colon$ recall that $\nabla g ( \overline { { \gamma } } _ { i } ^ { n } )$ is well defined because on $( A _ { i } ^ { n } ) ^ { c }$ we have $\overline { { \gamma } } _ { i } ^ { n } \in B ^ { c }$ while $\nabla g ( \beta _ { i } ^ { n } )$ is a.s. well defined because either B is empty, or it has Lebesgue measure 0 and $\beta _ { i } ^ { n }$ has a density. Analogously, $h ( \sqrt { n } \ \varDelta _ { i + 1 } ^ { n } Y ) - h ( \beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } )$ can be written likewise, provided we replace $\varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } Y , \beta _ { i } ^ { n } , A _ { i } ^ { n } , \bar { \gamma } _ { i } ^ { \bar { n } ^ { * } } \bar { \mathrm { b y } } \varDelta _ { i + 1 } ^ { n } Y , \beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } , A _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ $\overline { { \gamma } } _ { i } ^ { m }$ 

Now observe that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \delta_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) \Big (h (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) - h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \Big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad + \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \Big (g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \Big) h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}), \end{array}
$$

Therefore we deduce from the decomposition (8.2) and the analogous one for $h ,$ and also from (7.3) and (7.4), that $\begin{array} { r } { \delta _ { i } ^ { n } = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { 6 } \delta _ { i } ^ { n } ( k ) } \end{array}$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (1) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) \nabla h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime n},} \\ & {\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (2) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) \nabla h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \widetilde {\xi} _ {i + 1} ^ {n},} \\ & {\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (3) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n},} \\ & {\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (4) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \Big (g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) \nabla h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {\prime n} + h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} \Big),} \\ & {\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (5) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) \Big ((h (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y) - h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n})) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {\prime n}}} \\ & {- \nabla h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {\prime n}}} \\ & {+ (\nabla h (\overline {{\gamma}} _ {i} ^ {\prime n}) - \nabla h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n})) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i + 1} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) 1 _ {(A _ {i} ^ {\prime n}) ^ {c}} \Big),} \\ & {\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (6) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \Big ((g (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n})) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}}} \\ & {- \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n}) 1 _ {A _ {i} ^ {n}}} \\ & {+ (\nabla g (\overline {{\gamma}} _ {i} ^ {n}) - \nabla g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n})) (\sqrt {n} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y - \beta_ {i} ^ {n}) 1 _ {(A _ {i} ^ {n}) ^ {c}} \Big).} \end{array}
$$

If we combine (5.2) with Lemma 7.9, we readily get $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \mathbf { E } ( \| \delta _ { i } ^ { n } ( k ) \| )  0 } \end{array}$ when $k = 4 , 5 , 6$ . So we are left to proving that 

$$
\text { the   array } \quad \left\{\mu_ {i} ^ {n} (k) = \mathbf {E} \Big (\delta_ {i} ^ {n} (k) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big) \right\} \text { is   AN. }\tag{8.3}
$$

for $k = 1 , 2 , 3$ 

4) Let us introduce the $\mathcal { M } _ { d , d ^ { \prime } }$ –valued martingales 

$$
M (n, i) _ {t} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0 & \text {if} t \leq \frac {i - 1}{n} \\ v _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} (V _ {t} - V _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {t} \int_ {E _ {n}} w (\frac {i - 1}{n}, x) (\mu - \nu) (d s, d x) \text {otherwise.} \end{array} \right.
$$

We see that $\widetilde { \xi } _ { i } ^ { n } = \zeta ( 2 ) _ { i } ^ { n } + \zeta ( 5 ) _ { i } ^ { n } + \zeta ( 7 ) _ { i } ^ { n } = \sqrt { n } \left( \eta _ { i } ^ { n } + \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } \right)$ , where 

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {n} = \frac {1}{n} a _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} + \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} (W _ {u} - W _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}) d W _ {u},
$$

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} = \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} M (n, i) _ {u} d W _ {u} = \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} M (n, i) \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W - \int_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\frac {i}{n}} d M (n, i) _ {u} W _ {u}.
$$

Now we can write 

$$
\mu_ {i} ^ {n} (3) = \rho_ {i - 1} ^ {n} (h)   \mathbf {E} \Big (\nabla g (\sqrt {n}   \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W) (\eta_ {i} ^ {n} + \eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big).
$$

g is even, so $\nabla g$ is odd; hence the variable $\nabla g ( \sqrt { n } ~ \sigma _ { \perp - 1 } \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } W ) \eta _ { i } ^ { n }$ is multiplied $\mathrm { b y \_ - 1 }$ if we change the sign of the process $( W _ { s } \mathrm { ~ - ~ } \stackrel { \mathrm { \tiny ~ \wedge ~ } } { W } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) _ { s \ge ( i - 1 ) / n }$ , and this sign change does not afect the $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n ^ { - } }$ –conditional distribution of this process. Hence we get 

$$
\mathbf {E} \left(\nabla g (\sqrt {n} \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Delta_ {i} ^ {n} W) \eta_ {i} ^ {n} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}\right) = 0.
$$

On the other hand, the processes $M ( n , i )$ and $W _ { s } \mathrm { ~ - ~ } W _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ are independent, conditionally on $\mathcal F _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ , when the times goes through $( ( i \textrm { -- }$ $1 ) / n , i / n ]$ . So if $\mathcal { F } _ { s } ^ { 0 }$ denotes the $\sigma \mathrm { \cdot }$ –field generated by $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ and by $( W _ { u } - W _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) _ { ( i - 1 ) / n \leq u \leq s } .$ we get that $M ( n , i )$ is an ( <sup>0</sup>)–martingale for $s \in ( ( i - 1 ) / n , i / n ]$ , and thus $\mathbf { E } ( \eta _ { i } ^ { \prime n } | \mathcal { F } _ { i / n } ^ { 0 } ) = 0$ . By successive conditioning, we immediately deduce that 

$$
\mathbf {E} \left(\nabla g (\sqrt {n} \sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W) \eta_ {i} ^ {\prime n} | | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}\right) = 0,
$$

$$
\mathbf {E} \Big (\nabla h (\beta_ {i} ^ {\prime n}) \widetilde {\xi} _ {i + 1} ^ {n} | \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i}{n}} \Big) = 0,
$$

and therefore $\mu _ { i } ^ { n } ( 3 ) = 0$ . In a similar way, h is odd and $\beta _ { i } ^ { \prime n }$ is the product of an $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ –measurable variable, times $\varDelta _ { i + 1 } ^ { n } W$ . So exactly as above we have 

and so a fortiori $\mu _ { i } ^ { n } ( 2 ) = 0$ 

5) It remains to study $\mu _ { i } ^ { n } ( 1 )$ . With the previous notation $M ( n , i )$ , it is easy to check that 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mu_ {i} ^ {n} (1)\\= \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {d} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {d ^ {\prime}} z _ {i} ^ {n, l m}   \mathbf {E} \left(g (\sqrt {n}   \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} Y) (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W + \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} M (n, i)) ^ {l m}\right) |   \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}}\left. \right),\end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { z _ { i } ^ { n , l m } = \int \partial _ { x _ { l } } h ( \sigma _ { \frac { i - 1 } { n } } x ) } \end{array}$ x<sub>m</sub> ρ(dx) and $\rho$ is $\mathcal { N } ( 0 , I _ { d ^ { \prime } } )$ (the law of $W _ { 1 } )$ , so $\| z _ { i } ^ { n , l m } \| \leq C$ . Recalling once more $\sqrt { n } ~ \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } Y = \beta _ { i } ^ { n } + \widehat { \xi } _ { i } ^ { n } + \widetilde { \xi } _ { i } ^ { n }$ , we see that 

$$
\mu_ {i} ^ {n} (1) = \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {d} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {d ^ {\prime}} \left(\mathbf {E} \Big (\mu_ {i} ^ {n} (l, m) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big) + \mathbf {E} \Big (\mu_ {i} ^ {\prime n} (l, m) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} \Big)\right),
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu_ {i} ^ {n} (l, m) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}}   z _ {i} ^ {n, l m} \Big (g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n} + \widehat {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n} + \widetilde {\xi} _ {i} ^ {n}) - g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n}) \Big) \Big (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W + \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} M (n, i) \Big) ^ {l m}, \\ \mu_ {i} ^ {\prime n} (l, m) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}}   z _ {i} ^ {n, l m} g (\beta_ {i} ^ {n})   \Big (\sigma_ {\frac {i - 1}{n}} ^ {\prime} \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} W + \varDelta_ {i} ^ {n} M (n, i) \Big) ^ {l m}. \end{array}
$$

Use (5.2) and (7.37) and the property $\mathbf { E } ( \| \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } W \| ^ { q } ) + \mathbf { E } ( \| \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } M ( n , i ) \| ^ { q } ) \leq$ $C _ { q } / n$ for all $q \geq 2$ to get that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { [ n t ] } \mathbf { E } ( | \mu _ { i } ^ { n } ( l , m ) | )  0 } \end{array}$ . Finally, since $g$ is even and $\varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } W$ and $\varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } M ( n , i )$ are independent conditionally on $\mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n }$ and $\mathbf { E } \left( \varDelta _ { i } ^ { n } M ( n , i ) \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } \right) = 0$ , we find that indeed $\mathbf { E } ( \mu _ { i } ^ { \prime n } ( l , m ) \mid \mathcal { F } _ { ( i - 1 ) / n } ) = 0$ So we get (8.3) for $k = 1$ , and we are done.
