# A Didactic Note on Afine Stochastic Volatility Models

Jan KALLSEN∗ 

HVB-Stiftungsinstitut f¨ur Finanzmathematik, Zentrum Mathematik TU M¨unchen, Boltzmannstraße 3, D-85747 Garching bei M¨unchen, Germany. kallsen@ma.tum.de 

Summary. Many stochastic volatility (SV) models in the literature are based on an afine structure, which makes them handy for analytical calculations. The underlying general class of afine Markov processes has been characterized completely and investigated thoroughly by Dufie, Filipovic, and Schachermayer (2003). In this note, we take a look at this set of processes and, in particular, afine SV models from the point of view of semimartingales and time changes. In the course of doing so, we explain the intuition behind semimartingale characteristics. 

Key words: semimartingale characteristics, afine process, time change, stochastic volatility 

Mathematics Subject Classification (2000): 60G99, 91B70 

## 1 Introduction

Semimartingale calculus is by now a standard tool which is covered in many textbooks. However, this holds true to a lesser extent for the notion of semimartingale characteristics – despite of its practical use in many applications. A first goal of this note is to convince readers (who are not already convinced) that semimartingale characteristics are a very natural and intuitive concept. 

We do so in Section 2 by taking ordinary calculus as a starting point and by restricting attention to the important special case of absolutely continuous characteristics. We argue that diferential characteristics and certain martingale problems can be viewed as natural counterparts or extensions of derivatives and ordinary diferential equations (ODE’s). In this sense, afine processes are the solutions to particularly simple martingale problems, which extend afine ODE’s to the stochastic case. They are considered in Section 3. 

Afine processes have been characterized completely and investigated thoroughly in an extremely useful and impressive paper by Dufie et al. ([7], henceforth DFS). They work predominantly in the context of Markov processes and their generators. But in a semimartingale setting, their results yield an explicit solution to the afine martingale problem. 

Next to interest rate theory and credit risk, stochastic volatility (SV) models constitute one of the main areas in finance where the power of the afine structure has been exploited. In Section 4 we review a number of afine SV models under the perspective of semimartingale characteristics. 

Unexplained notation is typically used as in [12]. Superscripts refer generally to coordinates of a vector or vector-valued process rather than powers. The few exceptions as e.g. $e ^ { x } , \sigma ^ { 2 } , v _ { t } ^ { 1 / \alpha }$ should be obvious from the context. The notion of a L´evy process $X = ( X _ { t } ) _ { t \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } }$ is applied slightly ambigiously. In the presence of a given filtration $\mathbf { F } = ( \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) _ { t \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } } , X$ is supposed to denote a L´evy process relative to this filtration (PIIS in the language of [12]), otherwise an intrinsic L´evy process in the sense of [19], i.e. a PIIS relative to its own natural filtration. 

## 2 Diferential semimartingale calculus

In this section we want to provide non-experts in the field with an intuitive feeling for semimartingale characteristics. It is not the aim to explain the mathematics behind this concept in detail. This is done exemplarily in the standard reference [12] (henceforth JS) or in [11], [23]. 

We hope that the reader does not feel ofended by the following digression on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } .$ -valued deterministic functions $X = ( X _ { t } ) _ { t \in \mathbb { R } } .$ 1 of time. Specifically, linear functions $X _ { t }$ = bt are distinguished by constant growth. They are completely characterized by a single vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . Many arbitrary functions behave “locally” as linear ones. This local behavior is expressed in terms of the derivative $\textstyle { \frac { d } { d t } } X _ { t }$ of X at time $t \in \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ . Of course, linear functions are up to the starting value $X _ { 0 }$ the only ones with constant derivative. In many applications, functions occur as solutions to ODE’s rather than explicitly, i.e. their derivative is expressed implicitly as 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} X _ {t} = f (X _ {t}), \quad X _ {0} = x _ {0}.\tag{2.1}
$$

In simple cases, the solution to the initial value problem (2.1) can be found in a closed form, $\mathrm { e . g . }$ , if f is a linear or, more generally, an afine function. Linear ODE’s are solved by exponential functions. 

We now want to extend the above concepts to a probabilistic setting. Firstly note that stochastic processes $( X _ { t } ) _ { t \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } }$ are nothing else but random functions of time. A natural interpretation of constant growth in stochastic terms is stationary, independent increments. Therefore, the L´evy pocesses (processes with stationary, independent increments) can be viewed as random counterparts of linear functions. This is also reflected by the importance of L´evy processes in applications. The slope b of a linear function is paralleled by the L´evy–Khintchine triplet $( b , c , F )$ of a L´evy process, where the vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ stands for a linear drift as in the deterministic case, the symmetric non-negative d d matrix c denotes the covariance matrix of the Brownian motion part of the process, and the L´evy measure $F$ on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ reflects the intensity of jumps of diferent sizes. By virtue of the L´evy–Khintchine formula, this triplet characterizes the distribution of a L´evy process X uniquely. Indeed, we have $E e ^ { i \lambda ^ { \top } X _ { t } } = e ^ { t \psi ( i \lambda ) }$ , where the L´evy exponent ψ is given by 

$$
\psi (u) = u ^ {\top} b + \frac {1}{2} u ^ {\top} c u + \int (e ^ {u ^ {\top} x} - 1 - u ^ {\top} h (x)) F (d x)\tag{2.2}
$$

and $h : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ denotes a fixed truncation function as, e $. \mathrm { g } . , h ( x ) = x 1 _ { \{ | x | \leq 1 \} }$ If h is replaced with another truncation function ${ \widetilde { h } } .$ , only the drift coeficient b changes according to 

$$
b (\widetilde {h}) = b (h) + \int (\widetilde {h} (x) - h (x)) F (d x).\tag{2.3}
$$

It may seem less obvious how to extend derivatives and initial value problems to the stochastic case. A classical approach is provided within the theory of Markov processes. Infinitesimal generators describe the local behaviour of a Markov process X in terms of the current value $X _ { t } ,$ , which means that they naturally generalize ODE’s. In this note, however, we focus instead on semimartingale characteristics and martingale problems as an alternative tool. Although the general theory behind Markov processes and semimartingales looks quite diferent in the first place, there exist close relationships between the corresponding concepts (cf. [11], [8]). 

Finally, one can use stochastic diferential equations (SDE’s) to describe a process in terms of its local behavior. Even though there is a natural connection between martingale problems and SDE’s, “linear” martingale problems do not correspond to linear SDE’s as we shall see below. 

The characteristics of a $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ -valued semimartingale X can be defined in several equivalent ways. In the following definition they occur in an equation which resembles (2.2). 

Definition 1. Suppose that B is a predictable $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ -valued process, $C$ a predictable process whose values are non-negative symmetric d d matrices, both with components of finite variation, and ν a predictable random measure on $\mathbb { R } _ { + } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ~ ( i . e$ . a family $( \nu ( \omega ; \cdot ) ) _ { \omega \in \varOmega }$ of measures on $\mathbb { R } _ { + } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ with a certain predictability property, cf. JS for details). Then (B, C, ν) is called characteristics of X if and only $\begin{array} { r } { i f e ^ { i \lambda ^ { \top } X } - \int _ { 0 } ^ { \cdot } e ^ { i \lambda ^ { \top } X _ { t - } } d \varPsi _ { t } ( i \lambda ) } \end{array}$ is a local martingale for any $\boldsymbol { \lambda } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , where 

$$
\varPsi_ {t} (u) := u ^ {\top} B _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} u ^ {\top} C _ {t} u + \int_ {[ 0, t ] \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} (e ^ {u ^ {\top} x} - 1 - u ^ {\top} h (x)) \nu (d (s, x)).
$$

It can be shown that any semimartingale has unique characteristics up to a P-null set. This integral version of the characteristics can alternatively be written in diferential form. More specifically, there exist an increasing predictable process $A ,$ , predictable processes $b , c ,$ , and a transition kernel $F$ from $( \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } _ { + } , \mathscr { P } )$ into $( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , \mathcal { B } ^ { d } )$ such that 

$$
B _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} b _ {s} d A _ {s}, \quad C _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} c _ {s} d A _ {s}, \quad \nu ([ 0, t ] \times G) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} F _ {s} (G) d A _ {s}, \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {d}.
$$

This decomposition ${ \mathrm { i s } } ,$ of course, not unique. However, in most applications the characteristics $( B , C , \nu )$ are actually absolutely continuous, which means that one may choose $A _ { t } = t .$ . In this case we call the triplet $( b , c , F )$ diferential characteristics of X. It is unique up to some $P ( d \omega )$ dt-null set. 

Definition 2. Suppose that b is a predictable $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ -valued process, c a predictable process whose values are non-negative symmetric d d matrices, and $F$ a transition kernel from $( \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } _ { + } , \mathscr { P } )$ to $( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , \mathcal { B } ^ { d } )$ such that $F _ { \cdot } ( \{ 0 \} ) = 0$ and $\textstyle \int ( 1 \wedge | x | ^ { 2 } ) F . ( d x ) < \infty$ . We call the triplet $( b , c , F )$ diferential characteristics of X $\begin{array} { r } { i f e ^ { i \lambda ^ { \top } X } - \int _ { 0 } ^ { \cdot } e ^ { i \lambda ^ { \top } X _ { t - } } \psi _ { t } ( i \lambda ) } \end{array}$ dt is a local martingale for any $\lambda \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , where 

$$
\psi_ {t} (u) := u ^ {\top} b _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} u ^ {\top} c _ {t} u + \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} (e ^ {u ^ {\top} x} - 1 - u ^ {\top} h (x)) F _ {t} (d x)
$$

denotes the L´evy exponent of $( b , c , F ) ( \omega , t )$ . For want of a handy notation in the literature, we write $\partial X : = ( b , c , F )$ in this case. 

From an intuitive viewpoint one can interpret the diferential characteristics as a local L´evy–Khintchine triplet. Very loosely speaking, a semimartingale with diferential characteristics $( b , c , F )$ resembles locally after t a L´evy process with triplet $( b , c , F ) ( \omega , t )$ . Since this local behaviour may depend on the history up to $t ,$ the diferential characteristics may be random albeit predictable. In this sense, the connection between L´evy processes and diferential characteristics parallels the one between linear functions and derivatives of deterministic functions. In fact, b equals the ordinary derivative if X has absolutely continuous paths (and $c = 0 , F = 0$ in this case). As is well-known, X is a L´evy process if and only if the diferential characteristics are deterministic and constant (cf. JS, II.4.19): 

Proposition 1 (L´evy process). A $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } .$ -valued semimartingale $X , X _ { 0 } = 0 \quad$ is a L´evy process if and only if it has a version $( b , c , F )$ of the diferential characteristic which does not depend on $( \omega , t )$ . In this case, $( b , c , F )$ equals the L´evy-Khintchine triplet. 

As for the ordinary derivative, a number of rules allows to calculate the diferential characteristics comfortably by using $\mathrm { L e v y }$ processes as building blocks. 

Proposition 2 (Stochastic integration). Let X be a $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ -valued semimartingale and $\dot { \textbf { \textit { H } } } a \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times d }$ -valued predictable process with $H ^ { j \cdot } \in \ U ^ { \chi } )$ , $j = 1 , \ldots , n ( i . e$ . integrable with respect to $X )$ $I f \partial X = ( b , c , F )$ , then the diferential characteristics of the $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ -valued integral process 

$$
H \cdot X := (H ^ {j \cdot} \cdot X) _ {j = 1, \dots , n}
$$

equals $\partial ( H \bullet X ) = ( \widetilde { b } , \widetilde { c } , \widetilde { F } )$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \widetilde {b} _ {t} = H _ {t} b _ {t} + \int (\widetilde {h} (H _ {t} x) - H _ {t} h (x)) F _ {t} (d x), \\ \widetilde {c} _ {t} = H _ {t} c _ {t} H _ {t} ^ {\top}, \\ \widetilde {F} _ {t} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (H _ {t} x) F _ {t} (d x), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {n}. \end{array}
$$

Here, $\widetilde { h } : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ denotes the truncation function which is used on $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ 

Variants of Proposition $2$ are stated in JS, IX.5.3 or $[ 1 7 ]$ , Lemma 3. The efect of $C ^ { 2 }$ -functions on the characteristics follows directly from Itˆo’s formula (cf. [9], Corollary A.6): 

Proposition 3 $( C ^ { 2 } .$ -function). Let X be a $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ -valued semimartingale with diferential characteristics $\partial X = ( b , c , F )$ . Suppose that $f : U \to \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is twice continuously diferentiable on some open subset $U \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ such that $X , X _ { - }$ are U-valued. Then the $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ -valued semimartingale $f ( X )$ has diferential characteristics $\partial ( f ( X ) ) = ( \widetilde { b } , \widetilde { c } , \widetilde { F } )$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {b} _ {t} ^ {i} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {d} \partial_ {k} f ^ {i} (X _ {t -}) b _ {t} ^ {k} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {k, l = 1} ^ {d} \partial_ {k l} f ^ {i} (X _ {t -}) c _ {t} ^ {k l} \\ \qquad + \int \left(\widetilde {h} ^ {i} \left(f (X _ {t -} + x) - f (X _ {t -})\right) - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {d} \partial_ {k} f ^ {i} (X _ {t -}) h ^ {k} (x)\right) F _ {t} (d x), \\ \widetilde {c} _ {t} ^ {i j} = \sum_ {k, l = 1} ^ {d} \partial_ {k} f ^ {i} (X _ {t -}) c _ {t} ^ {k l} \partial_ {l} f ^ {j} (X _ {t -}), \\ \widetilde {\nu} _ {t} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} \left(f (X _ {t -} + x) - f (X _ {t -})\right) F _ {t} (d x), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {n}. \end{array}

A Girsanov-type theorem due to Jacod and M´emin studies the behaviour of the characteristics under absolutely continuous changes of the probability measure (cf. JS, III.3.24). We state here the following version. 

Proposition 4 (Change of the probability measure). Let X be a $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ valued semimartingale with diferential characteristics $\partial X = ( b , c , F )$ ). Suppose that $ { \widetilde { P } } \ll  { \mathcal { P } }$ with the density process

Z = \mathcal {E} (H \bullet X ^ {c} + W * (\mu^ {X} - \nu^ {X}))\tag{2.4}

In applications, the density process can typically be stated in the form (2.4). Alternatively, one may use a version of Proposition 4 where $( \widetilde { b } , \widetilde { c } , \widetilde { F } )$ is ex-* * *pressed in terms of the joint characteristics of (X, Z) (cf. [15], Lemma 5.1). 

Finally, we consider the efect of absolutely continuous time changes (cf. [17], Lemma 5 and [11], Chapter 10 for details). They play an important role in SV models as we shall see in Section 4. 

Proposition 5 (Absolutely continuous time change). Let X be $a \mathbb { R } ^ { d } .$ valued semimartingale with diferential characteristics $\partial X = ( b , c , F )$ . Suppose that $( T _ { \theta } ) _ { \theta \in \mathbb { R } . }$ + is a finite, absolutely continuous time change $( i . e . \ T _ { \theta }$ is a finite stopping time for any θ and $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { \theta } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \theta } \dot { T } _ { \rho } d \rho } \end{array}$ with non-negative derivative $\dot { T } _ { \rho } )$ 

Then the time-changed process $( \widetilde { X } _ { \theta } ) _ { \theta \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } } : = ( ( X \circ T ) _ { \theta } ) _ { \theta \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } } : = ( X _ { T _ { \theta } } ) _ { \theta \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } }$ + *is a semimartingale relative to the time-changed filtration

$$

with diferential characteristics $\partial \widetilde { X } = ( \widetilde { b } , \widetilde { c } , \widetilde { F } )$ given by

\begin{array}{r} \widetilde {b} _ {\theta} = b _ {T _ {\theta}} \dot {T} _ {\theta}, \\ \widetilde {c} _ {\theta} = c _ {T _ {\theta}} \dot {T} _ {\theta}, \\ \widetilde {F} _ {\theta} (G) = F _ {T _ {\theta}} (G) \dot {T} _ {\theta}, G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {n}. \end{array}

Let us now turn to the stochastic counterpart of the initial value problem (2.1), where the local dynamics of X are expressed in terms of X itself. This can be interpreted as a special case of a martingale problem in the sense of JS, III.2.4 and III.2.18. 

Definition 3. Suppose that $P _ { 0 }$ is a distribution on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and functions $\beta : \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times$ $\mathbb { R } _ { + } \ \to \ \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , \ \gamma : \ \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } _ { + } \ \to \ \mathbb { R } ^ { d \times d } , \ \varphi : \ \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } _ { + } \times \ \mathbb { B } ^ { d } \ \to \ \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ are given. 

We call $( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \mathbf { F } , P , X )$ solution to the martingale problem related to $P _ { 0 }$ and $( \beta , \gamma , \varphi )$ if X is a semimartingale on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mathbf { F } , P )$ such that $\mathcal { L } ( X _ { 0 } ) = P _ { 0 }$ and $\partial X = ( b , c , F )$ with 

$$
\begin{array}{c} b _ {t} (\omega) = \beta (X _ {t -} (\omega), t), \\ c _ {t} (\omega) = \gamma (X _ {t -} (\omega), t), \\ F _ {t} (\omega , G) = \varphi (X _ {t -} (\omega), t, G). \end{array}\tag{2.5}
$$

More in line with the common language of martingale problems, one may also call the distribution $P ^ { X }$ of $X$ solution to the martingale problem. In any case, uniqueness refers only to the law $P ^ { X }$ because solution processes on diferent probability spaces cannot be reasonably compared otherwise. 

Since ODE’s are particular cases of this kind of martingale problems, one cannot expect that unique solutions generally exist, let alone to solve them (cf. JS, III.2c and [11] in this respect). In this note we will only consider particularly simple martingale problems, namely linear and afine ones. 

## 3 Afine processes

Parallel to afine ODE’s, we assume that the diferential characteristics (2.5) are afine functions of $X _ { t - }$ in the following sense: 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta ((x ^ {1}, \ldots , x ^ {d}), t) = \beta_ {0} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {d} x ^ {j} \beta_ {j}, \\ \gamma ((x ^ {1}, \ldots , x ^ {d}), t) = \gamma_ {0} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {d} x ^ {j} \gamma_ {j}, \\ \varphi ((x ^ {1}, \ldots , x ^ {d}), t, G) = \varphi_ {0} (G) + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {d} x ^ {j} \varphi_ {j} (G), \end{array}\tag{3.1}
$$

where $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , \ldots , d$ are given L´evy–Khintchine triplets on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . As in the deterministic case, it is possible not only to prove existence of a unique solution but also to solve the afine martingale problem related to (3.1) in a sense explicitly. This has been done by DFS. More precisely, they characterize afine Markov processes and their laws. However, applied to the present setup one obtains the statement below on afine martingale problems (cf. Theorem 3.1). 

It is obvious that the d + 1 L´evy–Khintchine triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } )$ cannot be chosen arbitrarily. It has to be ensured that the local covariance matrix c and the local jump measure $F$ in the diferential characteristics $\partial X = ( b , c , F )$ of the solution remain positive even if some of the components $X ^ { j }$ turn negative. This leads to a number of conditions: 

Definition 4. Let m, $ { n _ { \mathrm { ~ \scriptsize ~ \in ~ \mathbb ~ \mathbb ~ \mathbb \Lambda ~ } } }$ with $m + n \ = \ d .$ . L´evy–Khintchine triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , \dots , d$ are called admissible if the following conditions hold: 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} \beta_ {j} ^ {k} - \int h ^ {k} (x) \varphi_ {j} (d x) \geq 0 \\ \varphi_ {j} ((\mathbb {R} _ {+} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {n}) ^ {C}) = 0 \\ \int h ^ {k} (x) \varphi_ {j} (d x) <   \infty \\ \gamma_ {j} ^ {k l} = 0 & i f 0 \leq j \leq m, \quad 1 \leq k \leq m, \quad k \neq j; \\ \beta_ {j} ^ {k} = 0 & i f 0 \leq j \leq m, \quad 1 \leq k, l \leq m \quad u n l e s s k = l = j; \\ \gamma_ {j} = 0 \\ \varphi_ {j} = 0 \end{array} \right\}
$$

A deep result of DFS shows that the martingale problem related to (3.1) has a unique solution for essentially any admissible choice of triplets: 

Theorem 3.1. Let $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , \ j = 0 , \ldots , d ,$ be admissible L´evy–Khintchine triplets and denote $b y \ \psi _ { j }$ the corresponding L´evy exponents in the sense of (2.2). Suppose in addition that 

$$
\int_ {\{| x | \geq 1 \}} | x | ^ {k} \varphi_ {j} (d x) <   \infty , \quad 1 \leq j, k \leq m.\tag{3.2}
$$

Then the martingale problem related to $( \beta , \gamma , \varphi )$ as in $( 3 . 1 )$ and any initial distribution $P _ { 0 }$ on $\mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ has a solution $\left( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mathbf { F } , P , X \right)$ , where X is $\mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ -valued. Its distribution is uniquely characterized $b y$ its conditional characteristic function 

$$
E \left(e ^ {i \lambda^ {\top} X _ {s + t}} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {s}\right) = \exp \left(\Psi^ {0} (t, i \lambda) + \Psi^ {(1, \dots , d)} (t, i \lambda) ^ {\top} X _ {s}\right), \quad \lambda \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d},\tag{3.3}
$$

where the mappings $\psi ^ { ( 1 , \dots , d ) } = \bigl ( \psi ^ { 1 } , \dots , \psi ^ { d } \bigr ) : \mathbb { R } _ { + } \times \bigl ( \mathbb { C } _ { - } ^ { m } \times i \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \bigr ) \to \bigl ( \mathbb { C } _ { - } ^ { m } \times i \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \bigr )$ and $\varPsi ^ { 0 } : \mathbb R _ { + } \times ( \mathbb C _ { - } ^ { m } \times i \mathbb R ^ { n } ) \to \mathbb C$ solve the following system of generalized Riccati equations: 

$$
\varPsi^ {0} (0, u) = 0, \quad \varPsi^ {(1, \dots , d)} (0, u) = u,
$$

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \varPsi^ {j} (t, u) = - \psi_ {j} (\varPsi^ {(1, \dots , d)} (t, u)), \quad j = 0, \dots , d\tag{3.4}
$$

$$
(a n d \mathbb {C} _ {-} ^ {m} := \{z \in \mathbb {C} ^ {m}: \operatorname{Re} (z ^ {j}) \leq 0, j = 1, \dots , m \}).
$$

Proof. Up to two details, the assertion follows directly from DFS, Theorems 2.7, 2.12 and Lemma 9.2. Equation (3.3) is derived in DFS under the additional assumptions that the initial distribution is of degenerate form $P _ { 0 } = \epsilon _ { x }$ for $x \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and that the filtration F is generated by X. Hence, it sufices to reduce the general statement to this case. 

Let $( \mathbb { D } ^ { d } , \mathcal { D } ^ { d } , \mathbf { D } ^ { d } )$ be the Skorohod path space of R<sup>d</sup>-valued c`adl`ag functions on $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ endowed with its natural filtration (cf. JS, Chapter VI). Denote by Y the canonical process, i.e. $Y _ { t } ( \alpha ) = \alpha ( t )$ for α $\ b { \mathscr { r } } \in \mathbb { D } ^ { d }$ 

Fix $s \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } , \omega \in \varOmega$ . From the characterization in Definition 1 (more precisely, from the slightly more general formulation in JS, II.2.42, because we do not know in the first place that Y is a semimartingale) it follows that $Y$ has diferential characteristics of the form (2.5) and (3.1) relative to the probability measure $\widetilde { P } _ { s , \omega } : = P ^ { ( X _ { s + t } ) _ { t \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } } | \mathcal { F } _ { s } } ( \omega , \cdot )$ on $( \mathbb { D } ^ { d } , \mathcal { D } ^ { d } )$ (except for some P-null set of $\omega \mathrm { { s } } )$ *. Therefore, Y solves the afine martingale problem corresponding to (3.1) and it has degenerate initial distribution $\tilde { P } _ { s , \omega } ^ { Y _ { 0 } } = \epsilon _ { X _ { s } ( \omega ) }$ . Theorem 2.12 in DFS yields that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left(e ^ {i \lambda^ {\top} X _ {s + t}} \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {s}\right) (\omega) = \widetilde {E} _ {s, \omega} e ^ {i \lambda^ {\top} Y _ {t}} \\ \qquad = \widetilde {E} _ {s, \omega} \left(\widetilde {E} _ {s, \omega} \left(e ^ {i \lambda^ {\top} Y _ {t}} \Big | \mathcal {D} _ {0}\right)\right) \\ \qquad = \widetilde {E} _ {s, \omega} \exp \left(\varPsi^ {0} (t, i \lambda) + \varPsi^ {(1, \dots , d)} (t, i \lambda) ^ {\top} Y _ {0}\right), \\ \qquad = \exp \left(\varPsi^ {0} (t, i \lambda) + \varPsi^ {(1, \dots , d)} (t, i \lambda) ^ {\top} X _ {s} (\omega)\right) \end{array}
$$

for P-almost all $\omega \in \varOmega$ 

## Remarks.

1. The restriction $X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { m } \geq 0$ has to be naturally imposed because otherwise $\gamma ( X _ { t - } , t ) , \varphi ( X _ { t - } , t , G )$ in (3.1) may turn negative which does not make sense. The remaining n components $X ^ { m + 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d }$ , on the other hand, afect the characteristics of X only through the drift rate $\beta _ { j }$ . Due to the conditions $\gamma _ { j } = 0 , \varphi _ { j } = 0 , j \geq m + 1$ , parts of the ODE system (3.4) are reduced actually to simple integrals and linear equations which can be solved in closed form (cf. (2.13)–(2.15) in DFS and Corollary 3.2 below for a special case). 

2. Condition (3.2) guaranties that the solution process does not explode in finite time and hence is a semimartingale on $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ in the usual sense. It can be relaxed by a weaker necessary and suficient condition (cf. DFS, Proposition 9.1). 

3. By introducing the zeroth component $X _ { t } ^ { 0 } = 1$ , it is easy to see that an afine process in $\mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ can be interpreted as a process with linear characteristics in $\mathring { \mathbb { R } } _ { + } ^ { 1 + m } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 1 + d }$ . Since the solution to linear ODE’s are exponential functions, one could be tempted to call the solutions to such linear martingale problems “stochastic exponentials.” However, this notion usually refers to the solutions to linear SDE’s and the latter typically do not have linear characteristics. For example, Propositions 1 and 2 yield that the diferential characteristics of the geometric Wiener process $\begin{array} { r } { { \bf \tilde { \cal X } } _ { t } \ = \ 1 + \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } { \cal X } _ { s } d W _ { s } } \end{array}$ are of the form $\partial X = ( 0 , X ^ { 2 } , 0 )$ . Hence they are quadratic rather than linear in X. 

4. Observe that the solution depends on the involved triplets only through their L´evy exponents, which is agreeable for concrete models where the latter are known in closed form. 

For such applications as, e.g., estimation purposes it is useful to dispose of a closed form expression of the finite-dimensional marginals. It follows by induction from Theorem 3.1. 

Corollary 3.1. The joint characteristic function of $X _ { t _ { 1 } } , \ldots , X _ { t _ { \nu } }$ is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \exp \left(i \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\nu} \lambda^ {k \cdot} X _ {t _ {k}}\right) \\ = \hat {P} _ {0} \left(\Psi_ {\nu} (t _ {1} - t _ {0}, \ldots , t _ {\nu} - t _ {\nu - 1}; i \lambda^ {1 \cdot}, \ldots , i \lambda^ {\nu \cdot})\right) \exp \left(\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\nu} \Psi^ {0} (t _ {k} - t _ {k - 1}, i \lambda^ {k \cdot})\right). \end{array}
$$

for any $0 = t _ { 0 } \leq t _ { 1 } \leq \cdot \cdot \cdot \leq t _ { \nu }$ and any $\lambda \in \mathbb { R } ^ { \nu \times d }$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { P } _ { 0 } ( u ) : = \int e ^ { u x } P _ { 0 } ( d x ) } \end{array}$ and $\varPsi _ { \nu }$ is defined recursively via 

$$
\varPsi_ {1} (\tau_ {1}; u _ {1}) := \varPsi^ {(1, \dots , d)} (\tau_ {1}, u _ {1})
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varPsi_ {k} (\tau_ {1}, \ldots , \tau_ {k}; u _ {1}, \ldots , u _ {k}) \\ := \varPsi_ {k - 1} \left(\tau_ {1}, \ldots , \tau_ {k - 1}; u _ {1}, \ldots , u _ {k - 2}, u _ {k - 1} + \varPsi^ {(1, \ldots , d)} (\tau_ {k}, u _ {k})\right). \end{array}
$$

Since an afine process is characterized by at most $d + 1$ L´evy–Khintchine triplets, one may wonder whether it can in fact be expressed pathwise in terms of $d + 1 \ \mathrm { L e v y }$ processes with the corresponding triplets. We give a partial answer to this question. 

Theorem 3.2 (Time change representation of afine processes). Let X be an afine process as in Theorem 3.1. On a possibly enlarged probability space, there exist intrinsic $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ -valued L´evy processes $L ^ { \left( j \right) }$ with triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , \ldots , d .$ , such that 

$$
X _ {t} = X _ {0} + L _ {t} ^ {(0)} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {d} L _ {\Theta_ {t} ^ {j}} ^ {(j)},\tag{3.5}
$$

where 

$$
\Theta_ {t} ^ {j} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {s -} ^ {j} d s.\tag{3.6}
$$

## 4 Afine stochastic volatility models

In the empirical literature, a number of so-called stylized facts has been reported repeatedly, namely semi-heavy tails in the return distribution, volatility clustering, and a negative correlation between changes in volatility and asset prices (leverage efect). These features are reflected in the SV models that have been suggested. At the same time, it seems desirable to work in settings which are analytically tractable. Here, afine models play an important role. The fact that the characteristic function is known in closed or semiclosed form opens the door to derivative pricing, calibration, hedging, and estimation. 

If the model is set up under the risk-neutral measure, European option prices can be computed by Laplace transform methods. This approach relies on the fact that the characteristic function or Laplace transform can be interpreted as a set of prices of complex-valued contingent claims. A large class of arbitrary payofs can be represented explicitly as a linear combination or, more precisely, integral of such “simple” claims (cf. e.g. [4], [20]). As far as estimation is concerned, the knowledge of the joint characteristic function can be exploited for generalized moment estimators (cf. [13] and [26] for an overview). 

Typically, (broad-sense) stochastic volatility models fall into two groups. Either market activity is expressed in terms of the time-varying size or magnitude of price movements, or alternatively, by their speed or arrival rate. The models of the first group are often stated in terms of an equation 

$$
d X _ {t} = \sigma_ {t} d L _ {t},\tag{4.1}
$$

possibly modified by an additional drift term. Here, X denotes the logarithm of an asset price and L a L´evy process as, e.g., Brownian motion. In this equation, the SV process σ afects the size of relative price moves. 

Models of the second kind arise from time-changed L´evy processes 

$$
X _ {t} = X _ {0} + L _ {V _ {t}}.\tag{4.2}
$$

Again, L denotes a L´evy process and X the logarithm of the asset price. Here, the time change $\begin{array} { r } { V _ { t } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } v _ { s } d s } \end{array}$ afects the speed of price moves. Often V is interpreted as business time. Measured on this operational time scale, log prices evolve homogeneously but due to randomly changing trading activity $v _ { t }$ , this is not true relative to calender time. 

If the L´evy process L is a Wiener process and if $L , \sigma$ , respectively $L , v ,$ are independent, then the two approaches lead essentially to the same models. This fact is due to the self-similarity of Brownian motion and it is reflected by Propositions 2 and 5. where the choice $v _ { t } = \sigma _ { t } ^ { 2 }$ leads to the same dif ferential characteristics of X in either case. Again due to self-similarity, the correspondence between (4.1) and (4.2) remains true for α-stable L´evy motions L. In this case, $v _ { t } = \sigma _ { t } ^ { \alpha }$ leads to the same characteristics (cf. also [17] in this respect). For general L´evy processes, however, (4.1) and (4.2) lead to quite diferent models because the change of measure in Proposition 2 does not lead to a multiple of F as in Proposition 5. Except for α-stable L´evy motions L, models of type (4.1), in general, do not lead to afine processes. Typically, the distribution of X is not known in closed form. 

Another important distinction refers to the sources of randomness that drive the L´evy process L and the volatility process σ resp. v in (4.1) and (4.2). In the simplest case, these two are supposed to be independent. This, however, excludes the above-mentioned leverage efect, i.e. it does not allow for negative correlation between volatility and asset price changes. Whereas such a correlation can be incorporated easily in models of type (4.1), this is less obvious in (4.2) because L and v live on diferent time scales (business vs. calender time). 

The other extreme would be to use a common source of randomness for both L and σ or L and v, respectively. This can be interpreted in the sense that changes in volatility are caused by changes in asset prices. This spirit underlies the ARCH-type models in the econometric literature. An interesting and natural continuous-time extension of GARCH(1,1) has recently been suggested in [18]. But since ARCH models are based on rescaling the innovations in the sense of (4.1), they do not lead to an afine structure. Nevertheless, the idea to use a common driver for volatility and price moves can be carried out in the context of afine processes as well (cf. Subsection 4.6). 

We will now discuss a number of well-known afine SV models from the point of view of characteristics. For a more exhaustive coverage of the literature, see DFS and [5]. We express the characteristics of the afine processes in terms of triplets (3.1). By straightforward insertion one can derive closed-form expressions for the corresponding L´evy exponents $\psi _ { j } , j = 0 , \ldots , d ,$ , in terms of the L´evy exponents of the involved L´evy processes and the additional parameters in the corresponding model. 

In all the examples, it is implicitly assumed that the filtration is generated by the afine process under consideration (cf. the last remark of Subsection 4.8 in this context). Moreover, we assume generally that the identity $h ( x ) = x$ is used as “truncation” function because this simplifies some of the expressions considerably. This choice implies that the corresponding L´evy measures have first moments in the tails. The general formulation without such moment assumptions can be derived immediately from (2.3). 

## 4.1 Stein and Stein (1991)

Slightly generalized, the model in [24] is of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{r} d X _ {t} = (\mu + \delta \sigma_ {t} ^ {2}) d t + \sigma_ {t} d W _ {t}, \\ d \sigma_ {t} = (\kappa - \lambda \sigma_ {t}) d t + \alpha d Z _ {t} \end{array}\tag{4.3}
$$

with constants $\kappa \geq 0 , \mu , \delta , \lambda , \ :$ α and Wiener processes W, Z having constant correlation $\rho .$ As can be seen from straightforward application of Propositions 

1-3, neither $( \sigma , X )$ nor $( \sigma ^ { 2 } , X )$ have afine characteristics in the sense of (3.1) unless the parameters are chosen in a very specific way $( \mathrm { e . g . ~ } \kappa = 0 )$ . However, the $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ -valued process $( \sigma , \sigma ^ { 2 } , X )$ is “almos $\mathrm { t } ^ { \dag }$ the solution to an afine martingale problem related with (3.1), namely, for $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , \ldots , 3$ , given by 

$$
(\beta_ {0}, \gamma_ {0}, \varphi_ {0}) = \left(\binom{\kappa}{\alpha^ {2}} _ {\mu}, \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \alpha^ {2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right), 0\right),
$$

$$
(\beta_ {1}, \gamma_ {1}, \varphi_ {1}) = \left(\left( \begin{array}{c} - \lambda \\ 2 \kappa \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 0 & 2 \alpha^ {2} & \alpha \rho \\ 2 \alpha^ {2} & 0 & 0 \\ \alpha \rho & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right), 0\right),
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = \left(\left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ - 2 \lambda \\ \delta \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \alpha^ {2} & 2 \alpha \rho \\ 0 & 2 \alpha \rho & 1 \end{array} \right), 0\right), \\ (\beta_ {3}, \gamma_ {3}, \varphi_ {3}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

Since $\gamma _ { 1 }$ is not non-negative definite, $( \beta _ { 1 } , \gamma _ { 1 } , \varphi _ { 1 } )$ is not a L´evy–Khintchine triplet in the usual sense and hence Theorem 3.1 cannot be applied. Nevertheless, the Riccati-type equation (3.4) leads to the correct characteristic function in this case (see, e.g., the derivation in [22]). The process $( \sigma , \sigma ^ { 2 } , X )$ is closely related to the non-degenerate example in DFS, Subsection 12.2 of an afine Markov process with a non-standard maximal domain. 

## 4.2 Heston (1993)

If κ is chosen to be 0 in the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation (4.3), then the Stein and Stein model reduces to a special case of the model in [10]: 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d X _ {t} = (\mu + \delta v _ {t}) d t + \sqrt {v _ {t}} d W _ {t}, \\ d v _ {t} = (\kappa - \lambda v _ {t}) d t + \sigma \sqrt {v _ {t}} d Z _ {t}. \end{array}\tag{4.4}
$$

Here, $\kappa \geq 0 , \mu , \delta , \lambda , \sigma$ denote constants and $W , Z$ Wiener processes with constant correlation $\rho .$ Calculation of the characteristics yields that $( v , X )$ is an afine process with triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ , in (3.1) given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\beta_ {0}, \gamma_ {0}, \varphi_ {0}) = \left(\binom{\kappa}{\mu}, 0, 0\right), \\ (\beta_ {1}, \gamma_ {1}, \varphi_ {1}) = \left(\binom{- \lambda}{\delta}, \left( \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & \sigma \rho \\ \sigma \rho & 1 \end{array} \right), 0\right), \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

## 4.3 Barndorf-Nielsen and Shephard (2001)

In the article [1] (henceforth BNS) it is considered a model of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{r} d X _ {t} = (\mu + \delta v _ {t -}) d t + \sqrt {v _ {t -}} d W _ {t} + \rho d Z _ {t}, \\ d v _ {t} = - \lambda v _ {t -} d t + d Z _ {t}. \end{array}\tag{4.5}
$$

Here, $\mu , \delta , \rho , \lambda$ denote constants, W a Wiener processes, and $Z \mathrm { ~ a ~ }$ subordinator (i.e. an increasing L´evy process) with L´evy–Khintchine triplet $( b ^ { Z } , 0 , F ^ { Z } )$ Compared to the Heston model, the square-root process (4.4) is replaced with a L´evy-driven Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process. Since W and $Z$ are necessarily independent, leverage is introduced by the $\rho d Z _ { t }$ term. Again, Propositions 1 and 2 yield that $( v , X )$ is an afine process with triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } )$ $j = 0 , 1 , 2$ , in (3.1) of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta_ {0} = \binom{b ^ {Z}}{\mu + \rho b ^ {Z}}, \quad \gamma_ {0} = 0, \quad \varphi_ {0} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (y, \rho y) F ^ {Z} (d y), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2}, \\ (\beta_ {1}, \gamma_ {1}, \varphi_ {1}) = \left(\binom{- \lambda}{\delta}, \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right), 0\right), \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

Due to the simple structure of the characteristics, we are in the situation of Corollary 3.2. 

BNS consider also a slightly extended version of the above model. They argue that the autocorrelation pattern of volatility is not appropriately matched by a single OU process. As a way out they suggest a linear combination of independent OU processes, i.e. a model of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d X _ {t} = (\mu + \delta v _ {t -}) d t + \sqrt {v _ {t -}} d W _ {t} + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\nu} \rho_ {k} d Z _ {t} ^ {k}, \\ v _ {t} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\nu} \alpha_ {k} v _ {t} ^ {(k)}, \\ d v _ {t} ^ {(k)} = - \lambda_ {k} v _ {t -} ^ {(k)} d t + d Z _ {t} ^ {k}, \end{array}
$$

with constants $\alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { \nu } \geq 0 , \ \mu , \delta , \rho _ { 1 } , \ldots , \rho _ { \nu } , \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { \nu } , $ a Wiener processes $W$ , and a $\mathbb { R } ^ { \nu }$ -valued L´evy process Z with triplet $( b ^ { Z } , 0 , F ^ { Z } )$ whose components are independent subordinators. $( v ^ { ( 1 ) } , \ldots , \bar { v } ^ { ( \nu ) } , \dot { v } , X )$ is $\mathrm { ~ a ~ } \mathbb { R } ^ { \nu + 2 }$ -valued afine process whose triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , \ldots , \nu + 2$ are of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta_ {0} = \left( \begin{array}{c} b ^ {Z ^ {1}} \\ \vdots \\ b ^ {Z ^ {\nu}} \\ \sum_ {k} \alpha_ {k} b ^ {Z ^ {k}} \\ \mu + \sum_ {k} \rho_ {k} b ^ {Z ^ {k}} \end{array} \right), \quad \gamma_ {0} = 0, \\ \varphi_ {0} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (y ^ {1}, \ldots , y ^ {\nu}, \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\nu} \alpha_ {k} y ^ {k}, \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\nu} \rho_ {k} y ^ {k}) F ^ {Z} (d y), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {\nu + 2}, \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} (\beta_ {k}, \gamma_ {k}, \varphi_ {k}) = \left((0, \ldots , 0, - \lambda_ {k}, 0, \ldots , 0, - \alpha_ {k} \lambda_ {k}, 0) ^ {\top}, 0, 0\right), k = 1, \ldots , \nu , \\ (\beta_ {\nu + 1}, \gamma_ {\nu + 1}, \varphi_ {\nu + 1}) = \left(\left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ \delta \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right), 0\right), \\ (\beta_ {\nu + 2}, \gamma_ {\nu + 2}, \varphi_ {\nu + 2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

In order to preserve this afine structure, the subordinators $Z ^ { 1 } , \ldots , Z ^ { \nu }$ do not have to be independent. The other extreme case $Z ^ { 1 } = \dots = Z ^ { \nu }$ , leads to the realm of continuous-time ARMA processes proposed in [2]. 

## 4.4 Carr, Geman, Madan, Yor (2003)

The paper [3] (henceforth CGMY) generalizes both the Heston and the BNS model by allowing for jumps in the asset price. As noted at the beginning of this section, one must consider time changes in order to preserve the afine structure unless the driver of the asset price changes is a stable L´evy motion (cf. Subsection 4.5). 

The analogue of the Heston model is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {t} = X _ {0} + \mu t + L _ {V _ {t}} + \rho (v _ {t} - v _ {0}), \\ d V _ {t} = v _ {t} d t, \\ d v _ {t} = (\kappa - \lambda v _ {t}) d t + \sigma \sqrt {v _ {t}} d Z _ {t}, \end{array}\tag{4.6}
$$

where $\kappa \geq 0 , \mu , \rho , \lambda , \sigma$ are constants, L denotes a L´evy process with triplet $( b ^ { L } , c ^ { L } , F ^ { L } )$ and $Z$ an independent Wiener process. Again, $( v , X )$ is an afine process whose triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ meet the equations 

$$
(\beta_ {0}, \gamma_ {0}, \varphi_ {0}) = \left(\binom{\kappa}{\mu + \rho \kappa}, 0, 0\right),
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta_ {1} = \binom{- \lambda}{b ^ {L} - \rho \lambda},   \gamma_ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & \sigma^ {2} \rho \\ \sigma^ {2} \rho & \sigma^ {2} \rho^ {2} + c ^ {L} \end{array} \right),   \varphi_ {1} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (0, x) F ^ {L} (d x), \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

Observe that we recover the characteristics of the Heston model – up to a rescaling of the volatility process v – if L is chosen to be a Brownian motion with drift. 

Proof. It remains to be shown that the diferential characteristics of $( v , X )$ are as claimed above. Note that ∂v and $\partial ( L \circ V )$ are obtained from Propositions 2 and 5, respectively. For any $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } .$ -valued semimartingale Y with $\partial Y = ( b , c , F )$ 

we have $\partial Y ^ { 1 } = ( b ^ { 1 } , c ^ { 1 1 } , F ^ { 1 } )$ with $F ^ { 1 } ( G ) : = F ( ( G \setminus \{ 0 \} ) \times \mathbb { R } )$ and likewise for $Y ^ { 2 } , \mathrm { e . g . }$ , by Proposition 3. 

Since v does not jump, this yields $\begin{array} { r } { F _ { t } ( G ) = \int 1 _ { G } ( 0 , x ) F _ { t } ^ { L \circ V } ( d x ) , G \in \mathcal { B } } \end{array}$ , for the joint $\mathrm { L e v y }$ measure $F$ of $( v , L \circ V )$ . Consequently, $\partial ( v , L \circ V ) = : ( b , c , F )$ is completely determined if we know $c ^ { 1 2 } \ ( = c ^ { 2 1 } )$ . Since L is independent of Z and hence of $v ,$ it follows from some technical arguments that $\langle v , L \circ V \rangle = 0 .$ which implies that $c ^ { 1 2 } = 0$ by JS, II.2.6. Applying Proposition 3 to the mapping $f ( y , x ) = ( y , x + \rho y )$ yields $\partial ( v , X )$ in the case $\mu = 0$ . The modification $\mu \neq 0$ just afects the drift coeficient of $X$  

In order to generalize the BNS model, the square-root process (4.6) is replaced with a L´evy-driven OU process: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {t} = X _ {0} + \mu t + L _ {V _ {t}} + \rho Z _ {t}, \\ d V _ {t} = v _ {t -} d t, \\ d v _ {t} = - \lambda v _ {t -} d t + d Z _ {t}. \end{array}\tag{4.7}
$$

Here, $\mu , \rho , \lambda$ are constants and $L , Z$ denote independent L´evy processes with triplets $( b ^ { L } , c ^ { L } , \ F ^ { L } )$ and $( b ^ { Z } , 0 , F ^ { Z } )$ , respectively, and $Z$ is supposed to be increasing. The triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ , of the afine process $( v , X )$ are given by 

$$
\beta_ {0} = \binom{b ^ {Z}}{\mu + \rho b ^ {Z}}, \quad \gamma_ {0} = 0, \quad \varphi_ {0} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (y, \rho y) F ^ {Z} (d y), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2},
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta_ {1} = \binom{- \lambda}{b ^ {L}}, \quad \gamma_ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c ^ {L} \end{array} \right), \quad \varphi_ {1} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (0, x) F ^ {L} (d y), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2}, \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

For a Brownian motion with drift $L ,$ we recover the dynamics of the BNS model (4.5). As in that case, Corollary 3.2 can be applied. 

Proof. The diferential characteristics of $( v , X )$ are derived similarly as above. Again, ∂v and $\partial ( L \circ V )$ are obtained from Propositions 2 and $5 ,$ respectively. If we write $\partial ( v , L \circ V ) = : ( b , c , F )$ , then $c ^ { 1 \bar { 1 } } = 0$ and hence also $c ^ { \bar { 1 } 2 } = c ^ { 2 \bar { 1 } } = 0$ . The marginal of the instantaneous $\mathrm { L e v y }$ measure $F _ { t }$ are given by the corresponding L´evy measures of v and $L \circ V$ , respectively. Since $L$ is independent of $Z ,$ , we have that v and $L \circ V$ never jump at the same time (up to some P-null set). Consequently, F is concentrated on the coordinate axes, which implies that $\begin{array} { r } { F ( G ) \stackrel { \cdot } { = } \int 1 _ { G } ( y , 0 ) F ^ { v } ( d y ) + \int 1 _ { G } ( 0 , x ) F ^ { L \circ V } ( d x ) } \end{array}$ . As above, Proposition 3 yields the characteristics of $( v , { \tilde { X } } )$ for $\widetilde { X } : = L _ { V _ { t } } + \rho v _ { t }$ Since $d X _ { t } = d \widetilde { X } _ { t } + ( \mu + \lambda v _ { t } ) d t$ * *, a correction of the drift yields $\partial ( v , X )$  

## 4.5 Carr and Wu (2003)

The study [5] considers a modification of the Heston model where the Wiener process W is replaced by an α-stable L´evy motion L with $\alpha \in ( 1 , 2 )$ and L´evy–Khintchine triplet $( 0 , 0 , F ^ { L } )$ : 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d X _ {t} = \mu d t + v _ {t} ^ {1 / \alpha} d L _ {t}, \\ d v _ {t} = (\kappa - \lambda v _ {t}) d t + \sigma \sqrt {v _ {t}} d Z _ {t}. \end{array}
$$

The self-similarity of L is reflected by the fact that $\textstyle \int { 1 _ { G } ( c ^ { 1 / \alpha } x ) F ^ { L } ( d x ) } =$ $c F ^ { L } ( G )$ for $c > 0 , G \in \mathcal { B }$ . An application of Propositions 1 and 2 shows that $( v , X )$ is an afine process with triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ , of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (\beta_ {0}, \gamma_ {0}, \varphi_ {0}) = \left(\binom {\kappa} {\mu}, 0, 0\right), \\ \beta_ {1} = \binom {- \lambda} {0}, \quad \gamma_ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array} \right), \quad \varphi_ {1} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (0, x) F ^ {L} (d y), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2}, \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

## 4.6 Carr and Wu (2004) and afine ARCH-like models

In the paper [6] it is considered a number of models, two of which could be written in the form 

$$
X _ {t} = X _ {0} + \mu t + L _ {V _ {t}},\tag{4.8}
$$

$$
d V _ {t} = v _ {t -} d t,\tag{4.9}
$$

$$
v _ {t} = v _ {0} + \kappa t + Z _ {V _ {t}}\tag{4.10}
$$

with constants $\kappa ~ \geq ~ 0$ $\mu$ and a L´evy process $( Z , L )$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ with triplet $( b ^ { ( Z , L ) } , c ^ { ( Z , L ) } , F ^ { ( Z , L ) } )$ , where Z has only non-negative jumps and finite expected value $E ( Z _ { 1 } )$ 

Note that the above equation $\begin{array} { r } { v _ { t } = v _ { 0 } + \kappa t + Z _ { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } v _ { s } \_ d s } } \end{array}$ is implicit. It may not be evident in the first place that a unique solution to this time change equation exists. On the other hand, the afine martingale problem corresponding to triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ , of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\beta_ {0}, \gamma_ {0}, \varphi_ {0}) = \left(\binom {\kappa} {\mu}, 0, 0\right), \\ (\beta_ {1}, \gamma_ {1}, \varphi_ {1}) = \left(b ^ {(Z, L)}, c ^ {(Z, L)}, F ^ {(Z, L)}\right), \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0) \end{array}
$$

has a unique solution by Theorem 3.1. In view of Theorem 3.2, the solution process $( v , X )$ can be expressed in the form (4.8)–(4.10) for some L´evy process $( Z , L )$ with triplet $( b ^ { ( Z , \dot { L } ) } , c ^ { ( Z , L ) } , F ^ { ( Z , L ) } )$ . 

The paper [6] discusses two particular cases of the above setup, namely a joint compound Poisson process with drift $( Z , L )$ and, alternatively, the completely dependent case $Z _ { t } = - \lambda t - \sigma L _ { t }$ with constants $\lambda , \sigma$ and some totally skewed α-stable $\mathrm { L e v y }$ motion $L ,$ , where $\alpha \in ( 1 , 2 ]$ . The latter model has an ARCH-like structure in the sense that the same source of randomness L drives both the volatility and the asset price process. This extends to a more general situation where $L$ is an arbitrary L´evy process and $\varDelta Z _ { t } = f ( \varDelta L _ { t } )$ for some deterministic function $f : \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ <sub>+</sub> as e.g. $f ( x ) = x ^ { 2 }$ . If L or $f$ are asymmetric, such models allow for leverage. A drawback of this setup is that it is not of the simple structure in Corollary 3.2. Non-trivial ODE’s may have to be solved in order to obtain the characteristic function. 

## 4.7 A model with flexible leverage

Any afine SV model can be defined directly in terms of the involved L´evy– Khintchine triplets, sometimes in the simple form of Corollary 3.2. Since this leads automatically to handy formulas for characteristic functions as well as diferential characteristics, there is in principle no need for a stochastic diferential equation or the like. Still, concrete equations of the above type may be useful in order to reduce generality and to give more insight in the structure of a model. 

Observe that the dependence structure between changes in asset prices and volatility in (4.7) is quite restrictive in the sense that any rise $\varDelta Z _ { t }$ in volatility results in a perfectly correlated move $\rho \varDelta Z _ { t }$ of the asset. This cannot be relaxed easily by considering dependent $\mathrm { L e v y }$ processes $L , \ Z$ because these two live on diferent time scales. In this subsection, we suggest a class of models in the spirit of (4.7), which is more flexible as far as the leverage efect is concerned. Nevertheless, we retain the simple structure of Corollary 3.2, where no Riccatitype equations have to be solved. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} X _ {t} = X _ {0} + L _ {V _ {t}} + Y _ {t}, \\ d V _ {t} = v _ {t -} d t, \\ d v _ {t} = - \lambda v _ {t -} d t + d Z _ {t}. \end{array}\tag{4.11}
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is a constant and L a L´evy process with triplet $( b ^ { L } , c ^ { L } , F ^ { L } )$ , which is assumed to be independent of another L´evy process $( Z , Y )$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ with triplet $( b ^ { ( Z , Y ) } , c ^ { ( Z , Y ) } , F ^ { ( Z , \dot { Y } ) } )$ and $Z$ is supposed to be a subordinator. As before, $( v , X )$ is an afine process with triplets $( \beta _ { j } , \gamma _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ , given by 

$$
(\beta_ {0}, \gamma_ {0}, \varphi_ {0}) = (b ^ {(Z, Y)}, c ^ {(Z, Y)}, F ^ {(Z, Y)}),\tag{4.12}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta_ {1} = \binom{- \lambda}{b ^ {L}}, \quad \gamma_ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c ^ {L} \end{array} \right), \quad \varphi_ {1} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (0, x) F ^ {L} (d x), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2}, \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0). \end{array}
$$

Proof. This follows similarly as in Subsection 4.4. In a first step, one derives $\partial ( v , Y )$ and $\partial ( L \circ V )$ from Propositions 2 and 5. Since these two processes have zero covariation and never jump together, this leads to the joint characteristics $\partial ( v , Y , L \circ V )$ in the same way as for (4.7). Applying Proposition 3 yields $\partial ( v , X )$  

The model (4.11) remains vague about how to choose the dependence structure between Z and Y. Therefore, we consider the following more concrete special case of the above setup: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {t} = X _ {0} + \mu t + L _ {V _ {t}} + U _ {Z _ {t}}, \\ d V _ {t} = v _ {t -} d t, \\ d v _ {t} = (\kappa - \lambda v _ {t -}) d t + d Z _ {t}, \end{array}
$$

where $\kappa \geq 0 , \lambda$ are constants and $L , U , Z$ three independent L´evy processes. The triplet of L is denoted by $( b ^ { L } , c ^ { L } , F ^ { L } )$ and Z is supposed to be a subordinator which equals the sum of its jumps, i.e. with triplet $( b ^ { Z } , 0 , F ^ { Z } )$ where $\begin{array} { r } { b ^ { Z } = \int z F ^ { Z } ( d z ) } \end{array}$ . The triplets in (3.1) of the afine process (v, X) are of the form 

$$
\beta_ {0} = \binom{\kappa + b ^ {Z}}{\mu + b ^ {Z} E (U _ {1})}, \quad \gamma_ {0} = 0, \quad \varphi_ {0} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (z, x) P ^ {U _ {z}} (d x) F ^ {Z} (d z),
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \beta_ {1} = \binom{- \lambda}{b ^ {L}}, \quad \gamma_ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c ^ {L} \end{array} \right), \quad \varphi_ {1} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (0, x) \varphi^ {L} (d x), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2}, \\ (\beta_ {2}, \gamma_ {2}, \varphi_ {2}) = (0, 0, 0)  , \end{array}
$$

where $P ^ { U _ { \theta } }$ denotes the law of $U _ { \theta }$ for $\theta \in \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ . Since the structure of the corresponding L´evy exponent ψ is less obvious in this case, we express it explicitly in terms of the L´evy exponents $\psi ^ { L } , \psi ^ { U } , \psi ^ { Z }$ of $L , Z , U$ , respectively. 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \psi_ {0} (u ^ {1}, u ^ {2}) = \kappa u ^ {1} + \mu u ^ {2} + \psi^ {Z} (u ^ {1} + \psi^ {U} (u ^ {2})), \\ \psi_ {1} (u ^ {1}, u ^ {2}) = - \lambda u ^ {1} + \psi^ {L} (u ^ {2}) \end{array}
$$

Proof. To determine the triplets (4.12), it remains to derive the joint characteristics of $( \widetilde { Z } , \widetilde { Y } ) _ { t } : = ( \kappa t + Z _ { t } , \mu t + U _ { Z _ { t } } )$ . Note that $( \widetilde { Z } _ { t } - \kappa t , \widetilde { Y } _ { t } - \mu t ) = \widetilde { U } \circ Z$ * *for the R2-valued L´evy process $\widetilde { U } _ { \theta } = \left( \theta , U _ { \theta } \right)$ * * *. Here, Proposition 5 cannot be *applied because the time change Z is not continuous. But [21], Theorem 30.1, yields that $\widetilde { U } \circ Z$ is a L´evy process with triplet $( b ^ { \widetilde { U } \circ Z } , 0 , F ^ { \widetilde { U } \circ Z } )$ ), where 

$$
b ^ {\widetilde {U} \circ Z} = \binom{b ^ {Z}}{b ^ {Z} E (U _ {1})}, \quad F ^ {\widetilde {U} \circ Z} (G) = \int 1 _ {G} (z, x) P ^ {U _ {z}} (d x) F ^ {Z} (d z), \quad G \in \mathcal {B} ^ {2}.
$$

Since

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \exp \left(u ^ {1} \widetilde {Z} _ {t} + u ^ {2} \widetilde {Y} _ {t}\right) = E \left(E \left(\exp \left(u ^ {1} (\kappa t + Z _ {t}) + u ^ {2} (\mu t + U _ {Z _ {t}})\right) \big |   Z\right)\right) \\ = \exp (u ^ {1} \kappa t + u ^ {2} \mu t) E \exp \left(u ^ {1} Z _ {t} + Z _ {t} \psi^ {U} (u ^ {2})\right) \\ = \exp \left(t \left(\kappa u ^ {1} + \mu u ^ {2} + \psi^ {Z} \left(u ^ {1} + \psi^ {U} (u ^ {2})\right)\right)\right), \end{array}

the $\mathrm { L e v y }$ exponent of $( \widetilde Z , \widetilde Y )$ is given by

The L´evy exponents $\psi _ { 0 } , \psi _ { 1 }$ follow now directly from (4.12). 

To be more specific, assume that $U _ { \theta } = \rho + \sigma W _ { \theta }$ for some Wiener process $W$ and constants $\rho , \sigma _ { \mathrm { { : } } }$ , in which case $\begin{array} { r } { \psi ^ { U } ( u ) = \rho u + \frac { \sigma ^ { 2 } } { 2 } u } \end{array}$ . This means that, conditionally on an upward move $\varDelta v$ of the “volatili $\mathrm { { \bar { t y } ^ { \dag } } }$ process v, the log asset price X exhibits a Gaussian jump with mean $\rho \varDelta v$ and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 } \varDelta v$ For $\sigma = 0$ we are back in the setup of (4.7). ## 4.8 Further remarks

## Ordinary versus stochastic exponential

In the literature, positive asset prices are modelled typically either as ordinary or as stochastic exponential, i.e. 

$$
S _ {t} = S _ {0} e ^ {X _ {t}} = S _ {0} \mathcal {E} (\widetilde {X}) _ {t}.
$$

Above, we considered the first representation in terms of X or, more precisely, $X + \log ( S _ { 0 } )$ . In [16], the process $\widetilde { X }$ is called the exponential transform of X. One can compute $\widetilde { X }$ *from X and vice versa quite easily. It is well-known that $X$ *is a L´evy process if and only if $\widetilde { X }$ is a L´evy process. A similar statement *holds for the afine SV models above, where the diferential characteristics of $( v , X )$ (resp. $( v ^ { ( 1 ) } , \ldots , v ^ { ( \nu ) } , v , X )$ in the BNS case) do not depend on $X _ { t }$ . By applying Propositions 3 and 2 one observes in a straightforward manner that $( v , \tilde { X } )$ (resp. $( v ^ { ( 1 ) } , \ldots , v ^ { ( \nu ) } , v , \widetilde { X } ) )$ is afine as well. However, for purposes of * *estimation or option pricing it is often more convenient to work with $X$ rather than $\widetilde { X }$ 

## Statistical versus risk-neutral modelling

Statistical estimators based on historical data yield parameters of the mode under the physical probability measure P. By contrast, option pricing and calibration refers to expectations relative to some risk-neutral measure ${ \widetilde { P } } .$ *For both purposes, afine models ofer considerable computational advantages. Therefore one may wonder whether a given measure change preserves the afine structure. This can be checked quite easily with the help of Proposition 4. E.g., if X is a $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } .$ -valued afine process and if, in (2.4), $H _ { t } ( \omega )$ is constant and $W ( \omega , t , x )$ depends only on x, then the afine structure carries over to ${ \widetilde { P } } .$ Only the triplets in (3.1) have to be adapted accordingly. 

## Martingale property of the asset price

Suppose that the process X in the examples above denotes the logarithm of a discounted asset price. If the model is set up under some “risk-neutral” probability measure, one would like $e ^ { X }$ to be a martingale or at least a local martingale. The latter property can be directly read from the characteristics. If $\partial X = ( b , c , F )$ , then $e ^ { X }$ is a local martingale if and only if $E e ^ { X _ { 0 } } < \infty$ and 

$$
b _ {t} + \frac {c _ {t}}{2} + \int (e ^ {x} - 1 - h (x)) F _ {t} (d x) = 0, \quad t \in \mathbb {R} _ {+},\tag{4.13}
$$

(cf. [16], Theorems 2.19, 2.18). In the context of the afine SV processes $( v , X )$ in the previous examples $( { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ , in particular, with $\psi _ { 2 } = 0 )$ , Expression (4.13) equals 

$$
\psi_ {0} (0, 1) + \psi_ {1} (0, 1) v _ {t}.
$$

Since $v _ { t }$ is random, both $\psi _ { 0 } ( 0 , 1 )$ and $\psi _ { 1 } ( 0 , 1 )$ typically have to be 0 in order for $e ^ { X }$ to be a local martingale. 

It is a more delicate to decide whether $e ^ { X }$ is a true martingale. This holds automatically if X is a L´evy process (cf. [14], Lemma 4.4). In the afine case a suficient condition can be derived from DFS. 

Proposition 1. Let $( v , X )$ be an afine SV process as in the previous examples (and hence the conditions in Theorem 3.1 hold). Suppose that $( 0 , 1 ) \in U$ and $( 0 , 0 ) \in U$ for an open convex set $U \subset \mathbb { C } ^ { 2 }$ such that, for any $u \in U$ 

$$
1. \psi_ {j} (\operatorname{Re} (u)) <   \infty , \quad j = 0, 1,
$$

2. there exists an U-valued solution $\varPsi ^ { ( 1 , 2 ) } ( \cdot , u )$ on $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ to the initial value problem $( 3 . 4 )$ 

If $E e ^ { X _ { 0 } } < \infty$ and $\psi _ { 0 } ( 0 , 1 ) = 0 = \psi _ { 1 } ( 0 , 1 )$ , then $e ^ { X }$ is a martingale. 

Proof. From Lemmas 5.3, 6.5 and Theorem 2.16 in DFS it follows that (3.3) holds also for $\lambda = ( 0 , - i )$ , i.e. 

$$
E (e ^ {X _ {s + t}} | \mathcal {F} _ {s}) = \exp \left(\varPsi^ {0} (t, 0, 1) + \varPsi^ {1} (t, 0, 1) ^ {\top} (v _ {s}, X _ {s})\right) = e ^ {X _ {s}},
$$

which yields the assertion. 

The previous result carries over to the BNS case $( v ^ { ( 1 ) } , \ldots , v ^ { ( \nu ) } , v , X )$ or to more general afine situations. The point is to verify that exponential moments can actually be calculated from (3.3). 

## Observability of the volatility process

In the examples above we assumed implicitly that the afine process under consideration as, e.g., (v, X) is adapted to the given filtration. In practice, however, only the logarithmic asset price X but not the volatility process v can be observed directly. Therefore, the canonical filtration of X would be a natural choice. Fortunately, v is typically adapted to the latter if X is driven by an infinite activity process. The intuitive reason is that one can recover v in an almost sure fashion from X by observing the quadratic variation of the continuous martingale part or by counting the jumps in the purely discontinuous case (cf. e.g. [25], Theorem 1). This holds even in models with leverage as e.g. (4.7) if the L´evy measure of L has considerably more mass near the origin than the one of Z.
