$$

is defined. Direct calculations [12, Section 2.9] show that, for those $^ { g , }$ 

$$
S g (\sqrt {- 1} h) = \hat {g} (h) e ^ {\frac {1}{2} \| h \| _ {L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {\ell})} ^ {2}}.
$$

As a result, the Wick product can be interpreted as a convolution on the infinite-dimensional space $( S ) _ { - \rho } .$ 

In the study of stochastic parabolic equations, $\ell = d + 1$ , so that the generic point from $\mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ is written as $( t , x ) , t \in \mathbb { R } , x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . As was mentioned earlier, the terms of the type $f d W ( t )$ become $f \diamond \dot { W } d t$ . The precise connection between the Itˆo integral and Wick product is discussed, for example, in [12, Section 2.5]. 

As an example, consider the following equation: 

$$
u _ {t} (t, x) = a (x) u _ {x x} (t, x) + b (x) u _ {x} (t, x) + u _ {x} (t, x) \diamond \dot {W} (t, x), 0 <   t <   T, x \in \mathbb {R},\tag{3.8}
$$

with initial condition $u ( 0 , x ) = u _ { 0 } ( x )$ . In (3.8), 

(WN1) $\dot { W }$ is the white noise process on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ 

(WN2) The initial condition $u _ { 0 }$ and the coeficients $a ,$ b are bounded and have continuous bounded derivatives up to second order. 

(WN3) There exists a positive number ε such that $a ( x ) \geq \varepsilon , x \in \mathbb { R }$ 

(WN4) The second-order derivative of a is uniformly H¨older continuous. 

The equivalent Itˆo formulation of (3.8) is 

$$
d u (t, x) = \left(a (x) u _ {x x} (t, x) + b (x) u _ {x} (t, x)\right) d t + e _ {k} (x) u _ {x} (t, x) d w _ {k} (x),\tag{3.9}
$$

where $\{ e _ { k } , k \geq 1 \}$ is the Hermite basis in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ 

With $\mathcal { M } _ { k } v = e _ { k } v _ { x }$ , we see that condition (2.2) does not hold in any Sobolev space $H _ { 2 } ^ { \gamma } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . In fact, no traditional solution exists in any normal triple of Sobolev spaces. On the other hand, with a suitable definition of solution, equation (3.8) is solvable in the space $( S ) _ { - 0 }$ of Hida distributions. 

Definition 3.6 A mapping $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  ( S ) _ { - \rho }$ is called weakly diferentiable with respect to $x _ { i }$ at a point $x ^ { * } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { \ell } \ i f$ and only if there exists $U _ { i } ( x ^ { * } ) \in ( S ) _ { - \rho }$ so that, for all $\varphi \in ( S ) _ { \rho } , D _ { i } \langle u ( x ) , \varphi \rangle | _ { x = x ^ { * } } = \langle U _ { i } ( x ^ { * } ) , \varphi \rangle$ . In that case, we write $U _ { i } ( x ^ { * } ) = D _ { i } u ( x ^ { * } )$ 

Definition 3.7 A mapping u from $[ 0 , T ] \times \mathbb { R }$ to $( S ) _ { - 0 }$ is called a white noise solution of (3.8) if and only if 

1. The weak derivatives $u _ { t } , u _ { x } ,$ and $u _ { x x }$ exist, in the sense of Definition ${ \it 3 . 6 } ,$ for all $( t , x ) \in ( 0 , T ) \times \mathbb { R }$ 

2. Equality (3.8) holds $f o r \ a l l \ ( t , x ) \in ( 0 , T ) \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ 

3. $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \downarrow 0 } u ( t , x ) = u _ { 0 } ( x ) } \end{array}$ in the topology $o f \left( S \right) _ { - 0 }$ 

Theorem 3.3. Under assumptions $( W N 1 ) { - } ( W N \mathcal { 4 } )$ , there exists a white noise solution of (3.8). This solution is unique in the class of weakly measurable mappings v from $( 0 , T ) \times \mathbb { R }$ to $( S ) _ { - 0 }$ , for which there exists a non-negative integer q and a positive number K such that 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \| v (t, x) \| _ {- 0, - q} e ^ {- K x ^ {2}} d x d t <   \infty .
$$

Proof. Consider the S-transformed equation 

$$
F _ {t} (t, x; h) = a (x) F _ {x x} (t, x; h) + b (x) F _ {x} (t, x; h) + F _ {x} (t, x; h) h,\tag{3.10}
$$

$0 < t < T , \ x \in \mathbb { R } , \ h \in S ( \mathbb { R } )$ , with initial condition $F ( 0 , x ; h ) = u _ { 0 } ( x )$ . This a deterministic parabolic equation, and one can show, using the probabilistic representation of $F _ { \mathrm { { ; } } }$ , that $F , F _ { t } , F _ { x }$ , and $F _ { x x }$ belong to $\mathcal { U } ^ { 0 }$ . Then the inverse S-transform of $F$ is a solution of (3.8), and the uniqueness follows from the uniqueness for equation (3.10). The details of the proof are in [40], where a similar equation is considered for $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ 

Even though the initial condition in (3.8) is deterministic, there are no measurability restrictions on $u _ { 0 }$ for the white noise solution to exist; see [12] for more details. 

With appropriate modifications, the white noise solution can be defined for equations more general than (3.8). The solution $F = F ( t , x ; h )$ of the corresponding S-transformed equation determines the regularity of the white noise solution [12, Section 4.1]. 

Two main advantages of the white noise approach over the Hilbert space approach are: 

1. No need for parabolicity condition. 

2. No measurability restrictions on the input data. 

Still, there are substantial limitations: 

1. There seems to be little or no connection between the white noise solution and the traditional solution. While the white noise solution can, in principle, be constructed for equation (2.7), this solution will be very diferent from the traditional solution. 

2. There are no clear ways of computing the solution numerically, even with available representations of the Feynmann-Kac type [12, Chapter 4]. 

3. The white noise solution, being constructed on a special white noise probability space, is weak in the probabilistic sense. Path-wise uniqueness does not apply to such solutions because of the ”averaging” nature of the solution spaces. 

## 4 Generalized Functions on the Wiener Chaos Space

The objective of this section is to introduce the space of generalized random elements on an arbitrary stochastic basis. 

Let $\mathbb { F } = ( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { t \geq 0 } , \mathbb { P } )$ be a stochastic basis with the usual assumptions and $Y .$ , a separable Hilbert space with inner product $( \cdot , \cdot ) _ { Y }$ and an orthonormal basis $\{ y _ { k } , \ k \geq 1 \}$ . On $\mathbb { F }$ and $Y _ { z }$ , consider a cylindrical Brownian motion W, that is, a family of continuous -adapted Gaussian martingales $W _ { y } ( t ) , y \in Y$ , such that $W _ { y } ( 0 ) = 0$ and $\mathbb { E } ( W _ { y _ { 1 } } ( t ) W _ { y _ { 2 } } ( s ) ) = \operatorname* { m i n } ( t , s ) ( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } ) _ { Y }$ In particular, 

$$
w _ {k} (t) = W _ {y _ {k}} (t), k \geq 1, t \geq 0,\tag{4.1}
$$

are independent standard Wiener processes on F. 

Equivalently, instead of the process $W ,$ , the starting point can be a system of independent standard Wiener processes $\{ w _ { k } , \ k \ge 1 \}$ on F. Then, given a separable Hilbert space $Y$ with an orthonormal basis $\{ y _ { k } , \ k \ \ge \ 1 \}$ , the corresponding cylindrical Brownian motion W is defined by 

$$
W _ {y} (t) = \sum_ {k \geq 1} (y, y _ {k}) _ {Y} w _ {k} (t).\tag{4.2}
$$

Fix a non-random $T \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and denote by $\mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { W }$ the σ-algebra generated by $w _ { k } ( t ) , \ k \geq 1 , \ t < T$ . Denote by $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ the collection of $\mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { W }$ -measurable square integrable random variables. 

We now review construction of the Cameron–Martin basis in the Hilbert space $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ 

Let ${ \mathfrak { m } } = \{ m _ { k } , \ k \geq 1 \}$ be an orthonormal basis in $L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) )$ such that each $m _ { k }$ belongs to $L _ { \infty } ( ( 0 , T ) )$ ). Define the independent standard Gaussian random variables 

$$
\xi_ {i k} = \int_ {0} ^ {T} m _ {i} (s) d w _ {k} (s).
$$

Consider the collection of multi-indices 

$$
\mathcal {J} = \left\{\alpha = (\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}, i, k \geq 1): \alpha_ {i} ^ {k} \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots \}, \sum_ {i, k} \alpha_ {i} ^ {k} <   \infty \right\}.
$$

The set $\mathcal { I }$ is countable, and, for every $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ , only finitely many of $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k }$ are not equal to zero. The upper and lower indices in ${ \dot { \alpha } } _ { i } ^ { k }$ represent, respectively, the space and time components of the noise process W. For $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ , define 

$$
| \alpha | = \sum_ {i, k} \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}, \alpha ! = \prod_ {i, k} \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}!,
$$

and 

$$
\xi_ {\alpha} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \prod_ {i, k} H _ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} (\xi_ {i k}),\tag{4.3}
$$

where $H _ { n }$ is $n ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ Hermite polynomial. For example, if 

$$
\alpha = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c c c c} 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 & \dots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \dots \end{array} \right)
$$

with four non-zero entries $\alpha _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } = 1 ; ~ \alpha _ { 4 } ^ { 1 } = 3 ; ~ \alpha _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } = 2 ; ~ \alpha _ { 5 } ^ { 2 } = 4$ , then 

$$
\xi_ {\alpha} = \xi_ {2, 1} \cdot \frac {H _ {3} (\xi_ {4 , 1})}{\sqrt {3 !}} \cdot \frac {H _ {2} (\xi_ {1 , 2})}{\sqrt {2 !}} \cdot \frac {H _ {4} (\xi_ {5 , 2})}{\sqrt {4 !}}.
$$

There are two main diferences between (3.2) and (4.3): 

1. The basis (4.3) is constructed on an arbitrary probability space. 

2. In (4.3), there is a clear separation of the time and space components of the noise, and explicit presence of the time-dependent functions m<sub>i</sub> facilitates the analysis of evolution equations. 

Definition 4.1 The space $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ is called the Wiener Chaos space. The N-th Wiener Chaos is the linear subspace of $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ ), generated by $\xi _ { \alpha } , \ | { \boldsymbol { \alpha } } | = N$ 

The following is another version of the classical results of Cameron and Martin [3]. 

Theorem 4.1. The collection $\boldsymbol { \Xi } = \{ \xi _ { \alpha } , \ \alpha \in \mathcal { I } \}$ is an orthonormal basis in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ 

We refer to $\varXi$ as the Cameron–Martin basis in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ ). By Theorem 4.1, every element v of $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ can be written as 

$$
v = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} v _ {\alpha} \xi_ {\alpha},
$$

where $v _ { \alpha } = \mathbb { E } ( v \xi _ { \alpha } )$ 

We now define the space $\mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) )$ of test functions and the space $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ of X-valued generalized random elements. 

## Definition 4.2

(1) The space $\mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) )$ is the collection of elements from $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ that can be written in the form 

$$
v = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J} _ {v}} v _ {\alpha} \xi_ {\alpha}
$$

for some $v _ { \alpha } \in \mathbb { R }$ and a finite subset $\mathcal { I } _ { v }$ of $\mathcal { T }$ . 

(2) A sequence $v _ { n }$ converges to v in $\mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) )$ ) if and only if $\mathcal { I } _ { v _ { n } } \subseteq \mathcal { I } _ { v }$ for all n and lim $| v _ { n , \alpha } - v _ { \alpha } | = 0$ for all α. n→∞ 

Definition 4.3 For a linear topological space X define the space $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ of X-valued generalized random elements as the collection of continuous linear maps from the linear topological space $\mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) )$ to X. Similarly, the elements o ${ \ ' } \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) )$ are called X-valued generalized random processes. 

The element u of $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ can be identified with a formal Fourier series 

$$
u = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} u _ {\alpha} \xi_ {\alpha},
$$

where $u _ { \alpha } \in X$ are the generalized Fourier coeficients of $u .$ For such a series and $v \in \mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) )$ ), we have 

$$
u (v) = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J} _ {v}} v _ {\alpha} u _ {\alpha}.
$$

Conversely, for $u \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ , we define the formal Fourier series of u by setting $u _ { \alpha } = u ( \xi _ { \alpha } )$ . If $u \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ , then $u \in \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; \mathbb { R } )$ and $u ( v ) = \mathbb { E } ( u v )$ 

By Definition 4.3, a sequence $\{ u _ { n } , n \geq 1 \}$ converges to u in $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ if and only if $u _ { n } ( v )$ converges to u(v) in the topology of X for every $v \in \mathcal { D } ( \mathbb { W } )$ In terms of generalized Fourier coeficients, this is equivalent to $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } u _ { n , \alpha } = u _ { \alpha }$ in the topology of X for every $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ 

The construction of the space $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ can be extended to Hilbert spaces other than $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ . Let H be a real separable Hilbert space with an orthonormal basis $\{ e _ { k } , \ k \geq 1 \}$ . Define the space 

$$
\mathcal {D} (H) = \left\{v \in H: v = \sum_ {k \in \mathcal {J} _ {v}} v _ {k} e _ {k}, v _ {k} \in \mathbb {R}, \mathcal {J} _ {v} - \text { a   finite   subset   of } \{1, 2, \dots \} \right\}
$$

By definition, $v _ { n }$ converges to v in ${ \mathcal { D } } ( H )$ as $n \to \infty$ if and only if $\mathcal { I } _ { v _ { n } } \subseteq \mathcal { I } _ { v }$ for all n and $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } | v _ { n , k } - v _ { k } | = 0$ for all k. 

For a linear topological space $X , { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X )$ is the space of continuous linear maps from $\mathcal { D } ( H )$ to X. An element g of $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X )$ can be identified with a formal series $\sum _ { k \geq 1 } g _ { k } \otimes e _ { k }$ such that $g _ { k } = g ( e _ { k } ) \in X$ and, for $v \in { \mathcal { D } } ( H )$ $\begin{array} { r } { g ( v ) = \sum _ { k \in \mathcal { T } _ { v } } \mathcal { g } _ { k } \overline { { v } } _ { k } } \end{array}$ . If $X = \mathbb { R }$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { k > 1 } g _ { k } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { g = \sum _ { k > 1 } g _ { k } e _ { k } \in \sum _ { k } g _ { k } e _ { k } \ \in } \end{array}$ H and $g ( v ) \ { \stackrel { . } { = } } \ ( g , v ) _ { H }$ , the inner product in H. The space $X$ is naturally imbedded into ${ \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X ) { \mathrm { : i f ~ } } u \in X$ , then $\textstyle \sum _ { k > 1 } u \otimes e _ { k } \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X )$ 

A sequence $\begin{array} { r } { g _ { n } = \sum _ { k > 1 } g _ { n , k } \otimes e _ { k } , n \geq 1 } \end{array}$ , converges to $\begin{array} { r } { g = \sum _ { k > 1 } g _ { k } \otimes e _ { k } } \end{array}$ in $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X )$ ≥<sub>if and only if, for every</sub> $k \geq 1 .$ $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } g _ { n , k } = g _ { k }$ in the topology of X. 

A collection $\{ \mathcal { L } _ { k } , ~ k \ge 1 \}$ of linear operators from $X _ { 1 }$ to $X _ { 2 }$ naturally defines a linear operator $\mathcal { L }$ from $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X _ { 1 } )$ to $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X _ { 2 } )$ 

$$
\mathcal {L} \left(\sum_ {k \geq 1} g _ {k} \otimes e _ {k}\right) = \sum_ {k \geq 1} \mathcal {L} _ {k} (g _ {k}) \otimes e _ {k}.
$$

Similarly, a linear operator ${ \mathcal { L } } : { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X _ { 1 } ) \to { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X _ { 2 } )$ can be identified with a collection $\{ \mathcal { L } _ { k } , \ k \geq 1 \}$ of linear operators from $X _ { 1 }$ to $X _ { 2 }$ by setting $\mathcal { L } _ { k } ( u ) = \mathcal { L } ( u \otimes e _ { k } )$ . Introduction of spaces $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( H ; X )$ ) and the corresponding operators makes it possible to avoid conditions of the type (2.2). 

## 5 The Malliavin Derivative and its Adjoint

In this section, we define an analog of the Itˆo stochastic integral for generalized random processes. 

All notations from the previous section will remain in force. In particular, Y is a separable Hilbert space with a fixed orthonormal basis $\{ y _ { k } , \ k \geq 1 \}$ and $\boldsymbol { \Xi } = \{ \xi _ { \alpha } , \alpha \in \mathcal { I } \}$ , the Cameron–Martin basis in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ defined in (4.3). 

We start with a brief review of the Malliavin calculus $[ 3 7 ]$ 

The Malliavin derivative D is a continuous linear operator from 

S. Lototsky and B. Rozovskii 

$$
L _ {2} ^ {1} (\mathbb {W}) = \left\{u \in L _ {2} (\mathbb {W}): \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} | \alpha | u _ {\alpha} ^ {2} <   \infty \right\}\tag{5.1}
$$

to $L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; ( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ) \times Y ) \right)$ ). In particular, 

$$
(\mathbb {D} \xi_ {\alpha}) (t) = \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \xi_ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} m _ {i} (t) y _ {k},\tag{5.2}
$$

where $\alpha ^ { - } ( i , k )$ is the multi-index with the components 

$$
\Bigl (\alpha^ {-} (i, k) \Bigr) _ {j} ^ {l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \max (\alpha_ {i} ^ {k} - 1, 0), & \text { if   } i = j \text {   and   } k = l, \\ \alpha_ {j} ^ {l}, & \text { otherwise. } \end{array} \right.
$$

Note that, for each $t \in [ 0 , T ] , \mathbb { D } \xi _ { \alpha } ( t ) \in { \mathcal { D } } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) \times Y )$ . Using (5.2), we extend the operator D by linearity to the space $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) )$ 

$$
\mathbb {D} \left(\sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} u _ {\alpha} \xi_ {\alpha}\right) = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \left(u _ {\alpha} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \xi_ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} m _ {i} (t) y _ {k}\right).
$$

For the sake of completeness and to justify further definitions, let us establish connection between the Malliavin derivative and the stochastic Itˆo integral. 

If u is an arbitrary $\mathbf { \mathcal { F } } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted process from $L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right)$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { u ( t ) = \sum _ { k > 1 } u _ { k } ( t ) y _ { k } } \end{array}$ , where the random variable $u _ { k } ( t )$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { \dot { W } }$ -measurable for each t and $\bar { \boldsymbol { k } }$ , and 

$$
\sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \mathbb {E} | u _ {k} (t) | ^ {2} d t <   \infty .
$$

We define the stochastic Itˆo integral 

$$
U (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} (u (s), d W (s)) _ {Y} = \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} u _ {k} (s) d w _ {k} (s).\tag{5.3}
$$

Note that $U ( t )$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -measurable and $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { \Xi } | U ( t ) | ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { k > 1 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \mathbb { E } | u _ { k } ( s ) | ^ { 2 } d s . } \end{array}$ 

The next result establishes a connection between the Malliavin derivative and the stochastic Itˆo integral. 

## Lemma 5.1. Suppose that u is an $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted process from

$L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right)$ , and define the process U according to $( 5 . 3 )$ . Then, for every $t \leq T$ and $x \in \mathcal { I }$ 

$$
\mathbb {E} (U (t) \xi_ {\alpha}) = \mathbb {E} \int_ {0} ^ {t} (u (s), (\mathbb {D} \xi_ {\alpha}) (s)) _ {Y} d s.\tag{5.4}
$$

Proof. Define $\xi _ { \alpha } ( t ) = \mathbb { E } ( \xi _ { \alpha } | \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W } )$ . It is known (see [33] or Remark 8.2 below) that 

$$
d \xi_ {\alpha} (t) = \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \xi_ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (t) m _ {i} (t) d w _ {k} (t).\tag{5.5}
$$

Due to $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -measurability of $u _ { k } ( t )$ , we have 

$$
u _ {k, \alpha} (t) = \mathbb {E} \Big (u _ {k} (t) \mathbb {E} (\xi_ {\alpha} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {W}) \Big) = \mathbb {E} (u _ {k} (t) \xi_ {\alpha} (t)).\tag{5.6}
$$

The definition of U implies $\begin{array} { r } { d U ( t ) = \sum _ { k > 1 } u _ { k } ( t ) d w _ { k } ( t ) } \end{array}$ , so that, by (5.5), (5.6), and the Itˆo formula, 

$$
U _ {\alpha} (t) = \mathbb {E} (U (t) \xi_ {\alpha}) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} u _ {k, \alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s.\tag{5.7}
$$

Together with (5.2), the last equality implies (5.4). Lemma 5.1 is proved. 

Note that the coeficients $u _ { k , \alpha }$ of $u ~ \in ~ L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; H ) )$ belong to $L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) )$ ). We therefore define $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { k , \alpha , i } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } u _ { k , \alpha } ( t ) m _ { i } ( t ) d t . \mathrm { T h e n } } \end{array}$ , by (5.7), 

$$
U _ {\alpha} (T) = \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} u _ {k, \alpha^ {-} (i, k), i}.\tag{5.8}
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { U ( T ) = \sum _ { \alpha \in \mathcal { T } } U _ { \alpha } ( T ) \xi _ { \alpha } } \end{array}$ , we shift the summation index in (5.8) and conclude that 

$$
U (T) = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k} + 1} u _ {k, \alpha , i} \xi_ {\alpha^ {+} (i, k)},\tag{5.9}
$$

where 

$$
\Bigl (\alpha^ {+} (i, k) \Bigr) _ {j} ^ {l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \alpha_ {i} ^ {k} + 1, & \text { if   } i = j \text {   and   } k = l, \\ \alpha_ {j} ^ {l}, & \text { otherwise. } \end{array} \right.\tag{5.10}
$$

As a result, $U ( T ) = \delta ( u )$ , where $\delta$ is the adjoint of the Malliavin derivative, also known as the Skorohod integral (called also the Skorohod–Hitsuda integral); see [10], [37] or [38] for details. 

Lemma $5 . 1$ suggests the following definition. 

For an $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted process u from $L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ) \right)$ , let $\mathbb { D } _ { k } ^ { * } u$ be the $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted process from $L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ) \right)$ such that 

$$
\left(\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u\right) _ {\alpha} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s.\tag{5.11}
$$

If $u \in L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right) { \mathrm { ~ i s ~ } } \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W } { \mathrm { - a d a p t e d } }$ , then u is in the domain of the operator δ and $\begin{array} { r } { \delta ( u I ( s < t ) ) = \sum _ { k > 1 } ( \mathbb { D } _ { k } ^ { * } u _ { k } ) ( t ) } \end{array}$ 

We now extend the operators $\mathbb { D } _ { k } ^ { * }$ to the generalized random processes. Let X be a Banach space with norm $\| \cdot \| _ { X }$ 

Definition 5.1 If u is an X-valued generalized random process, then $\mathbb { D } _ { k } ^ { * } u$ is the X-valued generalized random process such that 

$$
\left(\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u\right) _ {\alpha} (t) = \sum_ {i} \int_ {0} ^ {t} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) d s.\tag{5.12}
$$

$I f g \in \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } \Big ( Y ; \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } \left( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) \right) \Big )$ , then $\mathbb { D } ^ { * } g$ is the X-valued generalized random process such that, $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { f o r } g = \sum _ { k > 1 } \tilde { g _ { k } } \otimes y _ { k } , \ g _ { k } \in \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) ) } \end{array}$ 

$$
(\mathbb {D} ^ {*} g) _ {\alpha} (t) = \sum_ {k} (\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} g _ {k}) _ {\alpha} (t) = \sum_ {i, k} \int_ {0} ^ {t} g _ {k, \alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) d s.\tag{5.13}
$$

Using (5.2), we get a generalization of equality (5.4): 

$$
(\mathbb {D} ^ {*} g) _ {\alpha} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} g (\mathbb {D} \xi_ {\alpha} (s)) (s) d s.\tag{5.14}
$$

Indeed, by linearity, 

$$
g _ {k} \left(\sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) \xi_ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)}\right) (s) = \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) g _ {k, \alpha^ {-} (i, k)}) (s).
$$

Theorem 5.1. $I f T < \infty$ , then $\mathbb { D } _ { k } ^ { * }$ and $\mathbb { D } ^ { * }$ are continuous linear operators. 

Proof. It is enough to show that, if $u , u _ { n } \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } \left( L _ { 2 } ( { \mathcal { F } } _ { T } ^ { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) \right)$ and lim $\ L _ { n \to \infty } \left\| u _ { \alpha } - u _ { n , \alpha } \right\| _ { L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) } = 0$ for every $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ , then, for every $k \geq 1$ and $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ 2 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \| (\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u) _ {\alpha} - (\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u _ {n}) _ {\alpha} \| _ {L _ {1} ((0, T); X)} = 0.
$$

Using (5.12), we find that 

$$
\| (\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u) _ {\alpha} - (\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u _ {n}) _ {\alpha} \| _ {X} (t) \leq \sum_ {i} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \| u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} - u _ {n, \alpha^ {-} (i, k)} \| _ {X} (s) | m _ {i} (s) | d s.
$$

Note that the sum contains finitely many terms. By assumption, $| m _ { i } ( t ) | \leq C _ { i }$ , and so 

$$
\left\| \left(\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u\right) _ {\alpha} - \left(\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} u _ {n}\right) _ {\alpha} \right\| _ {L _ {1} ((0, T); X)} \leq C (\alpha) \sum_ {i} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \| u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} - u _ {n, \alpha^ {-} (i, k)} \| _ {L _ {1} ((0, T); X)}.
$$

Theorem 5.1 is proved. 

## 6 The Wiener Chaos Solution and the Propagator

In this section we build on the ideas from [25] to introduce the Wiener Chaos solution and the corresponding propagator for a general stochastic evolution equation. The notations from Sections 4 and 5 will remain in force. It will be convenient to interpret the cylindrical Brownian motion $W$ as a collection $\{ w _ { k } , k \geq 1 \}$ of independent standard Wiener processes. As before, $T \in ( 0 , \infty )$ is fixed and non-random. Introduce the following objects: 

The Banach spaces A, X, and U such that $U \subseteq X$ 

Linear operators 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {A}: L _ {1} ((0, T); A) \to L _ {1} ((0, T); X), \\ \mathcal {M} _ {k}: L _ {1} ((0, T); A) \to L _ {1} ((0, T); X). \end{array}
$$

Generalized random processes $f \in \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } \left( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) \right)$ and $g _ { k } \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } \left( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) \right)$ 

The initial condition $u _ { 0 } \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } \left( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; U \right)$ 

Consider the deterministic equation 

$$
v (t) = v _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} v) (s) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varphi (s) d s,\tag{6.1}
$$

where $v _ { 0 } \in U$ and $\varphi \in L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X )$ 

Definition 6.1 A function v is called a $w ( A , X )$ solution of (6.1) if and only i $f v \in L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; A )$ and equality (6.1) holds in the space $L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; A )$ 

Definition 6.2 An A-valued generalized random process u is called a $w ( A , X )$ Wiener Chaos solution of the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d u (t) = (\mathcal {A} u (t) + f (t)) d t + \left(\mathcal {M} _ {k} u (t) + g _ {k} (t)\right) d w _ {k} (t), t \leq T, u | _ {t = 0} = u _ {0},\tag{6.2}
$$

if and only if the equality 

$$
u (t) = u _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} u + f) (s) d s + \sum_ {k \geq 1} (\mathbb {D} _ {k} ^ {*} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u + g _ {k})) (t)\tag{6.3}
$$

holds in ${ \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } \left( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X ) \right)$ ). 

Sometimes, to stress the dependence of the Wiener Chaos solution on the terminal time $T ,$ the notation $w _ { T } ( A , X )$ will be used. 

Equalities (6.3) (5.13) mean that, for every $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ , the generalized Fourier coeficient $u _ { \alpha }$ of u satisfies the equation 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t) = u _ {0, \alpha} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} u + f) _ {\alpha} (s) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u + g _ {k}) _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s.\tag{6.4}
$$

Definition 6.3 System $( 6 . 4 )$ is called the propagator for equation (6.2). 

The propagator is a lower triangular system. Indeed, If $\alpha = ( 0 )$ , that is, $| \alpha | = 0$ , then the corresponding equation in (6.4) becomes 

$$
u _ {(0)} (t) = u _ {0, (0)} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} u _ {(0)} (s) + f _ {(0)} (s)) d s.\tag{6.5}
$$

If $\alpha = ( j \ell )$ , that is, $\alpha _ { j } ^ { \ell } = 1$ for some fixed $j$ and ℓ and $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k } = 0$ for all other $i , k \geq 1$ , then the corresponding equation in (6.4) becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u _ {(j \ell)} (t) = u _ {0, (j \ell)} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} u _ {(j \ell)} (s) + f _ {(j \ell)} (s)) d s \\ + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {(0)} (s) + g _ {\ell , (0)} (s)) m _ {j} (s) d s. \end{array}\tag{6.6}
$$

Continuing in this way, we conclude that (6.4) can be solved by induction on α as long as the corresponding deterministic equation (6.1) is solvable. The precise result is as follows. 

Theorem 6.1. If, for every $v _ { 0 } \in U$ and $\varphi \in L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X )$ , equation $( 6 . 1 )$ has a unique $w ( A , X )$ solution $v ( t ) = V ( t , v _ { 0 } , \varphi )$ , then equation (6.2) has a unique $w ( A , X )$ Wiener Chaos solution such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u _ {\alpha} (t) = V (t, u _ {0, \alpha}, f _ {\alpha}) + \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} V (t, 0, m _ {i} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)}) \\ \qquad + \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} V (t, 0, m _ {i} g _ {k, \alpha^ {-} (i, k)}). \end{array}\tag{6.7}
$$

Proof. Using the assumptions of the theorem and linearity, we conclude that (6.7) is the unique solution of (6.4). 

To derive a more explicit formula for $u _ { \alpha }$ , we need some additional constructions. For every multi-index α with $| { \boldsymbol { \alpha } } | = n ,$ , define the characteristic set $K _ { \alpha }$ of α as 

$$
K _ {\alpha} = \{(i _ {1} ^ {\alpha}, k _ {1} ^ {\alpha}), \ldots , (i _ {n} ^ {\alpha}, k _ {n} ^ {\alpha}) \},
$$

$i _ { 1 } ^ { \alpha } \leq i _ { 2 } ^ { \alpha } \leq \ldots \leq i _ { n } ^ { \alpha }$ , and if $i _ { j } ^ { \alpha } = i _ { j + 1 } ^ { \alpha } ,$ then $k _ { j } ^ { \alpha } \leq k _ { j + 1 } ^ { \alpha }$ . The first pair $( i _ { 1 } ^ { \alpha } , k _ { 1 } ^ { \alpha } )$ in $K _ { \alpha }$ is the position numbers of the first nonzero element of α. The second pair is the same as the first if the first nonzero element of α is greater than one; otherwise, the second pair is the position numbers of the second nonzero element of α and so on. As a result, if $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k } > 0$ , then exactly $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k }$ pairs in $K _ { \alpha }$ are equal to (i, k). For example, if 

$$
\alpha = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c c c c} 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 3 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \dots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \dots \end{array} \right)
$$

with nonzero elements 

$$
\alpha_ {1} ^ {2} = \alpha_ {2} ^ {1} = \alpha_ {1} ^ {6} = 1, \alpha_ {2} ^ {2} = \alpha_ {4} ^ {1} = 2, \alpha_ {5} ^ {1} = 3,
$$

then the characteristic set is 

$$
K _ {\alpha} = \{(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 2), (4, 1), (4, 1), (5, 1), (5, 1), (5, 1), (6, 2) \}.
$$

## Theorem 6.2. Assume that:

1. For every $v _ { 0 } \in U$ and $\varphi \in L _ { 1 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; X )$ , equation $( 6 . 1 )$ has a unique w $( A , X )$ solution $v ( t ) = V ( t , v _ { 0 } , \varphi )$ 

2. The input data in (6.4) satisfy g<sub>k</sub> = 0 and $f _ { \alpha } = u _ { 0 , \alpha } = 0 \ i f \left| \alpha \right| > 0$ 

Let $u _ { ( 0 ) } ( t ) = V ( t , u _ { 0 } , 0 )$ be the solution of $\left( 6 . 4 \right) f o r \left| \alpha \right| = 0$ . For $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ with $| { \boldsymbol { \alpha } } | = n \geq 1$ and the characteristic set $K _ { \alpha }$ , define functions $F ^ { n } = F ^ { n } ( t ; \alpha )$ by induction as follows: 

$$
\begin{array}{c} F ^ {1} (t; \alpha) = V (t, 0, m _ {i} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {(0)}) \text { if } K _ {\alpha} = \{(i, k) \}; \\ F ^ {n} (t; \alpha) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} V (t, 0, m _ {i _ {j}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {j}} F ^ {n - 1} (\cdot ; \alpha^ {-} (i _ {j}, k _ {j}))) \\ \text { if } K _ {\alpha} = \{(i _ {1}, k _ {1}), \ldots , (i _ {n}, k _ {n}) \}. \end{array}\tag{6.8}
$$

Then 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} F ^ {n} (t; \alpha).\tag{6.9}
$$

Proof. $\mathrm { I f } \ | \alpha | = 1$ , then representation (6.9) follows from (6.6). For $| \alpha | > 1$ observe that: 

If $\bar { u } _ { \alpha } ( t ) = \sqrt { \alpha ! } u _ { \alpha }$ and $| \alpha | \geq 1$ , then (6.4) implies the relation 

$$
\bar {u} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathcal {A} \bar {u} _ {\alpha} (s) d s + \sum_ {i, k} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha_ {i} ^ {k} m _ {i} (s) \mathcal {M} _ {k} \bar {u} _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) d s.
$$

If $K _ { \alpha } = \{ ( i _ { 1 } , k _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , ( i _ { n } , k _ { n } ) \}$ , then, for every $j = 1 , \dotsc , n$ , the characteristic set $K _ { \alpha ^ { - } ( i _ { j } , k _ { j } ) }$ of $\alpha ^ { - } ( i _ { j } , k _ { j } )$ is obtained from $K _ { \alpha }$ by removing the pair $( i _ { j } , k _ { j } )$ 

By the definition of the characteristic set, 

$$
\sum_ {i, k} \alpha_ {i} ^ {k} m _ {i} (s) \mathcal {M} _ {k} \bar {u} _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} m _ {i j} (s) \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {j}} \bar {u} _ {\alpha^ {-} (i _ {j}, k _ {j})} (s).
$$

As a result, representation (6.9) follows by induction on α using (6.7): if $| \alpha | = n > 1$ , then 

S. Lototsky and B. Rozovskii 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \bar {u} _ {\alpha} (t) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} V (t, 0, m _ {i _ {j}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {j}} \bar {u} _ {\alpha^ {-} (i _ {j}, k _ {j})}) \\ = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} V (t, 0, m _ {i _ {j}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {j}} F ^ {(n - 1)} (\cdot ; \alpha^ {-} (i _ {j}, k _ {j})) = F ^ {n} (t; \alpha). \end{array}\tag{6.10}
$$

Theorem 6.2 is proved. 

Corollary 6.1 Assume that the operator is a generator of a strongly continuous semigroup $\varPhi = \varPhi _ { t , s } , \ t \geq s \geq 0$ , in some Hilbert space H such that $A \subset H$ , each $\mathcal { M } _ { k }$ is a bounded operator from A to H, and the solution $V ( t , 0 , \varphi )$ of equation (6.1) is written as 

$$
V (t, 0, \varphi) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} \Phi_ {t, s} \varphi (s) d s, \quad \varphi \in L _ {2} ((0, T); H)).\tag{6.11}
$$

Denote by P<sup>n</sup> the permutation group of $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \} . \ I f \ u _ { ( 0 ) } \in L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; H ) )$ 1 then, $f o r \left| \alpha \right| = n > 1$ with the characteristic set $K _ { \alpha } = \{ ( i _ { 1 } , k _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , ( i _ { n } , k _ { n } ) \}$ , representation (6.9) becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u _ {\alpha} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \sum_ {\sigma \in \mathsf {P} ^ {n}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \\ \Phi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {\sigma (n)}} \dots \Phi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {\sigma (1)}} u _ {(0)} (s _ {1}) m _ {i _ {\sigma (n)}} (s _ {n}) \dots m _ {i _ {\sigma (1)}} (s _ {1}) d s _ {1} \ldots d s _ {n}. \end{array}\tag{6.12}
$$

Also, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} u _ {\alpha} (t) \xi_ {\alpha} = \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \\ \Phi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \Phi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} \left(\mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} u _ {(0)} + g _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1})\right) d w _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1}) \dots d w _ {k _ {n}} (s _ {n}), n \geq 1, \end{array}\tag{6.13}
$$

and, for every Hilbert space X, the following energy equality holds: 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {X} ^ {2} = \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \\ \| \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \varPhi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} u _ {(0)} (s _ {1}) \| _ {X} ^ {2} d s _ {1} \dots d s _ {n}; \end{array}\tag{6.14}
$$

both sides in the last equality can be infinite. For $n = 1$ , formulas (6.12) and $( 6 . 1 4 )$ become 

$$
u _ {(i k)} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varPhi_ {t, s} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {(0)} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s;\tag{6.15}
$$

$$
\sum_ {| \alpha | = 1} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {X} ^ {2} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \varPhi_ {t, s} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {(0)} (s) \| _ {X} ^ {2} d s.\tag{6.16}
$$

Proof. Using the semigroup representation (6.11), we conclude that (6.12) is just an expanded version of (6.9). 

Since $\{ m _ { i } , \enspace i \geq 1 \}$ is an orthonormal basis in $L _ { 2 } ( 0 , T )$ , equality (6.16) follows from (6.15) and the Parcevall identity. Similarly, equality (6.14) will follow from (6.12) after an application of an appropriate Parcevall’s identity. 

To carry out the necessary arguments when $| \alpha | > 1$ , denote by $\mathcal { I } _ { 1 }$ the collection of one-dimensional multi-indices $\beta = ( \beta _ { 1 } , \beta _ { 2 } , \ldots )$ such that each $\beta _ { i }$ is a non-negative integer and $\begin{array} { r } { | \beta | = \sum _ { i > 1 } \beta _ { i } < \infty } \end{array}$ . Given a $\beta \in \mathcal { I } _ { 1 }$ with $| \beta | = n ,$ we define $K _ { \beta } = \{ i _ { 1 } , \ldots , i _ { n } \}$ , the characteristic set of $\beta$ and the function 

$$
E _ {\beta} (s _ {1}, \dots , s _ {n}) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\beta} ! n !} \sum_ {\sigma \in \mathsf {P} ^ {n}} m _ {i _ {1}} (s _ {\sigma (1)}) \dots m _ {i _ {n}} (s _ {\sigma (n)}).\tag{6.17}
$$

By construction, the collection $\{ E _ { \beta } , \beta \in \mathcal { I } _ { 1 } , | \beta | = n \}$ is an orthonormal basis in the subspace of symmetric functions in $L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ^ { n } ; X )$ 

Next, we rewrite (6.12) in a symmetrized form. To make the notations shorter, denote by $s ^ { ( n ) }$ the ordered set $( s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } )$ and write $d s ^ { n } = d s _ { 1 } \ldots d s _ { n } .$ Fix $t \in ( 0 , T ]$ and the set $k ^ { ( n ) } = \{ k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { n } \}$ of the second components of the characteristic set $K _ { \alpha }$ . Define the symmetric function 

$$
\begin{array}{l} G (t, k ^ {(n)}; s ^ {(n)}) \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n !}} \sum_ {\sigma \in \mathsf {P} ^ {n}} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {\sigma (n)}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \varPhi_ {s _ {\sigma (2)}, s _ {\sigma (1)}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} u _ {(0)} (s _ {\sigma (1)}) 1 _ {s _ {\sigma (1)} <   \dots <   s _ {\sigma (n)} <   t} (s ^ {(n)}). \end{array}\tag{6.18}
$$

Then (6.12) becomes 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t) = \int_ {[ 0, T ] ^ {n}} G (t, k ^ {(n)}; s ^ {(n)}) E _ {\beta (\alpha)} (s ^ {(n)}) d s ^ {n},\tag{6.19}
$$

where the multi-indices α and $\beta ( \alpha )$ are related via their characteristic sets: if 

$$
K _ {\alpha} = \{(i _ {1}, k _ {1}), \dots , (i _ {n}, k _ {n}) \},
$$

then 

$$
K _ {\beta (\alpha)} = \{i _ {1}, \dots , i _ {n} \}.
$$

Equality (6.19) means that, for fixed $k ^ { ( n ) }$ , the function $u _ { \alpha }$ is a Fourier coefficient of the symmetric function $G ( t , k ^ { ( n ) } ; s ^ { ( n ) } )$ in the space $L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ^ { n } ; X )$ Parcevall’s identity and summation over all possible $k ^ { ( n ) }$ yield the equality 

$$
\sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {X} ^ {2} = \frac {1}{n !} \sum_ {k _ {1}, \dots , k _ {n} = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {[ 0, T ] ^ {n}} \| G (t, k ^ {(n)}; s ^ {(n)}) \| _ {X} ^ {2} d s ^ {n},
$$

which, due to (6.18), is the same as (6.14). 

To prove equality (6.13), relating the Cameron–Martin and multiple Itˆo integral expansions of the solution, we use the following result [13, Theorem 3.1]: 

$$
\xi_ {\alpha} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} E _ {\beta (\alpha)} (s ^ {(n)}) d w _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1}) \dots d w _ {k _ {n}} (s _ {n});
$$

see also [37, pp. 12–13]. Since the collection of all $E _ { \beta }$ is an orthonormal basis, equality (6.13) follows from (6.19) after summation over al $k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { n }$ 

Corollary 6.1 is proved. 

We now present several examples to illustrate the general results. 

Example 6.1 Consider the following equation: 

$$
d u (t, x) = \left(a u _ {x x} (t, x) + f (t, x)\right) d t + \left(\sigma u _ {x} (t, x) + g (t, x)\right) d w (t), x \in \mathbb {R},\tag{6.20}
$$

where $a \ > \ 0 , \ \sigma \ \in \ \mathbb { R } , \ f \in L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) ) , \ g \ \in \ L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ , and $u | _ { t = 0 } = u _ { 0 } \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . By Theorem 2.2, if $\sigma ^ { 2 } < 2 a ,$ , then equation (6.20) has a unique traditional solution $u \in L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) ) \right)$ . 

By $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -measurability of $u ( t )$ , we have 

$$
\mathbb {E} (u (t) \xi_ {\alpha}) = \mathbb {E} (u (t) \mathbb {E} (\xi_ {\alpha} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {W})).
$$

Using the relation (5.5) and the Itˆo formula, we find that $u _ { \alpha }$ satisfy 

$$
d u _ {\alpha} = a (u _ {\alpha}) _ {x x} d t + \sum_ {i} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i}} \sigma (u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i)}) _ {x} m _ {i} (t) d t,
$$

which is precisely the propagator for equation (6.20). In other words, in the case $2 a > \sigma ^ { 2 }$ the traditional solution of (6.20) coincides with the Wiener Chaos solution. 

On the other hand, the heat equation 

$$
v (t, x) = v _ {0} (x) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} v _ {x x} (s, x) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varphi (s, x) d s, v _ {0} \in L _ {2} (\mathbb {R}),
$$

with $\varphi \in L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ has a unique $v ( H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ ) solution. Therefore, by Theorem $6 . 1$ , the unique $w ( H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , \bar { H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } } ( \bar { \mathbb { R } } ) )$ ) Wiener Chaos solution of (6.20) exists for all $\sigma \in \mathbb { R }$ 

In the next example, the equation, although not parabolic, can be solved explicitly. 

Example 6.2 Consider the following equation: 

$$
d u (t, x) = u _ {x} (t, x) d w (t), t > 0, x \in \mathbb {R}; u (0, x) = x.\tag{6.21}
$$

Clearly, $u ( t , x ) = x + w ( t )$ satisfies (6.21). 

To find the Wiener Chaos solution of (6.21), note that, with onedimensional Wiener process, $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k } = \alpha _ { i }$ , and the propagator in this case becomes 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = x I (| \alpha | = 0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i}} (u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i)} (s, x)) _ {x} m _ {i} (s) d s.
$$

Then $u _ { \alpha } = 0 \ \mathrm { i f } \ | \alpha | > 1$ , and 

$$
u (t, x) = x + \sum_ {i > 1} \xi_ {i} \int_ {0} ^ {t} m _ {i} (s) d s = x + w (t).\tag{6.22}
$$

Even though Theorem 6.1 does not apply, the above arguments show that $u ( t , x ) = x + w ( t )$ is the unique $w ( A , X )$ Wiener Chaos solution of (6.21) for suitable spaces A and X, for example, 

$$
X = \left\{f: \int_ {\mathbb {R}} (1 + x ^ {2}) ^ {- 2} f ^ {2} (x) d x <   \infty \right\} \text {   and   } A = \{f: f, f ^ {\prime} \in X \}.
$$

Section 14 provides a more detailed analysis of equation (6.21). 

If equation (6.2) is anticipating, that is, the initial condition is not deterministic and/or the free terms $f , g$ are not $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W } \mathrm { - a d a p t e d }$ , then the Wiener Chaos solution generalizes the Skorohod integral interpretation of the equation. 

Example 6.3 Consider the equation 

$$
d u (t, x) = \frac {1}{2} u _ {x x} (t, x) d t + u _ {x} (t, x) d w (t), x \in \mathbb {R},\tag{6.23}
$$

with initial condition $u ( 0 , x ) = x ^ { 2 } w ( T )$ . Since $w ( T ) = \sqrt { T } \xi _ { 1 }$ , we find that 

$$
(u _ {\alpha}) _ {t} (t, x) = \frac {1}{2} (u _ {\alpha}) _ {x x} (t, x) + \sum_ {i} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i}} m _ {i} (t) (u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i)}) _ {x} (t, x)\tag{6.24}
$$

with initial condition $u _ { \alpha } ( 0 , x ) = \sqrt { T } x ^ { 2 } I ( | \alpha | = 1 , \alpha _ { 1 } = 1 )$ . By Theorem 6.1, there exists a unique $w ( A , X )$ Wiener Chaos solution of (6.23) for suitable spaces A and X. For example, we can take 

$$
X = \left\{f: \int_ {\mathbb {R}} (1 + x ^ {2}) ^ {- 8} f ^ {2} (x) d x <   \infty \right\} \text {   and   } A = \{f: f, f ^ {\prime}, f ^ {\prime \prime} \in X \}.
$$

System (6.24) can be solved explicitly. Indeed, $u _ { \alpha } \equiv 0 { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } | \alpha | = 0 { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } | \alpha | > 3$ or if $\alpha _ { 1 } = 0$ . Otherwise, writing $\begin{array} { r } { M _ { i } ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } m _ { i } ( s ) d s } \end{array}$ , we find: 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = (t + x ^ {2}) \sqrt {T}, \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 1, \alpha_ {1} = 1; \\ & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = 2 \sqrt {2} x t, \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 2, \alpha_ {1} = 2; \\ & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = 2 \sqrt {T} x M _ {i} (t), \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 2, \alpha_ {1} = \alpha_ {i} = 1, 1 <   i; \\ & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = \sqrt {\frac {6}{T}} t ^ {2}, \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 3, \alpha_ {1} = 3; \\ & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = 2 \sqrt {2 T} M _ {1} (t) M _ {i} (t), \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 3, \alpha_ {1} = 2, \alpha_ {i} = 1, 1 <   i; \\ & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = \sqrt {2 T} M _ {i} ^ {2} (t), \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 3, \alpha_ {1} = 1, \alpha_ {i} = 2, 1 <   i; \\ & u _ {\alpha} (t, x) = 2 \sqrt {T} M _ {i} (t) M _ {j} (t), \mathrm{if} | \alpha | = 3, \alpha_ {1} = \alpha_ {i} = \alpha_ {j} = 1, 1 <   i <   j. \end{array}
$$

Then 

$$
u (t, x) = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} u _ {\alpha} \xi_ {\alpha} = w (T) w ^ {2} (t) - 2 t w (t) + 2 (W (T) w (t) - t) x + x ^ {2} w (T)\tag{6.25}
$$

is the Wiener Chaos solution of (6.23). It can be verified using the properties of the Skorohod integral [37] that the function u defined by (6.25) satisfies

u (t, x) = x ^ {2} w (T) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} u _ {x x} (s, x) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} u _ {x} (s, x) d w (s), t \in [ 0, T ], x \in \mathbb {R},

where the stochastic integral is in the sense of Skorohod. 

## 7 Weighted Wiener Chaos Spaces and S-Transform

The space $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ is too big to provide any reasonable information about regularity of the Wiener Chaos solution. Introduction of weighted Wiener chaos spaces makes it possible to resolve this dificulty. 

As before, let $\boldsymbol { \Xi } = \{ \xi _ { \alpha } , \alpha \in \mathcal { I } \}$ be the Cameron–Martin basis in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ , and $\mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ , the collection of finite linear combinations of $\xi _ { \alpha }$ with coeficients in a Banach space X. 

Definition 7.1 Given a collection $\{ r _ { \alpha } , \alpha \in \mathcal { I } \}$ of positive numbers, the space $\mathcal { R } L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ is the closure of $\mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ) ; X )$ with respect to the norm 

$$
\| v \| _ {\mathcal {R} L _ {2} (\mathbb {W}; X)} ^ {2} := \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} r _ {\alpha} ^ {2} \| v _ {\alpha} \| _ {X} ^ {2}.
$$

The operator defined by $( { \mathcal R } v ) _ { \alpha } : = r _ { \alpha } v _ { \alpha }$ is a linear homeomorphism from $\mathcal { R } L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ to $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ 

There are several special choices of the weight sequence $\mathcal { R } = \{ r _ { \alpha } , \alpha \in \mathcal { T } \}$ and special notations for the corresponding weighted Wiener Chaos spaces. 

If $Q = \{ q _ { 1 } , q _ { 2 } , . . . \}$ is a sequence of positive numbers, define 

$$
q ^ {\alpha} = \prod_ {i, k} q _ {k} ^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}.
$$

The operator $\mathcal { R }$ , corresponding to $r _ { \alpha } = q ^ { \alpha }$ , is denotes by . The space $\mathcal { Q } L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ is denoted by $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ and is called a Q-weighted Wiener Chaos space. The significance of this choice of weights will be explained shortly (see, in particular, Proposition 7.2). 

If 

$$
r _ {\alpha} ^ {2} = (\alpha !) ^ {\rho} \prod_ {i, k} (2 i k) ^ {\gamma \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}, \rho , \gamma \in \mathbb {R},
$$

then the corresponding space $\mathcal { R } L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ is denoted by $( S ) _ { \rho , \gamma } ( X )$ . As always, the argument X will be omitted if $X = \mathbb { R }$ . Note the analogy with Definition 3.2. 

The structure of weights in the spaces $L _ { 2 , Q }$ and $( S ) _ { \rho , \gamma }$ is diferent, and in general these two classes of spaces are not related. There exist generalized random elements that belong to some $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ , but do not belong to any $( S ) _ { \rho , \gamma } ( X )$ . For example, $\begin{array} { r } { u = \sum _ { k > 1 } e ^ { k ^ { 2 } } \xi _ { 1 , k } } \end{array}$ belongs to $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } )$ with $q _ { k } =$ $e ^ { - 2 k ^ { 2 } }$ , but to no $( S ) _ { \rho , \gamma }$ , because the sum $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k > 1 } e ^ { 2 k ^ { 2 } } ( k ! ) ^ { \rho } ( 2 k ) ^ { \gamma } } \end{array}$ diverges for every $\rho , \gamma \in \mathbb { R }$ . Similarly, there exist generalized random elements that belong to some $( S ) _ { \rho , \gamma } ( X )$ , but to no $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ . For example, $\begin{array} { r } { u = \sum _ { n \geq 1 } \sqrt { n ! } \xi _ { ( n ) } . } \end{array}$ where (n) is the multi-index with $\alpha _ { 1 } ^ { 1 } = n$ and $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k } = 0$ elsewhere, belongs to $( S ) _ { - 1 , - 1 }$ , but does not belong to any $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } )$ , because the sum $\textstyle \sum _ { n \geq 1 } q ^ { n } n !$ diverges for every $q > 0$ 

The next result is the space-time analog of Proposition 2.3.3 in [12]. 

Proposition 7.1 The sum 

$$
\sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \prod_ {i, k \geq 1} (2 i k) ^ {- \gamma \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}
$$

converges if and only $i f \gamma > 1$ 

Proof. Note that 

$$
\sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \prod_ {i, k \geq 1} (2 i k) ^ {- \gamma \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} = \prod_ {i, k \geq 1} \left(\sum_ {n \geq 0} ((2 i k) ^ {- \gamma}) ^ {n}\right) = \prod_ {i, k} \frac {1}{(1 - (2 i k) ^ {- \gamma})}, \gamma > 0\tag{7.1}
$$

The infinite product on the right of $( 7 . 1 )$ converges if and only if each of the sums $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i \geq 1 } i ^ { - \gamma } , \sum _ { k \geq 1 } k ^ { - \gamma } } \end{array}$ converges, that is, if an only if $\gamma > 1$ 

Corollary 7.1 For every $u \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ , there exists an operator such that $\mathscr { R } u \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ . 

Proof. Define 

$$
r _ {\alpha} ^ {2} = \frac {1}{1 + \| u _ {\alpha} \| _ {X} ^ {2}} \prod_ {i, k \geq 1} (2 i k) ^ {- 2 \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}.
$$

Then 

$$
\| \mathcal {R} u \| _ {L _ {2} (\mathbb {W}; X)} ^ {2} = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {\| u _ {\alpha} \| _ {X} ^ {2}}{1 + \| u _ {\alpha} \| _ {X} ^ {2}} \prod_ {i, k \geq 1} (2 i k) ^ {- 2 \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \leq \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \prod_ {i, k \geq 1} (2 i k) ^ {- 2 \alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} <   \infty .
$$

The importance of the operator $\mathcal { Q }$ in the study of stochastic equations is due to the fact that the operator $\mathcal { R }$ maps a Wiener Chaos solution to a Wiener Chaos solution if and only $\mathcal { R } = \mathcal { Q }$ for some sequence $Q .$ . Indeed, direct calculations show that the functions $u _ { \alpha } , \alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ , satisfy the propagator (6.4) if and only if $\begin{array} { r } { v _ { \alpha } = ( \mathcal { R } u ) _ { \alpha } } \end{array}$ satisfy the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{l} {v _ {\alpha} (t) = (\mathcal {R} u _ {0}) _ {\alpha} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} v + \mathcal {R} f) _ {\alpha} (s) d s} \\ {\qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \frac {\rho_ {\alpha}}{\rho_ {\alpha^ {-} (i , k)}} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} \mathcal {R} u + \mathcal {R} g _ {k}) _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s.} \end{array}\tag{7.2}
$$

Therefore, the operator $\mathcal { R }$ preserves the structure of the propagator if and only if 

$$
\frac {\rho_ {\alpha}}{\rho_ {\alpha^ {-} (i , k)}} = q _ {k},
$$

that is, $\rho _ { \alpha } = q ^ { \alpha }$ for some sequence $Q .$ 

Below is the summary of the main properties of the operator $\mathcal { Q } .$

1. If $q _ { k } \le q < 1$ for all $k \geq 1$ , then $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ) \subset ( S ) _ { 0 , - \gamma }$ for some $\gamma > 0$ 

2. If $q _ { k } \ge q > 1$ for all k, then $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ) \subset L _ { 2 } ^ { n } ( \mathbb { W } ) f o r$ all $n \geq 1$ , that is, the (U) 1: cc 1 11

$$

3. If $u \in L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ ) with generalized Fourier coeficients $u _ { \alpha }$ satisfying the propagator $( 6 . 4 )$ , and $\ v \ = \ Q u$ , then the corresponding system for the generalized Fourier coeficients of v is

where, for $\begin{array} { r } { h \in Y , W _ { h } ^ { Q } ( t ) = \sum _ { k \geq 1 } ( h , y _ { k } ) _ { Y } q _ { k } w _ { k } ( t ) } \end{array}$ 

The following examples demonstrate how the operator helps with the analysis of various stochastic evolution equations. 

Example 7.1 Consider the $w ( H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ Wiener Chaos solution u of equation 

$$
d u (t, x) = \left(a u _ {x x} (t, x) + f (t, x)\right) d t + \sigma u _ {x} (t, x) d w (t), \quad x \in \mathbb {R},\tag{7.6}
$$

with $f \in L _ { 2 } ( \Omega \times ( 0 , T ) ; H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) ) , g \in L _ { 2 } ( \Omega \times ( 0 , T ) ; L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ , and the initial data $u | _ { t = 0 } = u _ { 0 } \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . Assume that $\sigma > 0$ and define the sequence $Q$ such that $q _ { k } = q$ for all $k \geq 1$ and $q < \sqrt { 2 a } / \sigma .$ . By Theorem 2.2, the equation 

$$
d v = (a v _ {x x} + f) d t + (q \sigma u _ {x} + g) d w
$$

with $v | _ { t = 0 } = u _ { 0 }$ , has a unique traditional solution 

$$
v \in L _ {2} \left(\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); H _ {2} ^ {1} (\mathbb {R}))\right) \bigcap L _ {2} \left(\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); L _ {2} (\mathbb {R}))\right).
$$

By Proposition 7.2, the $\begin{array} { r } { \upsilon ( H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) ) , } \end{array}$ ) Wiener Chaos solution u of equation (7.6) satisfies $u = \mathcal { Q } ^ { - 1 } \iota$ and 

$$
u \in L _ {2, Q} \left(\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); H _ {2} ^ {1} (\mathbb {R}))\right) \bigcap L _ {2, Q} \left(\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); L _ {2} (\mathbb {R}))\right).
$$

Note that if equation (7.6) is strongly parabolic, that is, $2 a > \sigma ^ { 2 } .$ , then the weight q can be taken bigger than one, and, according to the first statement of Proposition 7.2, regularity of the solution is better than the one guaranteed by Theorem 2.2. 

Example 7.2 The Wiener Chaos solutions can be constructed for stochastic ordinary diferential equations. Consider, for example, 

$$
u (t) = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {k \geq 1} u (s) d w _ {k} (s),\tag{7.7}
$$

which clearly does not have a traditional solution. On the other hand, the unique w(R, R) Wiener Chaos solution of this equation belongs to $L _ { 2 , Q } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ) \right)$ for every $Q$ satisfying $\textstyle \sum _ { k } q _ { k } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Indeed, for (7.7), equation (7.5) becomes 

$$
v (t) = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {k} v (s) q _ {k} d w _ {k} (s).
$$

If $\textstyle \sum _ { k } q _ { k } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , then the traditional solution of this equation exists and belongs to $L _ { 2 } \left( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ) \right)$ . 

There exist equations for which the Wiener Chaos solution does not belong to any weighted Wiener chaos space $L _ { 2 , Q }$ . An example is given below in Section 14. 

To define the S-transform, consider the following analog of the stochastic exponential (3.6). 

Lemma 7.1. $I f h \in \mathcal { D } \left( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right)$ and 

$$

$$

then 

$\mathcal { E } ( h ) \in L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } )$ for every sequence $Q$

Proof. Recall that, if $h \in \mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) )$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { h ( t ) = \sum _ { i , k \in I _ { h } } h _ { k , i } m _ { i } ( t ) y _ { k } } \end{array}$ , where $I _ { h }$ is a finite set. Direct computations show that

$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { h ^ { \alpha } = \prod _ { i , k } h _ { k , i } ^ { \alpha _ { i } ^ { k } } } \end{array}$ . In particular,

Consequently, for every sequence Q of positive numbers,

Similarly, for $\rho \in [ 0 , 1 )$ and $\gamma \geq 0$ ，
