$\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { i f ~ 2 ~ } \big ( \operatorname* { m a x } _ { ( m , n ) \in I _ { h } ) } ( m n ) ^ { \gamma } \big ) \sum _ { i , k } h _ { k , i } ^ { 2 } < 1 } \end{array}$ . Lemma 7.1 is proved. 

Remark 7.1 It is well-known (see, for example, [24, Proof of Theorem 5.5]) that the family $\{ \mathcal { E } ( h ) , h \in \mathcal { D } \left( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right) \}$ is dense in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } )$ and consequently in every $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } )$ and every $( S ) _ { \rho , \gamma } , - 1 < \rho \leq 1 , \gamma \in \mathbb { R }$ 

Definition 7.2 $I f u \in L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ for some Q, or if u $\textstyle \in \bigcup _ { q \geq 0 } ( S ) _ { - \rho , - \gamma } ( X )$ $0 \leq \rho \leq 1$ , then the deterministic function 

$$
S u (h) = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {u _ {\alpha} h ^ {\alpha}}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \in X\tag{7.12}
$$

is called the S-transform of u. Similarly, for $g \in \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } \left( Y ; L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X ) \right)$ the S-transform $S g ( h ) \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( Y ; X )$ is defined by setting $( S g ( h ) ) _ { k } = ( S g _ { k } ) ( h )$ 

Note that if $u ~ \in ~ L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ , then $S u ( h ) \ = \ \mathbb { E } ( u \mathcal { E } ( h ) )$ . If u belongs to $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ or to $\begin{array} { r } { \bigcup _ { a > 0 } ( S ) _ { - \rho , - \gamma } ( X ) , 0 \le \rho < 1 } \end{array}$ , then $S u ( h )$ is defined for all $h \in \mathcal { D } \left( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; \overline { { Y } } ) \right)$ . If $u \in \bigcup _ { \gamma > 0 } ( S ) _ { - 1 , - \gamma } ( X )$ , then $S u ( h )$ is defined only for h suficiently close to zero. 

By Remark 7.1, an element u from $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X )$ or $\begin{array} { r } { \bigcup _ { \gamma > 0 } ( S ) _ { - \rho , - \gamma } ( X ) , 0 \le } \end{array}$ $\rho < 1$ , is uniquely determined by the collection of deterministic functions $S u ( h )$ , $h \in \mathcal { D } \left( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right)$ . Since $\mathcal { E } ( h ) > 0$ for all $h \in \mathcal { D } \left( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right)$ , Remark 7.1 also suggests the following definition. 

Definition 7.3 An element u from $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } )$ or $\begin{array} { r } { \bigcup _ { \gamma > 0 } ( S ) _ { - \rho , - \gamma } , 0 \le \rho < 1 } \end{array}$ is called non-negative $( u \ge 0 )$ if and only if the inequality $S u ( h ) \geq 0$ holds whatever is $h \in \mathcal { D } \left( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) \right)$ . 

The definition of the operator $\mathcal { Q }$ and Definition 7.3 imply the following result. 

Proposition 7.3 A generalized random element u from $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } )$ is nonnegative if and only if $\mathcal { Q } u \geq 0$ 

For example, the solution of equation (7.7) is non-negative because 

$$
\mathcal {Q} u (t) = \exp \left(\sum_ {k \geq 1} (q _ {k} w _ {k} (t) - (1 / 2) q _ {k} ^ {2})\right).
$$

We conclude this section with one technical remark. 

Definition 7.2 expresses the S-transform in terms of the generalized Fourier coeficients. The following results makes it possible to recover generalized Fourier coeficients from the corresponding S-transform. 

Proposition 7.4 If u belongs to some $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \mathbb { W } ; X ) o r \bigcup _ { \gamma \geq 0 } ( S ) _ { - \rho , - \gamma } ( X )$ with $0 \leq \rho \leq 1$ , then 

$$
u _ {\alpha} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \left(\prod_ {i, k} \frac {\partial^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} S u (h)}{\partial h _ {k , i} ^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}}\right) \Bigg | _ {h = 0}.\tag{7.13}
$$

Proof. For each $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ with K non-zero entries, equality $\left( 7 . 1 2 \right)$ and Lemma 7.1 imply that the function $S u ( h )$ , as a function of K variables $h _ { k , i } ,$ , is analytic in some neighborhood of zero. Then (7.13) follows after diferentiation of the series (7.12). 

## 8 General Properties of the Wiener Chaos Solutions

Using notations and assumptions from Section 6, consider the linear evolution equation 

$$
d u (t) = (\mathcal {A} u (t) + f (t)) d t + (\mathcal {M} u (t) + g (t), d W (t)) _ {Y}, \quad u | _ {t = 0} = u _ {0}.\tag{8.1}
$$

The objective of this section is to study how the Wiener Chaos compares with the traditional and white noise solutions. 

To make the presentation shorter, we shall call an X-valued generalized random element S-admissible if and only if it belongs to $L _ { 2 , Q } ( \bar { \mathcal { F } } ^ { W } ; X )$ ) for some $Q$ or to $( S ) _ { \rho , q } ( X )$ for some $\rho \in [ - 1 , 1 ]$ and $q \in \mathbb { R }$ . It was shown in Section 7 that, for every S-admissible u, the S-transform $S u ( h )$ is defined when $\begin{array} { r } { h = \sum _ { i , k } h _ { k , i } m _ { i } y _ { k } \in \mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) ) } \end{array}$ and is an analytic function of $h _ { k , i }$ in some neighborhood of $h = 0$ 

The next result describes the S-transform of the Wiener Chaos solution. 

## Theorem 8.1. Assume that:

1. There exists a unique $w ( A , X )$ Wiener Chaos solution u $o f \left( 8 . 1 \right)$ and u is S-admissible. 

2. For each $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , the linear operators $\mathbf { \mathcal { A } } ( t ) , \mathbf { \mathcal { M } } _ { k } ( t )$ are bounded from A to X. 

3. The generalized random elements u<sub>0</sub>, $f , g _ { k }$ are S-admissible. 

Then, for every $h \in \mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) )$ with $\| h \| _ { L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) } ^ { 2 }$ suficiently small, the function $v = S u ( h )$ is $a \ w ( A , X )$ solution of the deterministic equation 

$$
v (t) = S u _ {0} (h) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Bigl (\mathcal {A} v + S f (h) + (\mathcal {M} _ {k} v + S g _ {k} (h)) h _ {k} \Bigr) (s) d s.\tag{8.2}
$$

Proof. By assumption, $S u ( h )$ exists for suitable functions $h .$ Then the $\mathrm { S } -$ transformed equation (8.2) follows from the definition of the S-transform (7.12) and the propagator equation (6.4) satisfied by the generalized Fourier coeficients of u. Indeed, continuity of operator implies 

$$
S (\mathcal {A} u) (h) = \sum_ {\alpha} \frac {h ^ {\alpha}}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \mathcal {A} u _ {\alpha} = \mathcal {A} \sum_ {\alpha} \frac {h ^ {\alpha}}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} u _ {\alpha} = \mathcal {A} (S u (h)).
$$

Similarly, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {\alpha} \frac {h ^ {\alpha}}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} m _ {i} = \sum_ {\alpha} \sum_ {i, k} \frac {h ^ {\alpha^ {-} (i , k)}}{\sqrt {\alpha^ {-} (i , k) !}} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} m _ {i} h _ {k, i} \\ = \sum_ {i, k} \left(\sum_ {\alpha} \frac {h ^ {\alpha}}{\sqrt {\alpha}} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha}\right) m _ {i} h _ {k, i} = \mathcal {M} _ {k} (S u (h)) h _ {k}. \end{array}
$$

Computations for the other terms are similar. Theorem 8.1 is proved. 

Remark 8.1 If $h \in \mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) )$ and 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {t} (h) = \exp \left(\int_ {0} ^ {t} (h (s), d W (s)) _ {Y} - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| h (t) \| _ {Y} ^ {2} d t\right),\tag{8.3}
$$

then, by the Itˆo formula, 

$$
d \mathcal {E} _ {t} (h) = \mathcal {E} _ {t} (h) (h (t), d W (t)) _ {Y}.\tag{8.4}
$$

If $u _ { 0 }$ is deterministic, $f$ and $g _ { k }$ are $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted, and u is a square-integrable solution of (8.1), then equality (8.2) is obtained by multiplying equations (8.4) and (8.1) according to the Itˆo formula and taking the expectation. 

Remark 8.2 Rewriting (8.4) as 

$$
d \mathcal {E} _ {t} (h) = \mathcal {E} _ {t} (h) h _ {k, i} m _ {i} (t) d w _ {k} (t)
$$

and using the relations 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {t} (h) = \mathbb {E} (\mathcal {E} _ {T} (h) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {W}), \xi_ {\alpha} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \left(\prod_ {i, k} \frac {\partial^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \mathcal {E} _ {T} (h)}{\partial h _ {k , i} ^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}}\right) \Bigg | _ {h = 0},
$$

we arrive at representation (5.5) for $\mathbb { E } ( \xi _ { \alpha } \vert \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W } )$ . 

A partial converse of Theorem 8.1 is that, under some regularity conditions, the Wiener Chaos solution can be recovered from the solution of the $\mathrm { S } -$ transformed equation (8.2). 

Theorem 8.2. Assume that the linear operators $\mathcal { A } ( t ) , \ \mathcal { M } _ { k } ( t ) , t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , are bounded from A to X, the input data u , $f , \ g _ { k }$ are S-admissible, and, for every $h \in \mathcal { D } ( L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) )$ with $\| h \| _ { L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y ) } ^ { 2 }$ suficiently small, there exists a $w ( A , X )$ solution $v = v ( t ; h )$ of equation (8.2). We write $h = h _ { k , i } m _ { i } y _ { k }$ and consider v as a function of the variables $h _ { k , i } .$ . Assume that all the derivatives of v at the point $h = 0$ exists, and, for $\alpha \in \mathcal { I }$ , define 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \left(\prod_ {i, k} \frac {\partial^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} v (t ; h)}{\partial h _ {k , i} ^ {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}}}\right) \Bigg | _ {h = 0}.\tag{8.5}
$$

Then the generalized random process $\begin{array} { r } { u ( t ) ~ = ~ \sum _ { \alpha \in \mathcal { T } } u _ { \alpha } ( t ) \xi _ { \alpha } } \end{array}$ is a w(A, X) Wiener Chaos solution of (8.1). 

Proof. Diferentiation of (8.2) and application of Proposition 7.4 show that the functions $u _ { \alpha }$ satisfy the propagator (6.4). 

Remark 8.3 The central part in the construction of the white noise solution of (8.1) is proving that the solution of (8.2) is an S-transform of a suitable generalized random process. For many particular cases of equation (8.1), the corresponding analysis is carried out in [10, 12, 33, 40]. The consequence of Theorems 8.1 and 8.2 is that a white noise solution of (8.1), if exists, must coincide with the Wiener Chaos solution. 

The next theorem establishes the connection between the Wiener Chaos solution and the traditional solution. Recall that the traditional, or squareintegrable, solution of (8.1) was introduced in Definition 2.2. Accordingly, the notations from Section 2 will be used. 

Theorem 8.3. Let $( V , H , V ^ { \prime } )$ be a normal triple of Hilbert spaces. Take a deterministic function u and $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted random processes f and g so that (2.3) holds. Under these assumptions we have the following two statements. 

1. An $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted traditional solution of $( 8 . 1 )$ is also a Wiener Chaos solution. 

2. If u is a $v ( V , V ^ { \prime } )$ Wiener Chaos solution of (8.1) such that 

$$
\sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {V} ^ {2} d t + \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq T} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2}\right) <   \infty ,\tag{8.6}
$$

then u is an $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted traditional solution of (8.1). 

Proof. (1) If $u = u ( t )$ is an $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted traditional solution, then 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t) = \mathbb {E} (u (t) \xi_ {\alpha}) = \mathbb {E} \left(u (t) \mathbb {E} (\xi_ {\alpha} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {W})\right) = \mathbb {E} (u (t) \xi_ {\alpha} (t)).
$$

Then the propagator (6.4) for $u _ { \alpha }$ follows after applying the Itˆo formula to the product $u ( t ) \xi _ { \alpha } ( t )$ and using (5.5). 

(2) Assumption (8.6) implies that 

$$
u \in L _ {2} (\Omega \times (0, T); V) \bigcap L _ {2} (\Omega ; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); H)).
$$

Then, by Theorem 8.1, for every $\varphi \in V$ and $h \in \mathcal { D } ( ( 0 , T ) ; Y )$ , the S-transform $u _ { h }$ of u satisfies the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (u _ {h} (t), \varphi) _ {H} = (u _ {0}, \varphi) _ {H} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle \mathcal {A} u _ {h} (s), \varphi \rangle d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle f (s), \varphi \rangle d s \\ \qquad + \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {h ^ {\alpha}}{\alpha !} \sum_ {i, k} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) \big ((\mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s), \varphi) _ {H} \\ \qquad + (g _ {k} (s), \varphi) _ {H} I (| \alpha | = 1) \big) d s. \end{array}
$$

If $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } ( \mathcal { M } _ { k } u ( s ) , \varphi ) _ { H } d w _ { k } ( s ) } \end{array}$ , then 

$$
\mathbb {E} (I (t) \xi_ {\alpha} (t)) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s), \varphi) _ {H} d s.\tag{8.7}
$$

Similarly, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\xi_ {\alpha} (t) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(g _ {k} (s), \varphi\right) _ {H} d w _ {k} (s)\right) = \sum_ {i, k} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) \left(g _ {k} (s), \varphi\right) _ {H} I (| \alpha | = 1) d s.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {h ^ {\alpha}}{\alpha !} \sum_ {i, k} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} m _ {i} (s) (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s), \varphi) _ {H} d s \\ = \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) \int_ {0} ^ {t} ((\mathcal {M} _ {k} u (s), \varphi) _ {H} + (g _ {k} (s), \varphi) _ {H})   d w _ {k} (s)\right). \end{array}
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) (u (t), \varphi) _ {H}\right) = \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) (u _ {0}, \varphi) _ {H}\right) \\ \qquad + \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle \mathcal {A} u (s), \varphi \rangle d s\right) + \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle f (s), \varphi \rangle d s\right) \\ \qquad + \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) \int_ {0} ^ {t} ((\mathcal {M} _ {k} u (s), \varphi) _ {H} + (g _ {k} (s), \varphi) _ {H})   d w _ {k} (s)\right). \end{array}\tag{8.8}
$$

Equality (8.8) and Remark 7.1 imply that, for each t and each $\varphi , \ ( 2 . 4 )$ holds with probability one. Continuity of u implies that, for each $\varphi _ { ; }$ , a single probability-one set can be chosen for all $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ . Theorem 9.3 is proved. 

## 9 Regularity of the Wiener Chaos Solution

Let $\mathbb { F } = ( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { t > 0 } , \mathbb { P } )$ be a stochastic basis with the usual assumptions and $w _ { k } = w _ { k } ( t ) , \ k \geq 1 , \ t \geq 0$ , a collection of standard Wiener processes on F. As in Section 2, let $( V , H , V ^ { \prime } )$ be a normal triple of Hilbert spaces and $\mathcal { A } ( t ) : V  V ^ { \prime } , \mathcal { M } _ { k } ( t ) : V  H$ , linear bounded operators; $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ 

In this section we study the linear equation 

$$
u (t) = u _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} u (s) + f (s)) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u (s) + g _ {k} (s)) d w _ {k} (s), t \leq T,\tag{9.1}
$$

under the following assumptions: 

A1 There exist positive numbers $C _ { 1 }$ and δ such that 

$$
\langle \mathcal {A} (t) v, v \rangle + \delta \| v \| _ {V} ^ {2} \leq C _ {1} \| v \| _ {H} ^ {2}, v \in V, t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{9.2}
$$

A2 There exists a real number $C _ { 2 }$ such that 

$$
2 \langle \mathcal {A} (t) v, v \rangle + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k} (t) v \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq C _ {2} \| v \| _ {H} ^ {2}, v \in V, t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{9.3}
$$

A3 The initial condition $u _ { 0 }$ is non-random and belongs to $H ;$ the process $f = f ( t )$ is deterministic and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| f ( t ) \| _ { V ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 } d t < \infty ; } \end{array}$ each $g _ { k } = g _ { k } ( t )$ is a deterministic processes and $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k \geq 1 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| g _ { k } ( t ) \| _ { H } ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ 

Note that condition (9.3) is weaker than (2.5). Traditional analysis of equation (9.1) under (9.3) requires additional regularity assumptions on the input data and additional Hilbert space constructions beyond the normal triple [42, Section 3.2]. In particular, no existence of a traditional solution is known under assumptions A1-A3, and the Wiener Chaos approach provides new existence and regularity results for equation (9.1). A diferent version of the following theorem is presented in [29]. 

Theorem 9.1. Under assumptions $_ { A 1 - A 3 , }$ for every $T > 0$ , equation $( 9 . 1 )$ has a unique $w ( V , V ^ { \prime } )$ Wiener Chaos solution. This solution $u = u ( t )$ has the following properties: 

1. There exists a weight sequence $Q$ such that 

$$
u \in L _ {2, Q} (\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); V)) \bigcap L _ {2, Q} (\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); H)).
$$

2. For every $t \le T , u ( t ) \in L _ { 2 } ( \varOmega ; H )$ and 

$$
\mathbb {E} \| u (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq 3 e ^ {C _ {2} t} \left(\| u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} + C _ {f} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| f (s) \| _ {V ^ {\prime}} ^ {2} d s + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| g _ {k} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s\right),\tag{9.4}
$$

where the number $C _ { 2 }$ is from (9.3) and the positive number $C _ { f }$ depends only on δ and $C _ { 1 }$ from (9.2). 

3. For every $t \leq T$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u (t) = u _ {(0)} + \sum_ {n \geq 1} \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \\ \Phi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \Phi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} \left(\mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} u _ {(0)} + g _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1})\right) d w _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1}) \dots d w _ {k _ {n}} (s _ {n}), \end{array}\tag{9.5}
$$

where $\varPhi _ { t , s }$ is the semigroup of the operator $\mathcal { A }$ . 

Proof. Assumption A2 and the properties of the normal triple imply that there exists a positive number $C ^ { * }$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {k \geq 1} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k} (t) v \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq C ^ {*} \| v \| _ {V} ^ {2}, v \in V, t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{9.6}
$$

Define the sequence $Q$ such that 

$$
q _ {k} = \left(\frac {\mu \delta}{C ^ {*}}\right) ^ {1 / 2} := q, k \geq 1,\tag{9.7}
$$

where $\mu \in ( 0 , 2 )$ and δ is from Assumption A1. Then, by Assumption A2, 

$$
2 \langle A v, v \rangle + \sum_ {k \geq 1} q ^ {2} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k} v \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq - (2 - \mu) \delta \| v \| _ {V} ^ {2} + C _ {1} \| v \| _ {H} ^ {2}.\tag{9.8}
$$

It follows from Theorem 2.1 that equation 

$$
v (t) = u _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} v + f) (s) d s + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} q (\mathcal {M} _ {k} v + g _ {k}) (s) d w _ {k} (s)\tag{9.9}
$$

has a unique solution 

$$
v \in L _ {2} (\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); V)) \bigcap L _ {2} (\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); H)).
$$

Comparison of the propagators for equations (9.1) and (9.9) shows that $u =$ ${ \mathcal { Q } } ^ { - 1 } v$ is the unique $w ( V , V ^ { \prime } )$ solution of (9.1) and 

$$
u \in L _ {2, Q} (\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); V)) \bigcap L _ {2, Q} (\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); H)).\tag{9.10}
$$

If $C ^ { * } < 2 \delta$ , then equation (9.1) is strongly parabolic and $q > 1$ is an admissible choice of the weight. As a result, for strongly parabolic equations, the result (9.10) is stronger than the conclusion of Theorem 2.1. 

The proof of (9.4) is based on the analysis of the propagator 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u _ {\alpha} (t) = u _ {0} I (| \alpha | = 0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Big (\mathcal {A} u _ {\alpha} (s) + f (s) I (| \alpha | = 0) \Big) d s \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) + g _ {k} (s) I (| \alpha | = 1)) m _ {i} (s) d s. \end{array}\tag{9.11}
$$

We consider three particular cases: (1) $f = g _ { k } = 0$ (the homogeneous equation); ( $2 ) \ u _ { 0 } = g _ { k } = 0 ; \ ( 3 ) \ u _ { 0 } = f = 0$ . The general case will then follow by linearity and the triangle inequality. 

Let us denote by $( \phi _ { t , s } , \ t \geq s \geq 0 )$ the semigroup generated by the operator $\mathcal { A } ( t ) ; \varPhi _ { t } : = \varPhi _ { t , 0 } .$ . One of the consequence of Theorem 2.1 is that, under Assumption A1, this semigroup exists and is strongly continuous in $H$ 

Consider the homogeneous equation: $f = g _ { k } = 0$ . By Corollary 6.1, 

$$
\sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} = \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \varPhi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n},\tag{9.12}
$$

where $d s ^ { n } = d s _ { 1 } . . . d s _ { n }$ . Define $\begin{array} { r } { F _ { n } ( t ) = \sum _ { | \alpha | = n } \| u _ { \alpha } ( t ) \| _ { H } ^ { 2 } , \ n \geq 0 . } \end{array}$ . Direct application of (9.3) shows that 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} F _ {0} (t) \leq C _ {2} F _ {0} (t) - \sum_ {k \geq 1} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k} \Phi_ {t} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2}.\tag{9.13}
$$

For $n \geq 1$ , equality (9.12) implies that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} F _ {n} (t) = \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n - 1}} \dots \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n - 1} \\ + \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \langle \mathcal {A} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0}, \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \rangle d s ^ {n}. \end{array}\tag{9.14}
$$

By (9.3), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \langle \mathcal {A} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \ldots \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0}, \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \ldots \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \rangle d s ^ {n} \\ \leq - \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n + 1} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n + 1}} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \ldots \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n} \\ + C _ {2} \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \ldots \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n}. \end{array}\tag{9.15}
$$

As a result, for $n \geq 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} F _ {n} (t) \leq C _ {2} F _ {n} (t) \\ + \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n - 1}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n - 1}} \ldots \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n - 1} \\ - \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n + 1} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n + 1}} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \ldots \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n}. \end{array}\tag{9.16}
$$

Consequently, 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq C _ {2} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2},\tag{9.17}
$$

so that, by the Gronwall inequality, 

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq e ^ {C _ {2} t} \| u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2}\tag{9.18}
$$

or 

$$
\mathbb {E} \| u (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq e ^ {C _ {2} t} \| u _ {0} \| _ {H} ^ {2}.\tag{9.19}
$$

Next, let us assume that $u _ { 0 } = g _ { k } = 0$ . Then the propagator (9.11) becomes 

$$
u _ {\alpha} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\mathcal {A} u _ {\alpha} (s) + f (s) I (| \alpha | = 0)) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s.\tag{9.20}
$$

Denote by $u _ { ( 0 ) } ( t )$ the solution corresponding to $\alpha = 0$ . Note that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| u _ {(0)} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} = 2 \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle \mathcal {A} u _ {(0)} (s), u _ {(0)} (s) \rangle d s + 2 \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle f (s), u _ {(0)} (s) \rangle d s \\ \leq C _ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| u _ {(0)} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {k > 1} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {(0)} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s + C _ {f} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| f (s) \| _ {V ^ {\prime}} ^ {2} d s. \end{array}
$$

By Corollary 6.1, 

$$
\sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} = \sum_ {k _ {1}, \dots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \Phi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {1}} u _ {(0)} (s _ {1}) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n}\tag{9.21}
$$

for $n \geq 1$ . Then, repeating the calculations (9.14)–(9.16), we conclude that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq C _ {f} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| f (s) \| _ {V ^ {\prime}} ^ {2} d s + C _ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s,\tag{9.22}
$$

and, by the Gronwall inequality, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \| u (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq C _ {f} e ^ {C _ {2} t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| f (s) \| _ {V ^ {\prime}} ^ {2} d s.\tag{9.23}
$$

Finally, let us assume that $u _ { 0 } = f = 0$ . Then the propagator (9.11) becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u _ {\alpha} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathcal {A} u _ {\alpha} (s) d s \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(\sum_ {i, k} \sqrt {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k}} \mathcal {M} _ {k} u _ {\alpha^ {-} (i, k)} (s) + g _ {k} (s) I (| \alpha | = 1)\right) m _ {i} (s) d s. \end{array}\tag{9.24}
$$

Even though $u _ { \alpha } ( t ) = 0$ if $\alpha = 0$ , we have 

$$
u _ {(i k)} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varPhi_ {t, s} g _ {k} (s) m _ {i} (s) d s,\tag{9.25}
$$

and then the arguments from the proof of Corollary 6.1 apply, resulting in 

$$
\sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} = \sum_ {k _ {1}, \dots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \Phi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \dots \Phi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} g _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1}) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s ^ {n}
$$

for $n \geq 1 .$ . Note that 

$$
\sum_ {| \alpha | = 1} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} = \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| g _ {k} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s + 2 \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \langle \mathcal {A} \varPhi_ {t, s} g _ {k} (s), \varPhi_ {t, s} g _ {k} (s) \rangle d s.
$$

Then, repeating the calculations (9.14)–(9.16), we conclude that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| g _ {k} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s + C _ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u _ {\alpha} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s,\tag{9.26}
$$

and, by the Gronwall inequality, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \| u (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq e ^ {C _ {2} t} \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| g _ {k} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s.\tag{9.27}
$$

To derive (9.4), it remains to combine (9.19), (9.23), and (9.27) with the elementary inequality $( a + b + c ) ^ { 2 } \leq 3 ( a ^ { 2 } + b ^ { 2 } + c ^ { 2 } )$ 

Representation (9.5) of the Wiener Chaos solution as a sum of iterated Itˆo integrals now follows from Corollary 6.1. Theorem 9.1 is proved. 

$$
\text {   Corollary   9.1   } \text {   If   } \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| u _ {\alpha} (s) \| _ {V} ^ {2} d s <   \infty , \text {   then   } \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq T} \| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2} <   \infty .

Proof. The proof of Theorem 9.1 shows that it is suficient to consider the homogeneous equation. Then, by inequalities (9.15)–(9.16),

By Corollary 6.1, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| u _ {\alpha} (s) \| _ {V} ^ {2} d s \\ = \sum_ {n \geq 1} \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \ldots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \| \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \varPhi_ {t, s _ {n}} \mathcal {M} _ {k _ {n}} \ldots \varPhi_ {s _ {1}} u _ {0} \| _ {V} ^ {2} d s ^ {n} d t <   \infty . \end{array}\tag{9.29}

As a result, (9.6) and (9.29) imply that

which, by (9.28), implies uniform, with respect to $t ,$ convergence of the series $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { \alpha \in \mathcal { T } } \| u _ { \alpha } ( t ) \| _ { H } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Corollary 9.1 is proved.

Remark 9.1 

(1) If (2.5) holds instead of (9.3), then the proof of Theorem 9.1, in particular, (9.15)–(9.16), shows that the term $\mathbb { E } \| u ( t ) \| _ { H } ^ { 2 }$ in the left-hand-side of inequality (9.4) can be replaced with

One of applications of the Wiener Chaos solution is new numerical methods for solving the evolution equations. Indeed, an approximation of the solution is obtained by truncating the sum $\textstyle \sum _ { \alpha \in \mathcal { I } } u _ { \alpha } ( t ) \xi _ { \alpha }$ . For the Zakai filtering equation, these numerical methods were studied in [25, 26, 27]; see also Section 11 below. The main question in the analysis is the rate of convergence, in $n ,$ of the series $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n \geq 1 } \sum _ { | \alpha | = n } \| u ( t ) \| _ { H } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . In general, this convergence can be arbitrarily slow. For example, consider the equation 

$$
d u = \frac {1}{2} u _ {x x} d t + u _ {x} d w (t), t > 0, x \in \mathbb {R},
$$

in the normal triple $( H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ , with the initial condition $u | _ { t = 0 } = u _ { 0 } \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . It follows from (9.12) that 

$$
F _ {n} (t) = \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} \| u \| _ {L _ {2} (\mathbb {R})} ^ {2} (t) = \frac {t ^ {n}}{n !} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | y | ^ {2 n} e ^ {- y ^ {2} t} | \hat {u} _ {0} | ^ {2} d y,
$$

where $\hat { u } _ { 0 }$ is the Fourier transform of $u _ { 0 }$ . If 

$$
| \hat {u} _ {0} (y) | ^ {2} = \frac {1}{(1 + | y | ^ {2}) ^ {\gamma}}, \gamma > 1 / 2,
$$

then the rate of decay of $F _ { n } ( t )$ is close to $n ^ { - ( 1 + 2 \gamma ) / 2 }$ . Note that, in this example, $\mathbb { E } \| u \| _ { L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ) } ^ { 2 } ( t ) = \| u _ { 0 } \| _ { L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ) } ^ { 2 }$ 

An exponential convergence rate that is uniform in $\| u _ { 0 } \| _ { H } ^ { 2 }$ is achieved under strong parabolicity condition (2.5). An even faster factorial rate is achieved when the operators $\mathcal { M } _ { k }$ are bounded on H.

As was mentioned earlier, the Wiener Chaos solution can be constructed for anticipating equations, that is, equations with $\mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { W }$ -measurable input data. With obvious modifications, inequality (9.4) holds if each of the input functions $u _ { 0 } , f ,$ and $g _ { k }$ in (9.1) is a finite linear combination of the basis elements $\xi _ { \alpha } .$ . The following example demonstrates that inequality (9.4) is impossible for a general anticipating equation. 

Example 9.1 Let $u = u ( t , x )$ be a Wiener Chaos solution of an ordinary differential equation 

$$
d u = u d w (t), t \leq 1,\tag{9.36}
$$

with $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { 0 } = \sum _ { \alpha \in \mathcal { I } } a _ { \alpha } \xi _ { \alpha } } \end{array}$ . For $n \geq 0$ , denote by $( n )$ the multi-index with $\alpha _ { 1 } = n$ and $\alpha _ { i } = 0 , i \geq 2$ , and assume that $a _ { ( n ) } > 0 , n \geq 0$ . Then 

$$
\mathbb {E} u ^ {2} (1) \geq C \sum_ {n \geq 0} e ^ {\sqrt {n}} a _ {(n)} ^ {2}.\tag{9.37}
$$

Indeed, the first column of propagator for $\alpha = ( n )$ is $u _ { ( 0 ) } ( t ) = a _ { ( 0 ) }$ and 

$$
u _ {(n)} (t) = a _ {(n)} + \sqrt {n} \int_ {0} ^ {t} u _ {(n - 1)} (s) d s,
$$

so that 

$$
u _ {(n)} (t) = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \frac {\sqrt {n !}}{\sqrt {(n - k) ! k !}} \frac {a _ {(n - k)}}{\sqrt {k !}} t ^ {k}.
$$

Then $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { ( n ) } ^ { 2 } ( 1 ) \geq \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { n } { \binom { n } { k } } \frac { a _ { ( n - k ) } ^ { 2 } } { k ! } } \end{array}$ and 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 0} u _ {(n)} ^ {2} (1) \geq \sum_ {n \geq 0} \left(\sum_ {k \geq 0} \frac {1}{k !} \binom {n + k} {n}\right) a _ {(n)} ^ {2}.
$$

Since 

$$
\sum_ {k \geq 0} \frac {1}{k !} \binom {n + k} {n} \geq \sum_ {k \geq 0} \frac {n ^ {k}}{(k !) ^ {2}} \geq C e ^ {\sqrt {n}},
$$

the result follows. 

The consequence of Example 9.1 is that it is possible, in (9.1), to have $u _ { 0 } \in L _ { 2 } ^ { n } ( \mathbb { W } ; H )$ for every n, and still get $\mathbb { E } \Vert u ( t ) \Vert _ { H } ^ { 2 } = + \infty$ for all $t > 0$ More generally, the solution operator for (9.1) is not bounded on any $L _ { 2 , Q }$ or $( S ) _ { - \rho , - \gamma }$ . On the other hand, the following result holds. 

Theorem 9.4. In addition to Assumptions A1, A2, let $u _ { 0 }$ be an element of $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } ( \mathbb { W } ; H ) , f ,$ an element of ${ \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) , V ^ { \prime } ) )$ , and each $g _ { k }$ , an element $o f ~ { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } ( \mathbb { W } ; L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) , H ) )$ ). Then the Wiener Chaos solution of equation (9.1) satisfies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {\| u _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2}}{\alpha !}} \leq C \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {1}{\sqrt {\alpha !}} \Bigg (\| u _ {0 \alpha} \| _ {H} + \bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {t} \| f _ {\alpha} (s) \| _ {V ^ {\prime}} ^ {2} d s \bigg) ^ {1 / 2} \\ \qquad + \left(\sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| g _ {k, \alpha} (s) \| _ {H} ^ {2} d s\right) ^ {1 / 2} \Bigg), \end{array}\tag{9.38}
$$

where $C > 0$ depends only on $T$ and the numbers $\delta , C _ { 1 }$ , and $C _ { 2 }$ from (9.2) and (9.3). 

Proof. To simplify the presentation, assume that $f = g _ { k } = 0$ . For fixed $\gamma \in \mathcal { I }$ denote by $u ( t ; \varphi ; \gamma )$ the Wiener Chaos solution of the equation (9.1) with initial condition $u ( 0 ; \varphi ; \gamma ) = \varphi \xi _ { \gamma }$ . Denote by (0) the zero multi-index. The structure of the propagator implies the following relation: 

$$
\frac {u _ {\alpha + \gamma} (t ; \varphi ; \gamma)}{\sqrt {(\alpha + \gamma) !}} = \frac {u _ {\alpha} \left(t ; \frac {\varphi}{\sqrt {\gamma !}} ; (0)\right)}{\sqrt {\alpha !}}.\tag{9.39}
$$

Clearly, $u _ { \alpha } ( t ; \varphi ; \gamma ) = 0 \ \mathrm { i f } \ | \alpha | < | \gamma |$ . If 

$$
\| v (t) \| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, 0} (H)} ^ {2} = \sum_ {\alpha \in \mathcal {J}} \frac {\| v _ {\alpha} (t) \| _ {H} ^ {2}}{\alpha !},
$$

then, by linearity and the triangle inequality, 

$$
\left\| u (t) \right\| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, 0} (H)} \leq \sum_ {\gamma \in \mathcal {J}} \left\| u (t; u _ {0 \gamma}; \gamma) \right\| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, 0} (H)}.
$$

We also have by (9.39) and Theorem 9.1 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| u (t; u _ {0 \gamma}; \gamma) \| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, 0} (H)} ^ {2} = \left\| u \left(t; \frac {u _ {0 \gamma}}{\sqrt {\gamma !}}; (0)\right) \right\| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, 0} (H)} ^ {2} \\ \qquad \leq \mathbb {E} \left\| u \left(t; \frac {u _ {0 \gamma}}{\sqrt {\gamma !}}; (0)\right) \right\| _ {H} ^ {2} \leq e ^ {C _ {2} t} \frac {\| u _ {0 \gamma} \| _ {H} ^ {2}}{\gamma !}. \end{array}
$$

Inequality (9.38) then follows. Theorem 9.4 is proved. 

Remark 9.2 Using Proposition 7.1 and the Cauchy–Schwartz inequality, (9.38) can be rewritten in a slightly weaker form to reveal continuity of the solution operator for equation (9.1) from $( S ) _ { - 1 , \gamma } ~ \mathrm { t o } ~ ( S ) _ { - 1 , 0 }$ for every $\gamma > 1 $ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\| u (t) \| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, 0} (H)} ^ {2} \leq C \Bigg (\| u _ {0} \| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, \gamma} (H)} ^ {2} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| f (s) \| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, \gamma} (V ^ {\prime})} ^ {2} d s} \\ & {\qquad + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| g _ {k} (s) \| _ {(\mathcal {S}) _ {- 1, \gamma} (H)} ^ {2} d s \Bigg).} \end{array}
$$

## 10 Probabilistic Representation of Wiener Chaos Solutions

The general discussion so far has been dealing with the abstract evolution equation 

$$
d u = (\mathcal {A} u + f) d t + \sum_ {k \geq 1} (\mathcal {M} _ {k} u + g _ {k}) d w _ {k}.
$$

By further specifying the operators and $\mathcal { M } _ { k }$ , as well as the input data $u _ { 0 } , f ,$ and $g _ { k }$ , it is possible to get additional information about the Wiener Chaos solution of the equation. 

Definition 10.1 For $r \in \mathbb { R }$ , the space $L _ { 2 , ( r ) } = L _ { 2 , ( r ) } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ is the collection of real-valued measurable functions such that $f \in L _ { 2 , ( r ) }$ if and only if 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} | f (x) | ^ {2} (1 + | x | ^ {2}) ^ {r} d x <   \infty .
$$

The space $H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 } = H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ is the collection of real-valued measurable functions such that $f \in H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 }$ if and only if f and all the first-order generalized derivatives $D _ { i } f$ of f belong to $\boldsymbol { L } _ { 2 , ( r ) }$ 

It is known, for example, from Theorem 3.4.7 in [42], that $L _ { 2 , ( r ) }$ is a Hilbert space with the norm 

$$
\| f \| _ {0, (r)} ^ {2} = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} | f (x) | ^ {2} (1 + | x | ^ {2}) ^ {r} d x,
$$

and $H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 }$ is a Hilbert space with the norm 

$$
\| f \| _ {1, (r)} = \| f \| _ {0, (r)} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d} \| D _ {i} f \| _ {0, (r)}.
$$

Denote by $H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { - 1 }$ the dual of $H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 }$ with respect to the inner product in $\boldsymbol { L } _ { 2 , ( r ) }$ Then $( H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 } , L _ { 2 , ( r ) } , H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { - 1 } )$ is a normal triple of Hilbert spaces. 

Let $\mathbb { F } = ( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { t \geq 0 } , \mathbb { P } )$ be a stochastic basis with the usual assumptions and $w _ { k } = w _ { k } ( t ) , k \geq 1 , t \geq 0$ , a collection of standard Wiener processes on F. Consider the linear equation 

$$
d u = (a _ {i j} D _ {i} D _ {j} u + b _ {i} D _ {i} u + c u + f) d t + (\sigma_ {i k} D _ {i} u + \nu_ {k} u + g _ {k}) d w _ {k}\tag{10.1}
$$

under the following assumptions: 

B0 All coeficients, free terms, and the initial condition are non-random. 

B1 The functions $a _ { i j } = a _ { i j } ( t , x )$ and their first-order derivatives with respect to x are uniformly bounded in $( t , x )$ , and the matrix $( a _ { i j } )$ is uniformly positive definite, that is, there exists $\delta \ > \ 0$ such that, for all vectors $y \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and all $( t , x ) , a _ { i j } y _ { i } y _ { j } \geq \delta | y | ^ { 2 }$ 

B2 The functions $b _ { i } = b _ { i } ( t , x ) , c = c ( t , x )$ , and $\nu _ { k } = \nu _ { k } ( t , x )$ are measurable and bounded in $( t , x )$ 

B3 The functions $\sigma _ { i k } = \sigma _ { i k } ( t , x )$ are continuous and bounded in $( t , x )$ 

B4 The functions $f = f ( t , x )$ and $g _ { k } = g _ { k } ( t , x )$ belong to $L _ { 2 } ( ( 0 , T ) ; L _ { 2 , ( r ) } )$ for some $r \in \mathbb { R }$ 

B5 The initial condition $u _ { 0 } = u _ { 0 } ( x )$ belongs to $\boldsymbol { L } _ { 2 , ( r ) }$ 

Under Assumptions B2–B4, there exists a sequence $Q = \{ q _ { k } , k \ge 1 \}$ of positive numbers with the following properties: 

P1 The matrix A with $\begin{array} { r } { A _ { i j } = a _ { i j } - ( 1 / 2 ) \sum _ { k \geq 1 } q _ { k } \sigma _ { i k } \sigma _ { j k } } \end{array}$ satisfies the inequality 

$$
A _ {i j} (t, x) y _ {i} y _ {j} \geq 0,
$$

$$
x, y \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}, 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

P2 There exists a number $C > 0$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {k \geq 1} \left(\sup _ {t, x} | q _ {k} \nu_ {k} (t, x) | ^ {2} + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| q _ {k} g _ {k} \| _ {0, (r)} ^ {p} (t) d t\right) \leq C.
$$

For the matrix A and each $t , x ,$ we have $A _ { i j } ( t , x ) = \tilde { \sigma } _ { i k } ( t , x ) \tilde { \sigma } _ { j k } ( t , x )$ where the functions $\tilde { \sigma } _ { i k }$ are bounded. This representation might not be unique; see, for example, [7, Theorem III.2.2] or [44, Lemma 5.2.1]. Given any such representation of $A ,$ consider the following backward Itˆo equation 

S. Lototsky and B. Rozovskii 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {t, x, i} \left(s\right) = x _ {i} + \int_ {s} ^ {t} B _ {i} \left(\tau , X _ {t, x} \left(\tau\right)\right) d \tau + \sum_ {k \geq 1} q _ {k} \sigma_ {i k} \left(\tau , X _ {t, x} \left(\tau\right)\right) \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} \left(\tau\right) \\ \quad + \int_ {s} ^ {t} \tilde {\sigma} _ {i k} \left(\tau , X _ {t, x} \left(\tau\right)\right) \overleftarrow {d \tilde {w}} _ {k} \left(\tau\right); s \in (0, t), t \in (0, T ], t - \text { fixed }, \end{array}\tag{10.2}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { i } = b _ { i } - \sum _ { k > 1 } q _ { k } ^ { 2 } \sigma _ { i k } \nu _ { k } } \end{array}$ and $\tilde { w } _ { k } , \ k \geq 1$ , are independent standard Wiener processes on F that are independent of $w _ { k } , k \ge 1$ . This equation might not have a strong solution, but does have a weak, or martingale, solution due to Assumptions B1–B3 and properties P1 and P2 of the sequence $Q ;$ this weak solution is unique in the sense of probability law [44, Theorem 7.2.1]. 

The following result is a variation of Theorem 4.1 in [29]. 

Theorem 10.1. Under assumptions B0–B5 equation (10.1) has a unique w $\ d _ { 7 } ( H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 } , H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { - 1 } ) \ d _ { }$ Wiener Chaos solution. If Q is a sequence with properties P1 and P2, then the solution of (10.1) belongs to 

$$
L _ {2, Q} \left(\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); H _ {2, (r)} ^ {1})\right) \bigcap L _ {2, Q} \left(\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); L _ {2, (r)})\right)
$$

and has the following representation: 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u (t, x) = \mathcal {Q} ^ {- 1} \mathbb {E} \Bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {t} f (s, X _ {t, x} (s)) \gamma (t, s, x) d s \\ + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} q _ {k} g _ {k} (s, X _ {t, x} (s)) \gamma (t, s, x) \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} (s) + u _ {0} (X _ {t, x} (0)) \gamma (t, 0, x) \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {W} \Bigg), t \leq T, \end{array}\tag{10.3}
$$

where $X _ { t , x } ( s )$ is a weak solution of (10.2), and 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\gamma (t, s, x) = \exp \left(\int_ {s} ^ {t} c (\tau , X _ {t, x} (\tau)) d \tau + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {s} ^ {t} q _ {k} \nu_ {k} (\tau , X _ {t, x} (\tau)) \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} (\tau) \right.\\\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {s} ^ {t} \sum_ {k \geq 1} q _ {k} ^ {2} | \nu_ {k} (\tau , X _ {t, x} (\tau)) | ^ {2} d \tau\left. \right).\end{array}\tag{10.4}
$$

Proof. It is enough to establish (10.3) when $t = T$ . Consider the equation 

$$
d U = (a _ {i j} D _ {i} D _ {j} U + b _ {i} D _ {i} U + c U + f) d t + \sum_ {k \geq 1} (\sigma_ {i k} D _ {i} U + \nu_ {k} U + g _ {k}) q _ {k} d w _ {k}\tag{10.5}
$$

with initial condition $U ( 0 , x ) = u _ { 0 } ( x )$ . Applying Theorem 2.1 in the normal triple $( H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 } , L _ { 2 , ( r ) } , H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { - 1 } )$ , we conclude that there is a unique solution 

$$
U \in L _ {2} \left(\mathbb {W}; L _ {2} ((0, T); H _ {2, (r)} ^ {1})\right) \bigcap L _ {2} \left(\mathbb {W}; \mathbf {C} ((0, T); L _ {2, (r)})\right)
$$

of this equation. By Proposition 7.2, the process $u = \mathcal { Q } ^ { - 1 } U$ is the corresponding Wiener Chaos solution of (10.1). To establish representation (10.3), consider the S-transform $U _ { h }$ of $U$ . According to Theorem 8.1, the function $U _ { h }$ is the unique w $( H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { 1 } , H _ { 2 , ( r ) } ^ { - 1 } )$ solution of the equation 

$$
d U _ {h} = (a _ {i j} D _ {i} D _ {j} U _ {h} + b _ {i} D _ {i} U _ {h} + c U _ {h} + f) d t + \sum_ {k \geq 1} (\sigma_ {i k} D _ {i} U _ {h} + \nu_ {k} U _ {h} + g _ {k}) q _ {k} h _ {k} d t\tag{10.6}
$$

with initial condition $U _ { h } | _ { t = 0 } = u _ { 0 }$ . We also define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y (T, x) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} f (s, X _ {T, x} (s)) \gamma (T, s, x) d s \\ \qquad + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {T} g _ {k} (s, X _ {T, x} (s)) \gamma (T, s) q _ {k} \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} (s) + u _ {0} (X _ {T, x} (0)) \gamma (T, 0, x). \end{array}\tag{10.7}
$$

By direct computation, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) Y (T, x) | \mathcal {F} _ {T} ^ {W}\right)\right) = \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) Y (T, x)\right) = \mathbb {E} ^ {\prime} Y (T, x),
$$

where $\mathbb { E } ^ { \prime }$ is the expectation with respect to the measure $d \mathbb { P } _ { T } ^ { \prime } = \mathcal { E } ( h ) d \mathbb { P } _ { T }$ and $\mathbb { P } _ { T }$ is the restriction of P to $\mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { W }$ 

To proceed, let us first assume that the input data $u _ { 0 } , f ,$ and $g _ { k }$ are all smooth functions with compact support. Then, applying the Feynmann–Kac formula to the solution of equation (10.6) and using Girsanov’s theorem (see, $\mathrm { e . g . }$ ., Theorems 3.5.1 and 5.7.6 in [15]), we conclude that $U _ { h } ( T , x ) = \mathbb { E } ^ { \prime } Y ( T , x )$ or 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) \mathbb {E} Y (t, x) | \mathcal {F} _ {T} ^ {W}\right) = \mathbb {E} \left(\mathcal {E} (h) U (T, x)\right).
$$

By Remark 7.1, the last equality implies $U \left( T , \cdot \right) = \mathbb { E } \left( Y ( T , \cdot ) | \mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { W } \right)$ as elements of $L _ { 2 } \left( \varOmega ; L _ { 2 , ( r ) } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) \right)$ 

To remove the additional smoothness assumption on the input data, let $u _ { 0 } ^ { n } , \ f ^ { n }$ , and $g _ { k } ^ { n }$ be sequences of smooth compactly supported functions such that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \Bigg (\| u _ {0} - u _ {0} ^ {n} \| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| f - f ^ {n} \| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} (t) d t \\ \qquad + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {T} q _ {k} ^ {2} \| g _ {k} - g _ {k} ^ {n} \| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} (t) d t \Bigg) = 0. \end{array}\tag{10.8}
$$

Denote by $U ^ { n }$ and $Y ^ { n }$ the corresponding objects defined by (10.5) and (10.7) respectively. By Theorem 9.1, we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mathbb {E} \| U - U ^ {n} \| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} (T) = 0.\tag{10.9}
$$

To complete the proof, it remains to show that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mathbb {E} \left\| \mathbb {E} \left(Y (T, \cdot) - Y ^ {n} (T, \cdot) \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {T} ^ {W}\right) \right\| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} = 0.\tag{10.10}
$$

To this end, introduce a new probability measure 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \mathbb {P} _ {T} ^ {\prime \prime} = \exp \left(2 \sum_ {k \geq 1} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \nu_ {k} (s, X _ {T, x} ^ {Q} (s)) q _ {k} \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} (s) \right. \\ \left. - 2 \int_ {0} ^ {T} \sum_ {k > 1} q _ {k} ^ {2} | \nu_ {k} (s, X _ {T, x} ^ {Q} (s)) | ^ {2} d s\right) d \mathbb {P} _ {T}. \end{array}
$$

By Girsanov’s theorem, equation (10.2) can be rewritten as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {T, x, i} (s) = x _ {i} + \int_ {s} ^ {T} \sum_ {k \geq 1} \sigma_ {i k} (\tau , X _ {T, x} (\tau)) h _ {k} (\tau) q _ {k} d \tau \\ \quad + \int_ {s} ^ {t} (b _ {i} + \sum_ {k \geq 1} q _ {k} ^ {2} \sigma_ {i k} \nu_ {k}) (\tau , X _ {T, x} (\tau)) d \tau \\ \quad + \int_ {s} ^ {t} \sum_ {k > 1} q _ {k} \sigma_ {i k} (\tau , X _ {T, x} (\tau)) \overleftarrow {d w _ {k} ^ {\prime \prime}} (\tau) + \int_ {s} ^ {t} \tilde {\sigma} _ {i k} (\tau , X _ {T, x} (\tau)) \overleftarrow {d w _ {k} ^ {\prime \prime}} (\tau), \end{array}\tag{10.11}
$$

where $w _ { k } ^ { \prime \prime }$ and $\tilde { w ^ { \prime \prime } } _ { k }$ are independent Wiener processes with respect to the measure $\mathbb { P } _ { T } ^ { \prime \prime }$ . Denote by $p ( s , y \vert x )$ the corresponding distribution density of $X _ { T , x } ( s )$ and write $\ell ( x ) = ( 1 + | x | ^ { 2 } ) ^ { \prime }$ <sup>r</sup>. It then follows by the H¨older and Jensen inequalities that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathbb {E} \left\| \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \gamma^ {2} (T, s, \cdot) (f - f ^ {n}) (s, X _ {T, \cdot} (s)) d s \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {T} ^ {W}\right) \right\| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2}} \\ & {\leq K _ {1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \mathbb {E} \left(\gamma^ {2} (T, s, x) (f - f ^ {n}) ^ {2} (s, X _ {T, x} (s))\right) d s\right) \ell (x) d x} \\ & {\qquad \leq K _ {2} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \mathbb {E} ^ {\prime \prime} (f - f ^ {n}) ^ {2} (s, X _ {T, x} (s)) d s\right) \ell (x) d x} \\ & {\quad = K _ {2} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} (f (s, y) - f ^ {n} (s, y)) ^ {2} p (s, y | x) d y d s \ell (x) d x,} \end{array}\tag{10.12}
$$

where the number $K _ { 1 }$ depends only on $T _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and the number $K _ { 2 }$ depends only on $T$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { ( t , x ) } | c ( t , x ) | + \sum _ { k \geq 1 } q _ { k } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ sup ν<sub>k</sub>(t, x) <sup>2</sup>. Assumptions B0–B2 <sub>imply that there exist positive numbers</sub> $K _ { 3 }$ and $K _ { 4 }$ such that 

$$
p (s, y | x) \leq \frac {K _ {3}}{(T - s) ^ {d / 2}} \exp \left(- K _ {4} \frac {| x - y | ^ {2}}{T - s}\right);\tag{10.13}
$$

see, for example, [6]. As a result, 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} p (s, y | x) \ell (x) d x \leq K _ {5} \ell (y),
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} (f (s, y) - f ^ {n} (s, y)) ^ {2} p (s, y | x) d y d s \ell (x) d x \\ \qquad \leq K _ {5} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| f - f ^ {n} \| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} (s) d s \to 0, n \to \infty , \end{array}\tag{10.14}
$$

where the number $K _ { 5 }$ depends only on $K _ { 3 } , K _ { 4 } , T$ , and $r .$ 

Calculations similar to (10.12)–(10.14) show that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \left\| \mathbb {E} \left(\gamma^ {2} (T, 0, \cdot) (u _ {0} - u _ {0} ^ {n}) (X _ {T, \cdot} (0)) \Big | \mathbb {W}\right) \right\| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} \\ + \mathbb {E} \left\| \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \sum_ {k \geq 1} (g _ {k} - g _ {k} ^ {n}) (s, X _ {T, \cdot} (s)) \gamma (t, s, \cdot) q _ {k} \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} (s) \Big | \mathbb {W}\right) \right\| _ {L _ {2, (r)} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} \to 0 \end{array}\tag{10.15}
$$

as $n  \infty$ . Then convergence (10.10) follows, which, together with (10.9), implies that $U \left( T , \cdot \right) = \mathbb { E } \left( \bar { U } ^ { Q } ( T , \cdot ) | \mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { W } \right)$ as elements of $L _ { 2 } \left( \varOmega ; L _ { 2 , ( r ) } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) \right)$ . It remains to note that $u = \mathcal { Q } ^ { - 1 } U$ . Theorem 10.1 is proved. 

Given $f \in L _ { 2 , ( r ) }$ , we say that $f \geq 0$ if and only if 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} f (x) \varphi (x) d x \geq 0
$$

for every non-negative $\varphi \in { \bf C } _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ . Then Theorem 10.1 implies the following result. 

Corollary 10.1 In addition to Assumptions B0–B5, let $u _ { 0 } \geq 0 , f \geq 0$ , and $g _ { k } = 0$ for all $k \geq 1$ . Then $u \geq 0$ 

Proof. This follows from (10.3) and Proposition 7.3. 

Example 10.1 (Krylov–Veretennikov formula) 

Consider the equation 

$$
d u = \left(a _ {i j} D _ {i} D _ {j} u + b _ {i} D _ {i} u\right) d t + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {d} \sigma_ {i k} D _ {i} u d w _ {k}, u (0, x) = u _ {0} (x).\tag{10.16}
$$

Assume B0–B5 and suppose that $\begin{array} { r } { a _ { i j } ( t , x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sigma _ { i k } ( t , x ) \sigma _ { j k } ( t , x ) } \end{array}$ . By Theorem 9.1, equation (10.16) has a unique Wiener chaos solution such that 

$$
\mathbb {E} \| u \| _ {L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} (t) \leq C ^ {*} \| u _ {0} \| _ {L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u (t, x) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {| \alpha | = n} u _ {\alpha} (t, x) \xi_ {\alpha} = u _ {0} (x) + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} = 1} ^ {d} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {s _ {2}} \\ \Phi_ {t, s _ {n}} \sigma_ {j k _ {n}} D _ {j} \dots \Phi_ {s _ {2}, s _ {1}} \sigma_ {i k _ {1}} D _ {i} \Phi_ {s _ {1}, 0} u _ {0} (x) d w _ {k _ {1}} (s _ {1}) \dots d w _ {k _ {n}} (s _ {n}), \end{array}\tag{10.17}
$$

where $\varPhi _ { t , s }$ is the semigroup generated by the operator $\mathcal { A } = a _ { i j } D _ { i } D _ { j } u + b _ { i } D _ { i } u .$ On the other hand, in this case, Theorem 10.1 yields

\begin{array}{c} X _ {t, x, i} \left(s\right) = x _ {i} + \int_ {s} ^ {t} b _ {i} \left(\tau , X _ {t, x} \left(\tau\right)\right) d \tau + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {d} \sigma_ {i k} \left(\tau , X _ {t, x} \left(\tau\right)\right) \overleftarrow {d w _ {k}} \left(\tau\right), \\ s \in (0, t), t \in (0, T ], t - \text { fixed }. \end{array}\tag{10.18}

## 11 Wiener Chaos and Nonlinear Filtering

In this section, we discuss some applications of the Wiener Chaos expansion to numerical solution of the nonlinear filtering problem for difusion processes; the presentation is essentially based on [25]. 

Let $( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \mathbb { P } )$ be a complete probability space with independent standard Wiener processes $W = W ( t )$ and $V = V ( t )$ of dimensions $d _ { 1 }$ and r respectively. Let $X _ { 0 }$ be a random variable independent of W and V. In the $d i f f u .$ sion filtering model, the unobserved d-dimensional state (or signal) process $X = X ( t )$ and the r-dimensional observation process $Y = Y ( t )$ are defined by the stochastic ordinary diferential equations 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d X (t) = b (X (t)) d t + \sigma (X (t)) d W (t) + \rho (X (t)) d V (t), \\ d Y (t) = h (X (t)) d t + d V (t), 0 <   t \leq T; \\ X (0) = X _ {0}, \quad Y (0) = 0, \end{array}\tag{11.1}
$$

where $b ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , \sigma ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d \times d _ { 1 } } , \rho ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d \times r } , h ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { r } .$ 

Denote by $\mathbf { C } ^ { n } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ the Banach space of bounded, n times continuously diferentiable functions on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ with finite norm 

$$
\| f \| _ {\mathbf {C} ^ {n} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})} = \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} | f (x) | + \max _ {1 \leq k \leq n} \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} | D ^ {k} f (x) |.
$$

Assumption R1. The components of the functions σ and $\rho$ are in $\mathbf { C } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ the components of the functions b are in $\mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ , the components of the function $h$ are bounded measurable, and the random variable $X _ { 0 }$ has a density $u _ { 0 }$ 

Assumption R2. The matrix $\sigma \sigma ^ { * }$ is uniformly positive definite: there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {d _ {1}} \sigma_ {i k} (x) \sigma_ {j k} (x) y _ {i} y _ {j} \geq \varepsilon | y | ^ {2}, x, y \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}.
$$

Under Assumption R1 system (11.1) has a unique strong solution [15, Theorems 5.2.5 and 5.2.9]. Extra smoothness of the coeficients in assumption R1 insure the existence of a convenient representation of the optimal filter. 

If f is a scalar measurable function on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { t < T } \mathbb { E } | f ( X ( t ) ) | ^ { 2 } < \infty } \end{array}$ then the filtering problem for (11.1) is to find the best mean square estimate $\hat { f } _ { t }$ of $f ( X ( t ) ) , \ t \leq T$ , given the observations $Y ( s ) , s \leq t .$ 

Denote by $\mathbf { \mathcal { F } } _ { t } ^ { Y }$ the σ-algebra generated by $Y ( s ) , s \leq t$ . Then the properties of the conditional expectation imply that the solution of the filtering problem is 

$$
\hat {f} _ {t} = \mathbb {E} \left(f (X (t)) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {Y}\right).
$$

To derive an alternative representation of $\hat { f } _ { t }$ , some additional constructions will be necessary. 

Define on $( \varOmega , \mathscr { F } )$ the probability measure $d \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } = Z _ { T } ^ { - 1 } d \mathbb { P }$ where 

$$
Z _ {t} = \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} h ^ {*} (X (s)) d Y (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} | h (X (s)) | ^ {2} d s \right\}
$$

(here and below, if $\zeta \in \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ , then $\zeta$ is a column vector, $\zeta ^ { * } = ( \zeta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \zeta _ { k } ) .$ , and $| \zeta | ^ { 2 } = \zeta ^ { * } \zeta )$ . If the function $h$ is bounded, then the measures P and $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ are equivalent. The expectation with respect to the measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ *will be denoted by E. 

*The following properties of the measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ are well known [14, 42]: 

P1. Under the measure ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ the distributions of the Wiener process $W$ and the random variable $X _ { 0 }$ are unchanged, the observation process $Y$ is a standard Wiener process, and, for $t \leq T$ , the state process X satisfies: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d X (t) = b (X (t)) d t + \sigma (X (t)) d W (t) + \rho (X (t)) \left(d Y (t) - h (X (t)) d t\right), \\ X (0) = X _ {0}. \end{array}

P2. Under the measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { \cdot }$ the Wiener processes $W$ and $Y$ and the random variable $X _ { 0 }$ *are independent of one another. 

P3. The optimal filter $\hat { f } _ { t }$ satisfies the relation

Because of property P2 of the measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ the filtering problem will be studied on the probability space $( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } )$ *. In particular, we will consider the stochastic basis $\widetilde { \mathbb { F } } = \{ \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { Y } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } , \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } \}$ and the Wiener Chaos space $\widetilde { L } _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { Y } )$ of $\mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { Y }$ *-measurable random variables $\eta$ *with $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } | \eta | ^ { 2 } < \infty$

Note that, under the assumptions R1 and R2, the operators ${ \mathcal { L } } , { \mathcal { L } } ^ { * }$ are bounded from $H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ to $H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb R ^ { d } )$ , operators $\mathcal { M } , \mathcal { M } ^ { * }$ are bounded from $H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ to $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ , and

where $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ is the duality between $H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ and $H _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ . The following result is well known [42, Theorem 6.2.1]. 

Proposition 11.1 In addition to Assumptions R1 and R1 suppose that the initial density u belongs to $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ . Then there is a random field $u = u ( t , x )$ 1 $t \in [ 0 , T ] , \ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , with the following properties:

*2. The function $u ( t , x )$ *is a traditional solution of the stochastic partial diferential equation

The random field $u = u ( t , x )$ is called the unnormalized filtering density (UFD) and the random variable $\varphi _ { t } [ f ] = \widetilde { \mathbb { E } } \left[ f ( X ( t ) ) Z _ { t } \vert \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { Y } \right]$ , the unnormalized optimal filter. 

A number of authors studied the nonlinear filtering problem using the multiple Itˆo integral version of the Wiener Chaos [2, 21, 39, 46, etc.]. In what follows, we construct approximations of u and $\varphi _ { t } [ f ]$ using the Cameron– Martin version. 

By Theorem 8.3,

We also need extra regularity of the coeficients in the state and observation equations — to have the semi-group generated by the operator $\mathcal { L } ^ { \ast }$ continuous not only in $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ but also in $H _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { \bar { d } } )$ . ## 12 Passive Scalar in a Gaussian Field

This section presents the results from [29] and [28] about the stochastic transport equation. 

The following viscous transport equation is used to describe the time evolution of a scalar quantity $\theta$ in a given velocity field v: 

$$
\dot {\theta} (t, x) = \nu \Delta \theta (t, x) - \mathbf {v} (t, x) \cdot \nabla \theta (t, x) + f (t, x); x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}, d > 1.\tag{12.1}
$$

The scalar θ is called passive because it does not afect the velocity field v. 

We assume that $\mathbf { v } = \mathbf { v } ( t , x ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is an isotropic Gaussian vector field with zero mean and covariance 

$$
\mathbb {E} (v ^ {i} (t, x) v ^ {j} (s, y)) = \delta (t - s) C ^ {i j} (x - y),
$$

where $C = ( C ^ { i j } ( x ) , i , j = 1 , \dots , d )$ is a matrix-valued function such that $C ( 0 )$ is a scalar matrix; with no loss of generality we will assume that $C ( 0 ) = I$ the identity matrix. 

It is known from [22, Section 10.1] that, for an isotropic Gaussian vector field, the Fourier transform $\hat { C } = \hat { C } ( z )$ of the function $C = C ( x )$ is 

$$
\hat {C} (y) = \frac {A _ {0}}{(1 + | y | ^ {2}) ^ {(d + \alpha) / 2}} \left(a \frac {y y ^ {*}}{| y | ^ {2}} + \frac {b}{d - 1} \left(I - \frac {y y ^ {T}}{| y | ^ {2}}\right)\right),\tag{12.2}
$$

where $y ^ { * }$ is the row vector $( y _ { 1 } , \ldots , y _ { d } )$ , y is the corresponding column vector, $| y | ^ { 2 } = y ^ { * } y ; \gamma > 0 , a \ge 0 , b \ge 0 , A _ { 0 } > 0$ are real numbers. Similar to [22], we assume that $0 < \gamma < 2$ . This range of values of $\gamma$ corresponds to a turbulent velocity field v, also known as the generalized Kraichnan model [8]; the original Kraichnan model $\lceil 1 8 \rceil$ corresponds to $a = 0$ . For small $x ,$ the asymptotics of $C ^ { i j } ( x )$ is $( \delta _ { i j } - c ^ { i j } | x | ^ { \gamma } )$ [22, Section 10.2]. 

By direct computation (cf. [1]), the vector field $\mathbf { v } = ( v ^ { 1 } , \ldots , v ^ { d } )$ can be written as 

$$
v ^ {i} (t, x) = \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} (x) \dot {w} _ {k} (t),\tag{12.3}
$$

where $\{ \sigma _ { k } , \ k \geq 1 \}$ is an orthonormal basis in the space $H _ { C } ,$ the reproducing kernel Hilbert space corresponding to the kernel function $C . \mathrm { I t }$ is known from [22] that $H _ { C }$ is all or a part of the Sobolev space $H ^ { ( d + \gamma ) / 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ . 

If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ , then the matrix $\hat { C }$ is invertible and 

$$
H _ {C} = \left\{f \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}: \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \hat {f} ^ {*} (y) \hat {C} ^ {- 1} (y) \hat {f} (y) d y <   \infty \right\} = H ^ {(d + \gamma) / 2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}),
$$

because $\| \hat { C } ( y ) \| \sim ( 1 + | y | ^ { 2 } ) ^ { - ( d + \gamma ) / 2 }$ 

If $a > 0$ and $b = 0 .$ , then 

$$
H _ {C} = \left\{f \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}: \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} | \hat {f} (y) | ^ {2} (1 + | y | ^ {2}) ^ {(d + \gamma) / 2} d y <   \infty ; y y ^ {*} \hat {f} (y) = | y | ^ {2} \hat {f} (y) \right\},
$$

the subset of gradient fields in $H ^ { ( d + \gamma ) / 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ , that is, the vector fields $f$ for which ${ \hat { f } } ( y ) = y { \hat { F } } ( y )$ for some scalar $F \in H ^ { ( d + \gamma + 2 ) / 2 } ( \mathbb R ^ { d } )$ 

If $a = 0$ and $b > 0$ , then 

$$
H _ {C} = \left\{f \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}: \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} | \hat {f} (y) | ^ {2} (1 + | y | ^ {2}) ^ {(d + \gamma) / 2} d y <   \infty ; y ^ {*} \hat {f} (y) = 0 \right\},
$$

the subset of divergence-free fields in $H ^ { ( d + \gamma ) / 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ 

By the embedding theorems, each $\sigma _ { k } ^ { i }$ is a bounded continuous function on $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } ;$ in fact, every $\sigma _ { k } ^ { i }$ is H¨older continuous of order $\gamma / 2$ . In addition, being an element of the corresponding space $H _ { C }$ , each $\sigma _ { k }$ is a gradient field if $b = 0$ and is divergence-free if $a = 0$ 

Equation (12.1) becomes 

$$
d \theta (t, x) = (\nu \Delta \theta (t, x) + f (t, x)) d t - \sum_ {k} \sigma_ {k} (x) \cdot \nabla \theta (t, x) d w _ {k} (t).\tag{12.4}
$$

We summarize the above constructions in the following assumptions: 

S1 There is a fixed stochastic basis $\mathbb { F } = ( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { t \geq 0 } , \mathbb { P } )$ with the usual assumptions and $( w _ { k } ( t ) , k \geq 1 , t \geq 0 )$ is a collection of independent standard Wiener processes on $\mathbb { F } .$ 

S2 For each $k ,$ the vector field $\sigma _ { k }$ is an element of the Sobolev space 

$$
H _ {2} ^ {(d + \gamma) / 2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}), 0 <   \gamma <   2, d \geq 2.
$$

To obtain the expressions of the higher-order moments in terms of the coeficients $\theta _ { \alpha } .$ , we need some auxiliary constructions. 

For $\alpha , ~ \beta \in { \mathcal { I } } ,$ , define $\alpha + \beta$ as the multi-index with components $\alpha _ { i } ^ { k } + \beta _ { i } ^ { k }$ Similarly, we define the multi-indices $| \alpha - \beta |$ and $\alpha \wedge \beta = \operatorname* { m i n } ( \alpha , \beta )$ . We write $\beta \leq \alpha$ if and only if $\beta _ { i } ^ { k } \le \alpha _ { i } ^ { k }$ for all $i , k \geq 1$ . If $\beta \leq \alpha .$ , we define 

$$
\binom{\alpha}{\beta} := \prod_ {i, k} \frac {\alpha_ {i} ^ {k} !}{\beta_ {i} ^ {k} ! (\alpha_ {i} ^ {k} - \beta_ {i} ^ {k}) !}.
$$

Definition 12.1 We say that a triple of multi-indices $( \alpha , \beta , \gamma )$ is complete and write $( \alpha , \beta , \gamma ) \in \triangle$ if all the entries of the multi-index $\alpha + \beta + \gamma$ are even numbers and $| \alpha - \beta | \leq \gamma \leq \alpha + \beta$ . For fixed α, $\beta \in \mathcal { I }$ , we write 

$$
\triangle (\alpha) := \{\gamma , \mu \in \mathcal {J}: (\alpha , \gamma , \mu) \in \triangle \}
$$

and 

$$
\triangle (\alpha , \beta) := \{\gamma \in \mathcal {J}: (\alpha , \beta , \gamma) \in \triangle \}.
$$

For $( \alpha , \beta , \gamma ) \in \triangle$ , we define 

$$
\Psi \left(\alpha , \beta , \gamma\right) := \sqrt {\alpha ! \beta ! \gamma !} \left(\left(\frac {\alpha - \beta + \gamma}{2}\right)! \left(\frac {\beta - \alpha + \gamma}{2}\right)! \left(\frac {\alpha + \beta - \gamma}{2}\right)!\right) ^ {- 1}.\tag{12.12}
$$

Note that the triple $( \alpha , \beta , \gamma )$ is complete if and only if any permutation of the triple $( \alpha , \beta , \gamma )$ is complete. Similarly, the value of $\varPsi \left( \alpha , \beta , \gamma \right)$ is invariant under permutation of the arguments. 

We also define 

$$
C \left(\gamma , \beta , \mu\right) := \left[ \binom{\gamma + \beta - 2 \mu}{\gamma - \mu} \binom{\gamma}{\mu} \binom{\beta}{\mu} \right] ^ {1 / 2},   \mu \leq \gamma \wedge \beta .\tag{12.13}
$$

It is readily checked that if $f$ is a function on $\mathcal { I }$ , then for $\gamma , \beta \in \mathcal { I }$ 

$$
\sum_ {\mu \leq \gamma \wedge \beta} C (\gamma , \beta , p) f (\gamma + \beta - 2 \mu) = \sum_ {\mu \in (\gamma , \beta)} f (\mu) \Phi (\gamma , \beta , \mu)\tag{12.14}
$$

The next theorem presents the formulas for the third and fourth moments of the solution of equation (12.6) in terms of the coeficients $\theta _ { \alpha }$ 

Theorem 12.3. In addition to $_ { S 1 - S 4 }$ , assume that each $\sigma _ { k }$ is divergence-free and the initial condition $\theta _ { 0 }$ belongs to $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) \cap L _ { 4 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ . Then 

$$
\mathbb {E} \theta (t, x) \theta \left(t ^ {\prime}, x ^ {\prime}\right) \theta (s, y) = \sum_ {(\alpha , \beta , \gamma) \in \triangle} \Psi (\alpha , \beta , \gamma) \theta_ {\alpha} (t, x) \theta_ {\beta} (t ^ {\prime}, x ^ {\prime}) \theta_ {\gamma} (s, y)\tag{12.15}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \theta (t, x) \theta (t ^ {\prime}, x ^ {\prime}) \theta (s, y) \theta (s ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}) \\ = \sum_ {\rho \in \triangle (\alpha , \beta) \cap \triangle (\gamma , \kappa)} \Psi (\alpha , \beta , \rho) \Psi (\rho , \gamma , \kappa) \theta_ {\alpha} (t, x) \theta_ {\beta} (t ^ {\prime}, x ^ {\prime}) \theta_ {\gamma} (s, y) \theta_ {\kappa} (s ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}). \end{array} \tag {12.16}
$$

Proof. It is known, [30], that 

$$
\xi_ {\gamma} \xi_ {\beta} = \sum_ {\mu \leq \gamma \wedge \beta} C (\gamma , \beta , \mu) \xi_ {\gamma + \beta - 2 \mu}.\tag{12.17}
$$

Let us consider the triple product $\xi _ { \alpha } \xi _ { \beta } \xi _ { \gamma }$ . By (12.17), 

$$
\mathbb {E} \xi_ {\alpha} \xi_ {\beta} \xi_ {\gamma} = \mathbb {E} \sum_ {\mu \in \triangle (\alpha , \beta)} \xi_ {\gamma} \xi_ {\mu} \Psi \left(\alpha , \beta , \mu\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \Psi \left(\alpha , \beta , \gamma\right), & (\alpha , \beta , \gamma) \in \triangle ; \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.\tag{12.18}
$$

Equality (12.15) now follows. 

To compute the fourth moment, note that 

496 S. Lototsky and B. Rozovskii 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \xi_ {\alpha} \xi_ {\beta} \xi_ {\gamma} = \sum_ {\mu \leq \alpha \wedge \beta} C (\alpha , \beta , \mu)   \xi_ {\alpha + \beta - 2 \mu} \xi_ {\gamma} \\ = \sum_ {\mu \leq \alpha \wedge \beta} C (\alpha , \beta , \mu) \sum_ {\rho \leq (\alpha + \beta - 2 \mu) \wedge \gamma} C (\alpha + \beta - 2 \mu , \gamma , \rho)   \xi_ {\alpha + \beta + \gamma - 2 \mu - 2 \rho}. \end{array}\tag{12.19}
$$

Repeated applications of (12.14) yield 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \xi_ {\alpha} \xi_ {\beta} \xi_ {\gamma} = \sum_ {\mu \leq \alpha \wedge \beta} C (\alpha , \beta , \mu) \sum_ {\rho \in \triangle (\alpha + \beta - 2 \mu , \gamma)} \xi_ {\rho} \Psi (\alpha + \beta - 2 \mu , \gamma , \rho) \\ = \sum_ {\mu \in \triangle (\alpha , \beta)} \sum_ {\rho \in \triangle (\mu , \gamma)} \Psi (\alpha , \beta , \mu) \Psi (\mu , \gamma , \rho) \xi_ {\rho} \end{array}
$$

Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathbb {E} \xi_ {\alpha} \xi_ {\beta} \xi_ {\gamma} \xi_ {\kappa} = \sum_ {\mu \in \triangle (\alpha , \beta)} \sum_ {\rho \in \triangle (\mu , \gamma)} \Psi (\alpha , \beta , \mu) \Psi (\mu , \gamma , \rho) I _ {\{\mu = \kappa \}} \\ = \sum_ {\rho \in \triangle (\alpha , \beta) \cap \triangle (\gamma , \kappa)} \Psi (\alpha , \beta , \rho) \Psi (\rho , \gamma , \kappa). \end{array}
$$

Equality (12.16) now follows. 

In the same way, one can get formulas for fifth- and higher-order moments. 

Remark 12.1 Expressions (12.15) and (12.16) do not depend on the structure of equation (12.6) and can be used to compute the third and fourth moments of any random field with a known Cameron–Martin expansion. The interested reader should keep in mind that the formulas for the moments of orders higher then two should be interpreted with care. In fact, they represent the pseudomoments (for detail see [35]).

The Q-weighted Wiener chaos spaces allow us to state a result that is fully analogous to Theorem 12.1. The proof is derived from Theorem 9.1; see [29] for details.

If $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m a x } _ { i } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { x } | \sigma _ { k } ^ { i } ( x ) | \leq C _ { k } , k \geq 1 } \end{array}$ , then a possible choice of $Q$ is

## 13 Stochastic Navier–Stokes Equation

In this section, we review the main facts about the stochastic Navier–Stokes equation and indicate how the Wiener Chaos approach can be used in the study of non-linear equations. Most of the results of this section come from the two papers [35] and [31]. 

A priori, it is not clear in what sense the motion described by Kraichnan’s velocity (see Section 12) might fit into the paradigm of Newtonian mechanics. Accordingly, relating the Kraichnan velocity field v to classic fluid mechanics naturally leads to the question whether we can compensate $\mathbf { v } \left( t , x \right)$ by a field $\mathbf { u } \left( t , x \right)$ that is more regular with respect to the time variable, so that there is a balance of momentum for the resulting field $\mathbf { U } \left( t , x \right) = \mathbf { u } \left( t , x \right) + \mathbf { v } \left( t , x \right)$ or, equivalently, that the motion of a fluid particle in the velocity field $\mathbf { U } \left( t , x \right)$ satisfies the Second Law of Newton. 

A positive answer to this question is given in $[ 3 5 ]$ , where it is shown that the equation for the smooth component $\mathbf { u } = ( u ^ { 1 } , \ldots , u ^ { d } )$ of the velocity is given by 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} d u ^ {i} = [ \nu \Delta u ^ {i} - u ^ {j} D _ {j} u ^ {i} - D _ {i} P + f _ {i} ] d t \\ + \left(g _ {k} ^ {i} - D _ {i} \tilde {P} _ {k} - D _ {j} \sigma_ {k} ^ {j} u ^ {i}\right) d w _ {k}, i = 1, \ldots , d, 0 <   t \leq T; \\ \operatorname{div} \mathbf {u} = 0, \mathbf {u} (0, x) = \mathbf {u} _ {0} (x). \end{array} \right.\tag{13.1}
$$

where $w _ { k } , \textit { k } \geq 1$ are independent standard Wiener processes on a stochastic basis $\mathbb { F } ,$ , the functions $\sigma _ { k } ^ { j }$ are given by (12.3), the known functions $\mathbf { f } = ( f ^ { 1 } , \ldots , f ^ { d } ) , \mathbf { g } _ { k } = ( g _ { k } ^ { i } ) , i = i , \ldots , d , k \geq 1$ , are, respectively, the drift and the difusion components of the free force, and the unknown functions $P , \tilde { P } _ { k }$ are the drift and difusion components of the pressure. 

Remark 13.1 It is useful to study equation (13.1) for more general coeficients $\sigma _ { k } ^ { j } . ~ \mathrm { S o }$ , in the future, $\sigma _ { k } ^ { j }$ are not necessarily the same as in Section 12. 

We make the following assumptions: 

NS1 The functions $\sigma _ { k } ^ { i } = \sigma _ { k } ^ { i } ( t , x )$ are deterministic and measurable, 

$$
\sum_ {k \geq 1} \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d} | \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} (t, x) | ^ {2} + | D _ {i} \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} (t, x) | ^ {2}\right) \leq K,
$$

and there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that, for all $\boldsymbol { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ 2 

$$
\nu | y | ^ {2} - \frac {1}{2} \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} (t, x) \sigma_ {k} ^ {j} (t, x) y _ {i} y _ {j} \geq \varepsilon | y | ^ {2}, \quad t \in [ 0, T ], x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}.
$$

NS2 The functions $f ^ { i } , g _ { k } ^ { i }$ are non-random and 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d} \left(\| f ^ {i} \| _ {L _ {2} ((0, T); H _ {2} ^ {- 1} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}))} ^ {2} + \sum_ {k \geq 1} \| g _ {k} ^ {i} \| _ {L _ {2} ((0, T); L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}))} ^ {2}\right) <   \infty .
$$

Remark 13.2 In NS1, the derivatives $D _ { i } \sigma _ { k } ^ { i }$ are understood as Schwartz distributions, but it is assumed that div $\textstyle \sigma : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } \partial _ { i } \sigma ^ { i }$ is a bounded $L _ { 2 }$ -valued function. Obviously, the latter assumption holds in the important case when $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } \partial _ { i } \sigma ^ { i } = 0 } \end{array}$ 

Our next step is to use the divergence-free property of u to eliminate the pressure $P$ and $\bar { P }$ from equation (13.1). For that, we need the decomposition of $L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ into potential and solenoidal components. 

Write $\mathfrak { S } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) ) = \{ \mathbf { V } \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ : div $\mathbf { V } = 0 \}$ . It is known (see $\mathrm { e . g . \ [ 1 6 ] ) }$ that 

$$
L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) = \mathfrak {G} (L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}; \mathbb {R} ^ {d})) \oplus \mathfrak {S} (L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}; \mathbb {R} ^ {d})),
$$

where $\mathfrak { G } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) )$ is a Hilbert subspace orthogonal to ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) )$ 

The functions ${ \mathfrak { G } } ( \mathbf { V } )$ and ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( \mathbf { V } )$ can be defined for V from any Sobolev space $H _ { 2 } ^ { \gamma } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ and are usually referred to as the potential and the divergence-free or solenoidal projections, respectively, of the vector field V. 

Now let u be a solution of equation (13.1). Since div $\mathbf u = 0$ , we have 

$$
D _ {i} (\nu \Delta u ^ {i} - u ^ {j} D _ {j} u ^ {i} - D _ {i} P + f ^ {i}) = 0; D _ {i} (\sigma_ {k} ^ {j} D _ {j} u ^ {j} u ^ {i} + g _ {k} ^ {i} - D _ {i} \tilde {P} _ {k}) = 0, k \geq 1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
D _ {i} P = \mathfrak {G} (\nu \Delta u ^ {i} - u ^ {j} D _ {j} u ^ {i} + f ^ {i}); D _ {i} \tilde {P} _ {k} = \mathfrak {G} (\sigma_ {k} ^ {j} D _ {j} u ^ {i} + g _ {k} ^ {i}), i = 1, \dots , d, k \geq 1.
$$

$\mathrm { S o } .$ , instead of equation (13.1), we can and will consider its equivalent form for the unknown vector $\mathbf { u } = ( u ^ { 1 } , \ldots , u ^ { d } )$ : 

$$
d \mathbf {u} = \mathfrak {S} (\nu \Delta \mathbf {u} - u ^ {j} D _ {j} \mathbf {u} + \mathbf {f}) d t + \mathfrak {S} (\sigma_ {k} ^ {j} D _ {j} \mathbf {u} + \mathbf {g} _ {k}) d w _ {k}, 0 <   t \leq T,\tag{13.2}
$$

with initial condition $\mathbf { u } | _ { t = 0 } = \mathbf { u } _ { 0 }$ 

Definition 13.1 An -adapted random process u $\in L _ { 2 } ( \varOmega \times [ 0 , T ] ; H _ { 2 } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) )$ is called a solution of equation $( 1 3 . 2 ) \ i f { \mathrm { : } }$

When $d \geq 3 .$ , the existence of a strong solution as well as uniqueness (strong or weak) for equation (13.2) are important open problems. 

By the Cameron–Martin theorem, 

$$

$$

If the solution of (13.2) is $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted, then, using the Itˆo formula together with relation (5.5) for the time evolution of $\mathbb { E } ( \xi _ { \alpha } \vert \bar { \mathcal { F } } _ { t } ^ { W } )$ and relation (12.17) for the product of two elements of the Cameron–Martin basis, we can derive the propagator system for coeficients u [31, Theorem 3.2]: 

Theorem 13.2. In addition to NS1 and NS2, assume that $\mathbf { u } _ { 0 } \in L _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ and equation (13.2) has an $\mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { W }$ -adapted solution u such that 

$$
\sup _ {t \leq T} \mathbb {E} \| \mathbf {u} \| _ {L _ {2} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}; \mathbb {R} ^ {d})} ^ {2} (t) <   \infty .\tag{13.4}

Then 

$$

$$
